title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: Give each affected tenant at least 90 days' written notice of any rent increase, and do not make an increase effective before the current fixed term ends. Use the state's Rent and Fee Increase Notice form and serve it the way eviction notices are served (personal delivery, or leaving it with a suitable person and mailing, or posting and mailing). 'Rent' here includes every recurring or periodic charge in the lease for use and occupancy, such as pet rent or parking, so a new or higher recurring fee is a rent increase. If rent is set by the tenant's income in a subsidized tenancy, 30 days' notice applies and the form is not required (a tenant paying with a portable voucher still gets the form). New rules other than rent changes take effect only after 30 days' written notice and at the end of the term, unless the tenant agrees sooner.

title: Statewide Rent Increase Limit
bodyText: Washington limits rent increases for every type of tenancy, month-to-month or fixed-term: no increase at all during the first 12 months of a tenancy, and in any 12-month period no more than 7% plus the Seattle-area CPI, or 10%, whichever is less. The Department of Commerce publishes each year's maximum. Rent includes recurring fees. You may reset rent freely only after a tenant vacates. Exempt: units whose first certificate of occupancy is 12 years old or less at the date of the notice; units owned by public housing or development authorities or by rent-regulated nonprofits; qualifying tax-credit housing; and, if the owner is not a REIT, a corporation or an LLC with a corporate member, rooms sharing a kitchen or bath with the owner, owner-occupied single-family homes renting up to two units or bedrooms, and owner-occupied duplexes to fourplexes. Claim an exemption by stating its supporting facts in the increase notice. If you overcharge, the tenant must first give you a written demand to cure, and may end the lease on 20 days' written notice before the increase takes effect, owing rent for the full month of moving out but no fee; courts award the excess, up to three months of the unlawful amount, and fees, and the Attorney General may seek civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. Do not report unpaid unlawful increases to a screening service. No city or county may otherwise regulate the amount of rent, but check local notice and fee ordinances (Seattle, Tacoma, Spokane and others).

title: Same Terms for Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases
bodyText: Washington bars terms of payment or other material conditions that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or the reverse. For any one unit, the rent you offer on different lease types may differ by no more than 5%, and that difference may not push the rent past the statewide increase limit. Offering a lower rent only for a 12-month lease, or a fee only for month-to-month, can therefore break the rule if the gap is larger than 5% or the burden is material.

title: Late Fees in Washington
bodyText: You may not charge a late fee for rent paid within five days after its due date; once rent is more than five days late, the fee may run from the first day after the due date. For these tenancies Washington sets no cap on the late fee itself (mobile home lot agreements have percentage caps), but in an eviction for nonpayment the court's judgment, and the amount the tenant pays to be reinstated, may include late fees only up to $75 in total. A lease term charging a late fee within the five days is void, and knowingly using a lease with that term exposes you to actual damages plus statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees. You may still serve a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice any time after rent is due.

title: Changing the Rent Due Date for Benefit Recipients
bodyText: Where your lease allows late fees, a tenant whose primary income is a regular monthly government benefit paid after the rent due date may ask in writing to move the due date. You must agree if the tenant shows that, and the new date is no more than five days after the date in the lease. This is separate from any reasonable-accommodation request.

title: What Counts as Rent
bodyText: In Washington, rent means the recurring and periodic charges in the lease for use and occupancy, which can include utilities, pet rent or parking. Late fees, damages, deposits, legal costs and other one-time fees are not rent, and a tenant's right to stay cannot be conditioned on paying them (except the court costs, late fees up to $75 and awarded attorneys' fees a tenant pays to be reinstated in a nonpayment eviction): put only rent in a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice, and collect other charges by other lawful means. The exception: if you gave an installment plan for deposits or nonrefundable fees at the start of the tenancy and the tenant defaults, the missed installment may be treated as rent owing. A fee in lieu of a deposit is never rent. Do not roll a balance from an earlier lease or unit into rent.

title: Rent Receipts and Accepted Payment Forms
bodyText: You may refuse cash, but if you accept cash you must give a receipt. For any other payment, give a written receipt when the tenant asks. You must accept a personal check (unless one bounced or hit a closed account in the past nine months), a cashier's check or a money order, must let the tenant pay by mail unless you have an accessible on-site payment location, and may not require electronic payment only.

title: Bounced Rent Checks
bodyText: After a tenant's personal check to you is returned for nonsufficient funds or a closed account, you may refuse personal checks from that tenant for nine months, but you must still accept a cashier's check or money order. Washington's dishonored-check law lets the payee collect a reasonable handling fee for each returned check; if the check is still unpaid 15 days after you send the statutory notice of dishonor, interest at 12% and collection costs of up to $40 (or the check amount, if less) may be added, and in a court action on the check further damages and fees apply. Keep your fee reasonable and state it in the lease.

title: Screening Charges for Applicants
bodyText: You may charge an applicant for a tenant screening report, or your own actual screening costs up to what local screening services customarily charge, only if before getting any information you told the applicant in writing (or by posting) what you will check, what criteria can lead to denial, the consumer reporting agency's name and address and the applicant's rights to a free copy and to dispute it, and whether you accept a comprehensive reusable screening report. If you accept a reusable report, you may run your own report but may not charge the applicant for it. You may never charge a fee or deposit just to put someone on a waiting list.

title: Screening Notices and Adverse Action
bodyText: Before you obtain any information about an applicant, give the screening notice in writing or by posting (types of information, denial criteria, the reporting agency's details and rights, and whether you accept a comprehensive reusable report). If you deny the application or approve it with conditions (a higher deposit, a guarantor, last month's rent or higher rent), give a written adverse action notice stating the reasons, in substantially the statutory format. If you have a website advertising rentals, its home page must say whether you accept comprehensive reusable reports. Do not use a victim's status or a tenant's lawful source of income against them. Screening companies may not report or score an eviction case a court has ordered limited, and treating such a case as unreported is good practice. Don't take adverse action over rent unpaid during the COVID-19 period (March 1, 2020 to six months after the moratorium ended); don't ask about, consider or require medical records or history except to evaluate an accommodation or modification request. A condominium or homeowners association may require owners to screen tenants but may not demand the report.

title: Holding Fees and Deposits
bodyText: After you offer a unit, you may take a fee or deposit to hold it, up to 25% of the first month's rent. Immediately on payment, give a receipt and a written statement of any conditions under which you may keep it. If the applicant moves in, credit it to the first month's rent or the security deposit; if not, you may keep it only as the written statement allows. You may not keep any of it if the unit fails a tenant-based rental assistance inspection; if that inspection doesn't happen within 10 days (or an agreed longer time), you may tell the applicant the unit is no longer held and must then promptly return the money. A screening charge is separate and is not a holding fee.

title: Source of Income Discrimination
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to, evict, or set different terms for an applicant or tenant because of a lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, public assistance, emergency rental assistance, veterans benefits, Social Security or SSI. Do not advertise preferences such as 'no Section 8'. If you use an income threshold, subtract the voucher or subsidy from the rent before applying it. A narrow exception lets you refuse where the voucher requires an inspection, the written estimate of repairs to pass is over $1,500, and you have not received landlord mitigation program money for the repairs. Violations cost up to four and one-half times the monthly rent plus fees.

title: Rent Concessions and the Increase Limit
bodyText: Washington has no statute written for rent concessions such as a free month or a move-in discount, but two rules reach them. A lease may not require the tenant to keep the concession, the rent or other offer terms confidential. And because rent includes recurring charges and the statewide limit caps any increase in a 12-month period, a recurring monthly discount that ends can look like a rent increase measured from the discounted rent; the statute does not say. To stay safe, put any concession in the lease as a one-time credit with its amount and timing. Treat the end of a recurring discount as an increase: no increase is allowed in the first 12 months of a tenancy or before a fixed term ends, so don't schedule a discount to end then, and otherwise give the 90-day notice and keep the change within the limit unless an exemption applies.

title: Interest on Money a Tenant Owes
bodyText: No Washington landlord-tenant statute sets interest on unpaid rent or damages. Washington's usury law sets 12% as the interest rate on a loan or forbearance of money when no rate is agreed in writing, and caps any rate at the higher of 12% or a Treasury-bill-based rate, and court judgments carry their own statutory interest (a judgment for unpaid consumer debt bears 9% unless a written contract rate applies). Whether a lease may add contractual interest on unpaid rent is not settled by statute, and a charge that works like a late fee within the first five days is void, so the library offers no interest clause.

title: Sales Tax and Long-Term Rent
bodyText: Washington's retail sales tax reaches lodging for less than a month, not ordinary residential rent: occupancy for a continuous period of one month or more is presumed to be a rental of real property rather than a license to use it. Short-term rentals of under 30 days, and local lodging taxes, are a separate regime.

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting Tools
bodyText: Washington has no state statute that regulates or bans software or algorithms used to set residential rent. Federal and state antitrust and consumer protection law still apply, and local ordinances may address these tools.

title: Advertising Rent and Fees
bodyText: No Washington statute requires an all-in price in rental advertising. Two rules still reach fees: recurring charges for use and occupancy count as rent (so they are capped by the increase limit and listed on the increase form), and a fee should be in the lease: obligations become part of the rental agreement when brought to the tenant's attention at move-in, and a nonrefundable fee must be written into the lease as nonrefundable. Local ordinances may require fee disclosure in ads.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Washington has no statute requiring or regulating a landlord's reporting of rent payments to credit bureaus. Two limits apply: you may not report a tenant to a screening service for failing to pay an unlawful rent increase, and damage charges not documented as the deposit law requires may not be reported to a consumer reporting agency or screening service.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, Washington sets no cap on pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent (mobile home lot agreements entered into on or after May 7, 2025, not renewals of earlier ones, cap move-in fees and deposits at one month's rent, or two months' if the tenant brings pets). A refundable pet deposit is a deposit under the deposit statute (written terms and the move-in checklist); a nonrefundable pet fee must be stated in writing as nonrefundable; monthly pet rent is a recurring charge, so it counts as rent for the increase limit and the increase notice. On written request, tenants may pay deposits and fees in installments unless deposits and nonrefundable fees total no more than 25% of the first full month's rent and no last month's rent is required upfront. Do not charge a pet deposit or pet fee for an assistance animal.

title: Rental Assistance Pledges
bodyText: If a government or nonprofit emergency rental assistance program gives the tenant a pledge, you must accept it if it arrives before a pay-or-vacate notice expires and covers the full rent owed; after the notice expires, you must accept a written pledge that will contribute to paying the full amount due. Once you give the program your payment information, suspend the court case for 14 court days so the funds can arrive. A pledge letter also extends the tenant's right to pay and be reinstated until the eviction date.

title: No Security Deposit Cap for Residential Landlord-Tenant Act Tenancies
bodyText: For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, Washington sets no maximum security deposit (mobile home lot agreements entered into on or after May 7, 2025 cap move-in fees and deposits combined at one month's rent, or two months' if the tenant brings pets). The limits that do apply: you may take no deposit at all without a written lease and a signed move-in condition checklist; on written request the tenant may pay deposits, nonrefundable fees and last month's rent in installments (unless deposits and fees total 25% or less of the first full month's rent and no last month's rent is required upfront); a holding fee is capped at 25% of the first month's rent; and nonrefundable money may never be called a deposit. Some cities cap deposits or move-in fees; check local ordinances.

title: Deposit Trust Account and Interest
bodyText: Promptly put every security deposit in a trust account kept for tenants' deposits at a financial institution or a licensed escrow agent located in Washington, give the tenant a written receipt, and tell the tenant in writing the name, address and location of the depository and any later change. Unless you agree otherwise in writing, you keep the interest. A tenant's claim to deposit money comes ahead of your creditors, even in bankruptcy.

title: Deposits When the Property Changes Hands
bodyText: If you sell or otherwise transfer your status as landlord during a tenancy, the deposit money must move at the same time to an equivalent trust account of the new landlord, who must promptly tell the tenant about the transfer and the new depository. If the property is foreclosed and the deposit is not transferred to the successor, the foreclosed-upon owner must refund the full deposit to the tenant immediately after the sale or transfer, or owe up to twice the deposit.

title: Penalties for Deposit Mistakes
bodyText: Miss the 30-day deadline for the itemized statement, documentation and refund, and you owe the tenant the full deposit. In the tenant's suit you also can't assert any claim or defense for keeping any of it, and an intentional refusal can cost up to twice the deposit, unless you show circumstances beyond your control prevented you or the tenant abandoned the unit. Taking a deposit without giving a move-in checklist makes you liable for the whole deposit. In a tenant's suit to recover the deposit, the prevailing party also recovers costs and reasonable attorneys' fees.

title: Move-In Condition Checklist
bodyText: Before taking any deposit, give the tenant a written checklist or statement at the start of the tenancy describing the condition and cleanliness of, and existing damage to, the premises, fixtures, equipment, appliances and furnishings, covering at least walls (paint and wallpaper), carpets and flooring, furniture and appliances. Both of you sign and date it, and the tenant gets a copy and may ask for one free replacement. At move-out you can't charge for repair or replacement of fixtures, equipment, appliances or furnishings whose condition the checklist didn't reasonably document, and never for ordinary wear. Taking a deposit without the checklist makes you liable to the tenant for the whole deposit.

title: Installment Payments of Move-In Costs
bodyText: On the tenant's written request, let them pay deposits, nonrefundable fees and last month's rent in installments: three equal monthly payments starting at move-in for a fixed term of three months or longer, otherwise two. You may refuse only if deposits and nonrefundable fees together are no more than 25% of the first full month's rent and you don't require last month's rent upfront. Charge no fee or interest, make the schedule written and signed by both of you, and set the due dates to match rent. Refusing costs one month's rent plus attorneys' fees. A missed installment may be treated as rent owing.

title: Last Month's Rent Paid in Advance
bodyText: You may require last month's rent at the start of the tenancy, but the tenant may pay it in installments with any deposits and nonrefundable fees, and requiring it removes your right to refuse installments under the 25% exception. Washington's deposit statutes do not treat prepaid last month's rent as a security deposit; keep it identified as rent and apply it to the last month. If you impose last month's rent on a particular applicant as a condition of approval, that is an adverse action needing a written notice.

title: Unclaimed Refunds and Sale Proceeds
bodyText: Washington's unclaimed property act has no entry written for an uncashed security deposit refund, but a refund the tenant never cashes is likely presumed abandoned three years after it became payable, under the act's entries for a business's debts or its catch-all; report it then. The act also reaches money from selling a tenant's property: excess sale proceeds after a writ of restitution, or after a sole tenant's death, are held for the tenant for one year and then reported to the Department of Revenue as unclaimed property. Excess proceeds from selling property left after an abandonment are held for one year and then become yours.

title: Charging Damage Beyond the Deposit
bodyText: Back every damage deduction with estimates or invoices; for work you or your employees do, include the materials receipt (or a vendor price list for stock on hand) and the time spent and hourly rate. Never withhold from the deposit for ordinary wear, for carpet cleaning without documented excess wear, for items the checklist didn't document, or more than the damaged part of an item, and apply the same limits to any claim beyond the deposit (where the statute bars wear and undocumented charges). You may sue for damage beyond the deposit, but for tenancies begun on or after July 23, 2023 you must file within three years after the tenancy ends. Undocumented or wear-and-tear charges may not be billed, sent to collections or reported to a screening service. If you claim from the state landlord mitigation program after a tenant ends the lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking, you may not keep the deposit or pursue that tenant for damage beyond it.

title: Fee in Lieu of a Deposit: Your Duties
bodyText:
If you offer a monthly fee instead of a deposit, keep it strictly optional, offer it to every approved applicant and never use the choice in deciding an application; any nonrefundable part must be disclosed in the lease and separately acknowledged by the tenant; the fee is not rent, and nonpayment is not a cause for eviction, though you may sue for it; give the statutory disclosure form with the lease and any renewal; disclose in writing the terms of the insurance you buy with the fees (coverage, exclusions and caps) and, if the insurer requires you to try the tenant first, that the fee doesn't stop you or the insurer pursuing the tenant; use the fee only to buy that insurance, charging no more than its cost and administration; still give the move-in checklist; and let the tenant switch to a deposit at any time.

Once the insurer pays a valid claim you may not seek those amounts from the tenant, and if it denies a claim as not a loss under the lease or for insufficient documentation you may not invoice or pursue the tenant for it; wait 60 days after notifying the tenant and sending documentation (and 60 days after filing the claim) before any collection; sue within one year after the tenancy ends.

If you stop offering the option, give 60 days' notice before the end of the term, credit the fees paid against the deposit and offer a three-month installment plan.

Don't discontinue or alter that insurance during the term. If you fail to keep it and the tenant has paid the fee as agreed, credit the coverage stated in the disclosure against what the tenant owes at move-out, unless through no fault of yours the insurer can no longer do business in Washington or meet its obligations.

title: Just Cause: When You May End a Tenancy
bodyText:
Washington requires a listed cause to evict, to refuse to continue a tenancy, or to end a month-to-month tenancy. The end of a fixed term does not by itself end possession: unless the lease uses one of two narrow options (a first lease of six to 12 months that rolls to month-to-month, ended with 60 days' notice before the first term ends; or a fixed term that has never been month-to-month, where the first lease was 12 months or more or every lease since the start was for six months or more, ended with 60 days' notice before the term ends), the tenancy becomes month-to-month.

The causes are: unpaid rent after a 14-day notice; a material breach not cured within a 10-day notice; waste, nuisance or unlawful activity after a 3-day notice; owner or immediate family move-in (90 days); sale of a single-family home (90 days); demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use (120 days); condominium conversion; a unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable (30 days); a shared unit with the owner (20 days); transitional housing ending (30 days); refusing a reasonable new lease offered at least 30 days before a fixed term ends (not for periodic tenancies); intentional, material application misrepresentations (30 days); other legitimate economic or business reasons (60 days); four or more cured violations in 12 months with written warnings (60 days); a sex-offender registration requirement (60 days); and sexual harassment of the owner, staff or another tenant based on race, gender or other protected status in violation of the lease (20 days).

Owner move-in, sale, and demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use can't end a fixed term early unless you and the tenant agree in writing and the tenant gets at least 60 days to vacate.

Each notice must be served as eviction notices are served and state the supporting facts. If you remove a tenant, or cause a tenant to be removed, in violation of this law, you owe the greater of the tenant's economic and noneconomic damages or three months' rent, plus attorneys' fees and court costs.

When a tenant permanently leaves other than because you ended the tenancy, give remaining occupants who lived there at least six months a 30-day notice to apply for the tenancy or vacate (not in subsidized housing). Some cities add their own just-cause rules.

title: Notice Periods to End a Tenancy
bodyText:
A tenant may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy with written notice of at least 20 days before the end of a rental period, and a fixed-term tenancy with written notice at least 20 days before the term ends; a servicemember (or spouse or dependent) with permanent change of station or deployment orders that don't allow 20 days' notice may give less, and a servicemember (or spouse or dependent) with permanent change of station or deployment orders meeting the statutory criteria may end a fixed term early on 20 days' written notice with a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's letter.

A landlord may end a tenancy only for a just cause, with that cause's notice period, except that a qualifying fixed term may be ended without cause at its end on 60 days' written notice (see the just-cause row and the two optional term clauses); longer periods apply to condominium conversion (120 days) and demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use (120 days).

A 90-day notice applies before changing to a policy of excluding children, but such a policy is lawful only where an exemption allows it (such as housing for older persons), and the change isn't a listed cause: the tenancy can still end only on a just cause (possibly the 'other good cause' ground, 60 days).

Every landlord notice ending a tenancy must be served by personal delivery; or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there and mailing a copy; or, if the tenant's residence isn't known or no such person can be found, by posting a copy conspicuously, delivering a copy to a resident if one can be found, and mailing a copy; it must state the date to vacate or comply; mailing from within Washington completes service, but you must wait five extra days before filing an eviction based on a mailed notice.

title: The 14-Day Pay or Vacate Notice
bodyText: For unpaid rent, serve a 14-day notice to pay or vacate in substantially the statutory form, which lists monthly rent, utilities and other recurring charges due (no late fees or other one-time charges), tells the tenant about the Attorney General's translated notices and rental assistance, the right to a lawyer and an interpreter, and mediation, and states where to pay. You may serve it any time after rent is due. Accept payment as the lease allows or by nonelectronic means, including (but not limited to) cashier's check, money order or other certified funds; any payment must go first to the amount on the notice. Serve it the way RCW 59.12.040 requires (personal delivery, or the substitute methods, which include mailing a copy); when a copy is mailed, allow five additional days before filing. State in the notice the date by which the tenant must pay or vacate, which the service statute now requires of every termination notice. You must accept a rental assistance pledge that covers the full rent before the notice expires.

title: Cure Periods for Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than unpaid rent or money damages, give a written 10-day notice to comply or vacate that specifies the acts or omissions; the tenant (or a subtenant or mortgagee) may cure within the 10 days and save the tenancy. A breach must be substantial and of a material lease term, a material subsidized-housing requirement, or a tenant duty imposed by law. No cure applies to waste, nuisance, unlawful activity affecting others' use and enjoyment, or other substantial or repeated and unreasonable interference: a 3-day notice to quit. Repeated cured violations can support a 60-day end-of-term notice only after four separate violations in 12 months, each with a written warning containing the statutory statements. For unpaid rent the tenant can still pay and be reinstated up to five court days after judgment.

title: The Eviction Court Process
bodyText: Only a court can evict. After the notice period runs, file an unlawful detainer case in superior court with the statutory Eviction Summons (Residential). You may ask for a show cause hearing 7 to 30 days after service, where the tenant may answer orally or in writing; if you prevail, the court issues a writ of restitution that the sheriff executes. If you can't serve the tenant personally after three attempts over at least two days at different times, you may post and mail (regular and certified) at least nine days before the return date, but then the court can only restore possession, not enter a money judgment. Subject to state funding, the court must appoint a lawyer for an indigent tenant, and hearings may be continued for that. Some superior courts add local rules: for example, requiring a copy of the lease with the complaint, pleading the just-cause basis, serving a local notice with the show cause order, or (in Skagit County) notifying the local legal aid office before filing. Check the county's local court rules.

title: Court Payment Plans and Stays in Nonpayment Cases
bodyText: In a nonpayment eviction, the tenant can end the case by paying the rent due, court costs, up to $75 in late fees and any awarded attorneys' fees before judgment or within five court days after it (longer with a rental assistance pledge letter), plus $50 for each prior post-judgment reinstatement in the last 12 months. Even after judgment the court may stay the writ for up to 90 days on a payment plan, weighing factors such as willfulness, hardship and payment history; the tenant must pay one month's rent within five court days. A tenant served three or more pay-or-vacate notices in the past 12 months generally can't get this stay. If the tenant later defaults on the plan, serve the statutory notice of default; the tenant then has three calendar days before the sheriff may execute the writ. The court may find the tenant eligible for the state landlord mitigation program to pay you.

title: Limited Dissemination of Eviction Records
bodyText: A court may order an eviction case to be of limited dissemination if your case lacked a basis in fact or law, if the tenancy was reinstated, or for other good cause. Once ordered, tenant screening services may not report that case or use it in a score. Expect courts to use this where a tenant paid and was reinstated. Separately, you may not deny or end a tenancy because someone was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because they ended a lease under the victim-protection statute.

title: No Lockouts, Utility Shutoffs or Property Seizures
bodyText: Never remove or exclude a tenant without a court order: no lock changes, removal of doors or belongings, or utility shutoffs. A tenant locked out may recover possession or end the lease, plus damages and fees. Intentionally causing termination of water, heat, electricity or gas (other than for a reasonable time to make repairs) costs actual damages plus up to $100 a day. Taking or keeping a tenant's belongings without specific written consent, after a written demand for their return, can cost up to $500 a day (capped at $5,000) if intentional. The police may remove a squatter on the owner's sworn declaration, but never a tenant or a tenant's guest.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Washington abolished the landlord's right of distress for rent. A lease clause creating a lien on the tenant's personal property, or authorizing you to seize it for rent, is void. You may take a tenant's property only with the tenant's specific written consent to that taking, after an abandonment, after a writ of restitution, or after a sole tenant's death, each under its own procedure.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: While a tenant complies with the landlord-tenant act, you may not retaliate (by eviction, a rent increase, reduced services or added obligations) for good-faith complaints to a government agency about code violations that may endanger health or safety, or for asserting rights under the act. Acting within 90 days after such a complaint or the resulting inspection creates a presumption of retaliation; a tenant behind on rent or in breach when you give a termination notice gets the opposite presumption; a rent increase notice that states reasonable grounds avoids the presumption; impracticality of repairs with the tenant in place can rebut it for an eviction, and a tenant complaint made within 90 days after your notice of a rent increase is presumed not made in good faith. Do not retaliate against a tenant who lets a code official inspect.

title: Property Left After an Abandonment
bodyText: If a tenant who owes rent has shown by words or actions an intent not to return, you may enter, take any property left, and store it somewhere reasonably secure. Mail a notice by first-class mail to the last known address and any other known address giving your name and address, where the property is, the sale or disposal date, and the tenant's right to get it back first. Return it if the tenant asks in writing before the sale and pays the lesser of actual or reasonable moving and storage costs. You may sell or dispose of it 45 days after the notice (7 days if its total value is $250 or less, except personal papers, family pictures and keepsakes). Apply proceeds to what you're owed and hold any excess for one year. A sole tenant's death follows a separate procedure.

title: Rent Owed After a Tenant Abandons
bodyText: When a tenant in default abandons, make a reasonable effort to re-rent. A month-to-month tenant owes rent for the 30 days after the earlier of the date you learn of the abandonment or the next rent due date. A tenant with a longer term owes the lesser of all rent for the rest of the term, or the rent accrued while re-renting at a fair rental, plus any shortfall in the new rent, plus your actual re-renting costs, statutory court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees. Your deposit statement is due within 30 days after you learn of the abandonment.

title: Tenant Property After a Writ of Restitution
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ, take possession of the tenant's property left in the unit. You must store it if the tenant served a written storage request (the sheriff gives the tenant a form you supply) within three days after service of the writ, and, if you know the tenant has a disability that impairs or prevents a request, must presume one unless the tenant objects in writing; if the tenant objects, or makes no request and you choose not to store, the property goes on the nearest public property. Return stored property when the tenant pays the lesser of actual or reasonable moving and storage costs. Before selling property worth over $250, give notice and wait 30 days; for $250 or less, 7 days (personal papers, family pictures and keepsakes may not be sold under the small-value rule). Hold excess sale proceeds for one year, then report them to the Department of Revenue as unclaimed property.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: You may ask a tenant to designate, in a writing separate from the lease, a person to act on the tenant's death if the tenant lives alone. When a sole occupant dies, promptly mail or hand-deliver (and email if you know an address) a notice to any known personal representative, designated person, emergency contact and likely successor, and to the tenant at the unit, stating the death, rent paid-through date, and that the tenancy ends 15 days after the notice or at the paid-through date, whichever is later, unless a representative arranges to prepay rent for up to 60 days from the death. Release property to a representative who asks in writing, takes an inventory and signs a possession-only acknowledgment. Refund unearned rent and account for the deposit within 30 days after removal. Before selling or disposing of unclaimed property, send a second notice and wait at least 45 days; property worth over $1,000 must be sold in a commercially reasonable manner, and personal papers and photographs may not be sold.

title: Early Termination by Victims
bodyText: A tenant who gives written notice that the tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking, and provides a protection order or a qualified third party's signed report, may end the lease without further obligation if the request is made within 90 days of the incident. The tenant owes no rent after the month of moving out, and owes that month's rent unless the termination also met the 20-day periodic notice rule, and gets the full deposit back, subject to lawful deductions (documented damage beyond ordinary wear, unpaid rent or charges), whatever the lease says about forfeiture. If you claim damages from the state landlord mitigation program, you may not keep any of that tenant's deposit or pursue the tenant for property damage beyond the deposit. Other co-tenants remain bound unless they are victims. If the tenant or a household member is a victim of sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment by the landlord (including the landlord's employees), the tenant may leave first and deliver the order or report within seven days of moving out, owing rent only until the later of moving out or delivering the report and notice, with a pro rata refund of prepaid rent. The tenant may instead change or add locks at the tenant's expense, giving you written notice and the documents within seven days; the lease then ends 90 days after that notice unless within 60 days the tenant tells you in writing they want to stay or ends it under the leave-first route, and rent continues until the lease ends and the tenant vacates; once you receive that notice your entry is restricted (emergencies with police or fire officials, or at least two days' written notice of date, time and purpose under RCW 59.18.150), including if the tenant stays.

title: No Adverse Action Against Victims
bodyText: You may not end, refuse to renew, or refuse to rent because a tenant, applicant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because they ended a lease under the victim-protection statute; doing so is a defense to eviction. Lawful factors unrelated to victim status may still be considered. The tenant-duty rule against assaults and weapon threats leading to arrest does not authorize evicting the victim.

title: Lock Changes for Protected Tenants
bodyText: If a tenant gives you a court order granting them possession to the exclusion of a co-tenant and asks you to replace or rekey the lock, do it at the tenant's expense and don't give the restrained person a key. You are held harmless for damages that result directly from the lock change. The excluded co-tenant stays liable under the lease unless they are a victim household member.

title: Servicemember Termination Rights
bodyText: A tenant in the armed forces (including the National Guard and reserves), or the tenant's spouse or dependent, may end a fixed-term lease on 20 days' written notice with a copy of permanent change of station or deployment orders, or a commanding officer's letter, showing a qualifying move of 35 miles or more, discharge, government housing, or orders of 90 days or more; and may end a month-to-month tenancy on less than 20 days' notice if the orders don't allow 20. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act also applies.

title: Other Statutory Ways a Tenant May Leave Early
bodyText:
Beyond the military and victim rights, a Washington tenant may end the lease without further obligation if: you fail to remedy a defective condition within the statutory period to start repairs after written notice and a reasonable time to finish; a court or arbitrator finds a defect too substantial to fix in time; you threaten the tenant with a firearm or deadly weapon and are arrested; another tenant threatens them with a firearm or deadly weapon, is arrested, the tenant notifies you, and you don't file an eviction within seven calendar days after law enforcement notifies you of the arrest; or you raise rent unlawfully above the statewide limit (after a written cure demand, on at least 20 days' written notice, ending before the increase takes effect, owing rent for the full month of moving out).

If you knowingly rent a unit an agency has condemned or declared unlawful to occupy, the tenant recovers the greater of three months' rent or up to three times actual damages, plus costs and attorneys' fees, and, on leaving, all deposits and prepaid rent; relocation assistance is owed where you knew or should have known of the conditions, with exceptions for tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of, natural disasters and eminent domain.

title: Premium Holdover Rates (Not Offered)
bodyText: Washington sets no statutory holdover measure for residential tenancies (the general double-damages rule for unlawful detainer doesn't apply to them), so a lease could set a stipulated daily charge for a tenant who stays after the tenancy lawfully ends. The library doesn't offer a premium rate: because a fixed term usually becomes month-to-month rather than ending, a holdover only arises after a just-cause ending, often for nonpayment, where the tenant can still pay and be reinstated and late fees in judgment are capped at $75, so a premium could be read as a penalty or a second late charge. The library's holdover clause charges daily rent instead. If you want a premium, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: Fire, Casualty and Uninhabitable Units
bodyText: Washington has no statute written for fire or casualty damage to a rental. If the unit becomes defective, the tenant uses the repair-notice remedies: if you don't start repairs within the statutory period after written notice and finish within a reasonable time, the tenant may end the lease, and a court may end it if the defect can't feasibly be fixed in time. You may end a tenancy for a damaged unit only on a just cause, for example a unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable by a local agency where continued occupancy would expose you to civil or criminal penalties (30 days' notice, or as much as the order allows) or demolition or substantial rehabilitation (120 days; not before a fixed term ends unless the tenant agrees in writing and gets at least 60 days). If a code agency condemns the unit and you knew or should have known of the conditions, you owe relocation assistance (not for natural disasters or tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of). A lease clause letting you end the lease after a casualty isn't offered: it would add a cause the statute doesn't list. If the tenant, family, guest or anyone under the tenant's control caused the damage, you have no repair duty for it and the tenant has no remedy for it under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Criminal Activity and Dangerous Conduct
bodyText: Washington's statute already makes these tenant duties: no drug-related activity at the premises (and not allowing it with the tenant's knowledge or consent); no imminently hazardous activity involving an assault or unlawful use of a firearm or deadly weapon that leads to an arrest; and no gang-related activity endangering two or more households. Waste, nuisance or unlawful activity affecting others' use and enjoyment lets you serve a 3-day notice to quit with no cure. Neighbors in the same building or complex, or within a one-block radius, whose safety or property is endangered by a tenant's gang activity may serve you a 10-day demand to file an eviction, and may petition the court if you don't investigate, if you investigate and find no gang activity, or if your steps don't stop it. The library offers no separate crime-free clause: the statute covers the ground, a broader lease definition could reach conduct the statute protects (victims), and city crime-free programs may not bar renting to someone solely for criminal history.

title: Drug Nuisance Abatement Against the Building
bodyText: A building or unit used to make, sell, store or give away illegal drugs is a public or private nuisance that can be enjoined and abated in superior court, including against the owner, after attempts to notify the owner. Act on tenant drug activity promptly: it is a tenant duty and an eviction ground with no cure period. Police seizure of illegal drugs at a unit triggers a notice to you under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Squatters and Remaining Occupants
bodyText: For a squatter who hasn't been a tenant, or an owner on title, in the last 12 months, you may give police a sworn declaration in the statutory form; an officer with probable cause of criminal trespass may remove them after letting them show evidence they are a tenant or guest. You may not use this for a tenant, a lawful occupant, or their guests, and a false declaration exposes you to damages and fees. When a tenant permanently leaves (other than because you ended the tenancy), for occupants who lived with the tenant for at least six months up to the move-out (except in subsidized housing), serve a 30-day notice to apply to become a party to the lease or vacate, and screen them like any applicant; use the eviction process if they don't apply or don't qualify.

title: Drug and Alcohol Free Housing Programs
bodyText: Washington has a special category of drug and alcohol free housing for recovery programs run by a nonprofit, corporation or housing authority providing federally assisted housing, where every unit has at least one tenant in recovery and the landlord provides monitoring and support. Its written rental agreement must contain specific terms (no use or possession of alcohol or unprescribed drugs on or off the premises, a described program of recovery, quarterly verification), and the program has its own termination rules. Ordinary landlords can't use this regime.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: If a rental is sold at a foreclosure (trustee's) sale, a tenant in possession must get 60 days' written notice to vacate before removal, except for waste or nuisance; where the trustee elects to foreclose the occupants' interests, it must also post and mail the statutory notice to residents when the sale is noticed. How Washington's just-cause rule applies to a purchaser at a trustee's sale is not settled by the statutes read; get advice before relying on the 60-day notice alone. The foreclosed-upon owner must refund the tenant's deposit immediately unless it is transferred to the successor. The 60-day rule doesn't apply where the borrower stays on as an occupant.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: To convert apartments to condominiums, the declarant must give each residential tenant at least 120 days' notice with the public offering statement, served like an eviction notice, describing tenant rights, the state tenant-to-homeowner program and any local relocation assistance. A tenant may not be required to leave on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment, waste, conduct disturbing other tenants, or another act of unlawful detainer, and the terms of the tenancy may not be changed during that period. For 60 days after the notice you must offer to sell each occupied unit to its tenant. If the tenant doesn't buy, for the next 180 days you may offer that unit to anyone else on better price or terms only after offering the same price and terms to the tenant in writing and giving the tenant 10 days to accept. Your city or county may also require you to pay relocation assistance of up to three months' rent to lower-income tenants who don't buy.

title: Condemned or Unlawful Units and Relocation Assistance
bodyText: Once a code agency notifies you that a unit is condemned or unlawful to occupy, you may not rent it until the conditions are fixed; knowingly doing so costs the greater of three months' rent or up to treble damages, plus all deposits and prepaid rent if the tenant leaves. If you knew or should have known of the conditions, you must pay displaced tenants relocation assistance of the greater of $2,000 per unit or three months' rent, plus deposits and prepaid rent, within seven days of the agency's notice (exceptions: tenant or third-party illegal conduct you didn't know of, natural disasters, eminent domain). From the agency's first notice of violations until relocation assistance is paid or the conditions are fixed, you may not evict, harass or intimidate tenants to avoid or reduce this duty, and may not reduce services, raise rent at all, or materially increase or change other obligations.

title: Selling or Changing Management
bodyText: A sale doesn't by itself end a Washington tenancy: the just-cause rules keep applying, and selling a single-family home is a cause only on 90 days' notice and only with a genuine listing for sale within 30 days after the tenant leaves; it can't end a fixed term early unless you and the tenant agree in writing and the tenant gets at least 60 days to vacate. When the landlord or the person designated as landlord changes, notify tenants immediately in writing (personal delivery, or mail plus conspicuous posting), and move the deposits to the new landlord's trust account and notify tenants of the new depository.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: No Washington statute says whether accepting rent after serving a notice waives your right to evict, with one exception: after a writ of restitution issues, accepting a payment that only partly satisfies the judgment doesn't invalidate the writ unless both parties sign a written agreement saying so. A tenant may pay the full amount owed and be reinstated up to five court days after judgment in a nonpayment case, and you must accept qualifying rental assistance pledges. For other notices, assume that accepting rent for a period after the notice's deadline may be treated as continuing the tenancy, and get advice before doing so.

title: Your Duty to Keep the Unit Fit
bodyText: Throughout the tenancy keep the premises fit for human habitation: substantially comply with codes where a violation endangers health or safety; keep structural parts usable and the unit weathertight; keep shared areas clean, sanitary and safe; provide pest control at the start of the tenancy and, except in a single-family residence, during it unless the tenant caused the infestation; repair everything except ordinary wear; provide adequate locks and keys and safeguard master keys; keep supplied electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances working; provide garbage receptacles and removal except in a single-family residence; and provide facilities for heat, water and hot water. These duties can't be waived in a standard lease. You have no repair duty, and the tenant no remedy, for a condition the tenant or the tenant's family, guests or people under their control caused, or where the tenant unreasonably refuses access for repairs.

title: Repair Deadlines and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: After a tenant's written repair notice, start repairs within 24 hours for loss of hot or cold water, heat or electricity or an imminent hazard to life; within 72 hours for loss of a refrigerator, range and oven or major plumbing fixture you supplied; and within 10 days otherwise, finishing promptly. If you don't, a tenant who is current on rent and agreed utilities may end the lease on written notice, sue or arbitrate for reduced rental value, or (after sending a good-faith estimate) hire a licensed or responsible person and deduct the cost from rent, up to two months' rent per repair and two months' rent in any 12 months, or do minor repairs within the unit personally, costing no more than one month's rent per repair and one month's rent in any 12 months. For conditions that substantially endanger health or safety, the tenant may ask the local government to inspect and certify the condition and then pay rent into an escrow account.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText: If a tenant breaks a statutory duty or a house rule in a way that substantially affects health or safety or substantially increases fire or accident hazards, and the problem can be fixed by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, give written notice specifying it. The tenant then has 30 days to comply (or as promptly as an emergency requires). If the tenant doesn't, you may enter, have the work done, and bill the tenant an itemized actual and reasonable cost, payable with the next rent (or immediately if the tenancy has ended). Enter with the usual two days' written notice unless it's an emergency. Other substantial breaches go to the unlawful detainer process instead, and drug activity, assaults or weapon use resulting in an arrest, and gang activity skip the cure period.

title: Tenants' Duties Under Washington Law
bodyText: Washington law requires every tenant to pay rent as agreed and obey applicable codes, and to: keep their part of the premises as clean and sanitary as conditions permit; dispose of garbage properly and pay for extermination of infestations they cause; use fixtures and appliances properly; not damage or remove any part of the dwelling or let others do so; not permit a nuisance or waste; not engage in or knowingly allow drug-related activity; maintain the smoke detector, including batteries; not engage in imminently hazardous assaults or unlawful weapon use leading to an arrest; not engage in gang-related activity; and at move-out restore the unit to its initial condition except ordinary wear and conditions you failed to fix. A tenant who paid a nonrefundable cleaning fee may not be charged for normal cleaning.

title: House Rules
bodyText: Tenants must follow reasonable rules about use, occupancy and maintenance that don't violate the landlord-tenant act or other law and were brought to their attention when they moved in. A new rule takes effect only after 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant and at the end of the lease term, or sooner if the tenant agrees; a rent increase or termination can't be imposed as a 'rule'.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to a Tenant
bodyText: A landlord and tenant may exempt themselves from the landlord's repair and habitability duties (and the related tenant remedies) only by a written agreement that is not in a standard form lease, between parties of roughly equal bargaining power, that doesn't undercut safe and sanitary housing, and that the county prosecutor, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's own attorney has approved in writing. A lease clause shifting those duties is otherwise void. Ordinary upkeep a tenant uses exclusively, such as a single-family home's yard or snow on the tenant's own walkway, is not one of the landlord's statutory duties. The library offers no tenant-repair agreement for Washington: one generated from a template is a standard form, and the approval must come from an official or the tenant's lawyer.

title: Heat, Water and Cooling
bodyText: Provide facilities adequate to supply heat, water and hot water as reasonably required, and keep supplied heating and appliances working. Loss of heat, hot or cold water or electricity requires repairs to start within 24 hours of the tenant's notice. Landlord-supplied electric or water service also has heat-alert rules (`edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`). Washington doesn't require landlords to supply air conditioning, but you must let tenants install portable cooling devices within the statutory limits.

title: Utility Shutoffs and Heat Alerts
bodyText: You may never intentionally cause a tenant's water, heat, electricity or gas to be shut off, except for a reasonable time to make repairs. The landlord-tenant act also contains rules for a landlord-supplied electric or water service disconnected for nonpayment: no involuntary disconnection on any day the National Weather Service has issued or announced a heat-related alert for the area, a disconnection notice that explains how to ask for reconnection, a prompt reconnection attempt on request on such a day, and any payment plan capped at 6% of the tenant's monthly income. Those rules assume such disconnections happen, but they don't authorize them, and the general shutoff ban has no nonpayment exception; don't disconnect a tenant's utilities without advice. Where a city or town utility serves the property and either several units share one account, the billing address differs from the service address, or the city has been told a tenant lives there, the city must make a good-faith effort to give seven days' written notice at the service address before cutting electricity or water for your nonpayment, and a tenant who puts the service in their own name may deduct those charges from rent.

title: City Utility Accounts and Liens
bodyText: If your rental is served by a city or town utility, you can ask in writing to be notified of a tenant's delinquency; once you have, the city must notify you and can't collect from you more than four months of a tenant's past-due electric charges, and it loses its lien if it fails to notify you. When a utility account in the tenant's name ends, tell the city in writing within 14 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant moves out, or the four-month limit may not protect you. City utility liens on the property itself are governed by separate statutes.

title: Locks and Keys
bodyText: Provide reasonably adequate locks and furnish keys to the tenant, and maintain and safeguard any master or duplicate keys with reasonable care. A tenant who does a lock repair under the repair-and-deduct remedy must give you a key. A tenant with a court order excluding a co-tenant may have the locks changed at their own expense. A tenant who is a victim of sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment by the landlord may change or add locks at the tenant's expense. From January 1, 2027, if you use a smart access system you must offer a tenant who asks a non-biometric, non-app key. Washington has no statewide rekeying-between-tenants, deadbolt or peephole statute.

title: Smart Locks and Access Systems (from 2027)
bodyText: Starting January 1, 2027, if you use a smart access system (app, biometric or electronic entry), a tenant who asks must get an alternative key that uses no biometrics and no phone app, such as a fob, card, physical key or keypad code. Make the system's written privacy policy available, and give tenants at lease signing (or within five days of installation) a plain-language policy covering the data collected (including about guests), safeguards, retention, breach handling, deletion and how temporary users are added. Collect only the minimum data the law lists for granting access. Biometric entry may also bring the state's consumer health data and biometric identifier laws; see `edu-key-control-policy-wa`.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Install smoke detection devices inside every rental dwelling unit, test them and make them work before each new occupancy, and instruct the occupants on their purpose, operation and maintenance; the tenant maintains them, including batteries. Agree in advance who pays for repair or replacement. Residential buildings must have carbon monoxide alarms under the state building code (owner-occupied single-family homes occupied before July 26, 2009 are exempt until sold, and existing buildings other than R-2 apartment-type occupancies need them only if they have a fuel-burning appliance, a fuel-burning fireplace or an attached garage), and the statute makes the tenant responsible for maintaining a CO alarm, including batteries, as the manufacturer specifies. Give the signed fire safety notice at lease signing. An owner who fails to comply faces a fine of up to $200, or $5,000 if after the failure a fire causes property damage, personal injury or death to a tenant or a member of the tenant's household.

title: Pests and Bed Bugs
bodyText: Provide a reasonable program to control insects, rodents and other pests when a tenancy starts and, except in a single-family residence, throughout the tenancy unless the tenant caused the infestation; a tenant pays for extermination of an infestation they caused. Washington has no bed-bug-specific disclosure, inspection or treatment statute for rentals, and no pesticide-notification rule written for tenants was found. Enter to treat only with the two-day written notice (or in an emergency).

title: Radon
bodyText: Washington has no statute requiring a residential landlord to test for or disclose radon. Radon appears in the building code for new construction and in the seller disclosure form for home sales, which don't reach leases.

title: Lead-Based Paint
bodyText: For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure rules apply to leases (the shared lead clause is tagged for Washington). Washington adds a state renovation, repair and painting program: renovation work in pre-1978 housing must be done by a state-certified renovation firm using certified renovators. Washington has no separate state lead disclosure for leases.

title: Meth and Hazardous Chemical Contamination
bodyText: If you believe a tenant contaminated a vacated or abandoned unit with hazardous chemicals (such as from making meth), you must contact the local health officer. When contamination is reported, the health officer posts a warning, inspects, and may order the property unfit and its use prohibited until it is decontaminated by a certified contractor; the order is recorded against the property. Washington has no separate lease disclosure statute for contaminated property, but renting a unit under a no-occupancy order is barred.

title: Deaths or Crimes on the Property
bodyText: Washington has no statute addressing whether a landlord must disclose that a death, crime or illness occurred at a rental. Don't misrepresent the property if asked.

title: Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: A tenant's requirement to register as a sex offender during the tenancy, or failure to disclose a registration requirement when the application asked or when it was otherwise known to you at the start, is a just cause to end the tenancy on at least 60 days' written notice before the end of the rental period or lease term. Washington has no landlord duty to disclose registered offenders nearby.

title: City Rental Inspection Programs
bodyText: Cities may require a certificate of inspection from a qualified inspector as a business license condition, no more than once every three years, and must limit a sample to at most four units at a property of 20 or fewer units, or 20% of the units (up to 50) at a larger property, as long as the first inspection finds no conditions endangering health or safety; if a sampled unit fails, or such conditions were reported since the last inspection, the city may require every unit. Units with a certificate of occupancy within the last four years and no reported violations are exempt. If you inspect only a sample, give all tenants written notice telling them how to request repairs, and give each inspected unit written notice of entry stating the date, approximate time and inspector and the tenant's right to see the inspector's identification. Check your city's rental registration and inspection ordinance.

title: Landlord Registration
bodyText: Washington has no statewide registration or licensing requirement for residential landlords under the landlord-tenant act (manufactured/mobile home communities register separately). Many cities require rental registration or business licenses and may tie them to inspections. Two general business-registration laws can also stop an eviction. If you rent under a trade name that is not your true and real name (for an LLC or corporation, its name on file with the Secretary of State), you must register the trade name with the Department of Revenue. Until you do, you may not maintain any suit in a Washington court, though the lease stays valid and you can still defend a suit (RCW 19.80.005, 19.80.010, 19.80.040). An out-of-state LLC, corporation or other entity must register with the Secretary of State before doing business here. Until it registers and pays any back fees and penalties, it may not maintain an action or proceeding, though its contracts stay valid and it can defend a suit. Owning property without more is not doing business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts and on case law; get advice before filing (RCW 23.95.505, 23.95.510, 23.95.520). And wherever you live, owning property here lets a Washington court hear a claim arising from that ownership, with the papers served on you personally outside the state (RCW 4.28.185).

title: Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no express covenant of quiet enjoyment for these tenancies (the mobile home act mentions quiet enjoyment only as a limit on the park's entry), but several duties protect it: you may not abuse your right of entry or use it to harass, may not unreasonably interfere by showing the unit excessively, may not lock out or cut utilities, and may not retaliate.

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no rule on tenants installing doorbell or security cameras. Treat a camera that needs drilling or wiring as an alteration under the lease, and keep the state privacy and recording statutes in mind for any camera, yours or the tenant's. Smart access systems from 2027 have their own data rules.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging
bodyText: No Washington statute gives residential tenants a right to install EV charging or sets landlord duties for it; the building code governs EV-ready parking in new construction, and association rules govern condominiums. Handle tenant charging requests by written agreement.

title: Balcony or Portable Solar
bodyText: Washington has no statute on tenants installing balcony or plug-in solar devices. Treat a request under the lease's alterations terms.

title: Cable and Internet Provider Access
bodyText: No Washington statute requires a residential landlord to give competing cable or internet providers access to a building, or limits exclusive provider agreements; federal FCC rules may apply.

title: Towing and Booting at a Rental
bodyText: On residential property (property with no more than four living units) you may have an unauthorized vehicle impounded immediately by giving a registered tow truck operator a signed written authorization containing the statutory liability statement. On a property with five or more units, a vehicle may be towed in less than 24 hours only if signs are posted near each entrance and on the property showing the times vehicles may be impounded and the towing firm's name, telephone number and address. You may never boot (immobilize) a vehicle owned by someone else: it is a gross misdemeanor. A person who authorizes an unlawful impound may be liable for the owner's costs.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: When a new tenant moves in, if hot water comes from an accessible water heater serving only that unit, set its thermostat no higher than 120 degrees Fahrenheit, or at the lowest setting if the heater can't be set that low (a mixing valve or system design that limits delivered water to 120 degrees also complies). The tenant may turn it up after moving in; if they do, you aren't liable for damage caused by their readjustment. The rule doesn't apply to buildings served by a central water heater system.

title: Lease Terms Washington Voids
bodyText: Any lease term waiving a section of the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable (the narrow exemption agreement aside), and a lease may not provide that the tenant: waives rights or remedies under the act; gives up the right to sue or join a class action against you or your agents; signs a nondisclosure agreement about the lease or the offer (rent, deposits, fees, concessions, move-in gifts, specials); authorizes a confession of judgment; agrees to pay your attorneys' fees except as the act allows and a court awards; exculpates or limits your liability under law, or indemnifies you for it; agrees in advance to a particular arbitrator, or to arbitrate unless you pay all its cost and the agreement is notarized; pays late fees on rent paid within five days of its due date; or must pay rent electronically only. A lease term creating a lien on the tenant's belongings is void. Agreements made in an eviction case that make the tenant pay more than the act allows, or waive the tenant's rights, are void too. Knowingly using a lease with a prohibited term exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent.

title: Penalty for Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: A prohibited term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees. A general 'nothing here limits your rights' sentence doesn't cure a prohibited term. Washington's collection agency law reaches people collecting claims owed to another, so a debt collector you hire, and possibly a property manager collecting for an owner, is bound by it; a landlord collecting its own debts in its own name in its own business appears to be outside it.

title: Attorneys' Fees
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees except as the landlord-tenant act authorizes and a court awards. Any lease clause giving one party fees is read to give fees to whichever party prevails, and can't be waived. In an eviction, a court may award you fees, but not after a default judgment, and not where the rent awarded is two months' rent or $1,200 or less, whichever is greater; if the tenant has moved to stay the writ, the court may award you fees only if the tenant is reinstated under the hardship-stay rules, and those fees are then subject to repayment under the stay order. Many sections (deposits, retaliation, lockouts, entry) give the prevailing party fees directly.

title: Jury Trial Waivers (Not Offered)
bodyText: The library offers no jury waiver for Washington. The state constitution keeps the right of jury trial inviolate while allowing a jury to be waived in civil cases with the parties' consent, and eviction cases are tried to a jury on factual issues unless a jury is waived 'as in other cases'. Whether a pre-dispute waiver signed in a residential lease counts as that consent is not settled by any statute found, and a lease can't make a tenant waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act.

title: Waiving Exemptions or Homestead (Not Offered)
bodyText: The library offers no clause waiving a tenant's exemptions from execution or homestead rights. No Washington statute authorizes such a waiver in a residential lease, and a lease term creating a lien on, or authorizing seizure of, a tenant's personal property is void.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no unconscionability section of its own, but it does void a long list of terms, and general contract law may let a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term. Keep terms within what the act allows.

title: The Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Washington's Consumer Protection Act declares unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful and allows treble damages (up to $25,000) and Attorney General penalties. The landlord-tenant act doesn't say its violations are CPA violations, and no enumerated list of landlord practices was found apart from one narrow rule: a landlord's violation of the weatherization program rules (no rent increase or eviction because of state-funded weatherization) is a per se CPA violation; whether a particular rental practice is 'unfair or deceptive' in trade or commerce is a matter of case law. The Attorney General separately enforces the rent increase limit with civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation.

title: Plain Language and Type Size
bodyText: Washington has no plain-language or minimum type-size rule for leases under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (mobile home lot agreements have a boldface, larger-type park-closure statement). Specific notices carry their own form rules (the 14-day notice, the rent increase notice, the fee-in-lieu disclosure), and from January 1, 2027 a smart access data policy must be in plain language.

title: Translated Notices
bodyText: Washington doesn't require you to translate the lease. The Attorney General publishes the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice in at least the ten most common languages, and some courts' local rules require serving notices in the tenant's language where the Attorney General has them; using the translated notice for a tenant who reads another language is good practice.

title: Blank Spaces and Lease Completeness
bodyText: Washington has no statute requiring a residential lease to be complete before signing or barring blanks filled in later. Several items must be in writing in the lease, though: deposit withholding terms, nonrefundable fees, the fee-in-lieu acknowledgment and, if you restrict window air conditioners, the cooling notice.

title: Written Leases and Long Terms
bodyText: Year-to-year tenancies exist only by express written contract. A lease of up to one year may be written or printed and needs no acknowledgment, witnesses or seals. A lease for longer than a year is a conveyance of an interest in land that must be made by deed (in writing and signed); it needs no acknowledgment unless you want to record it. Any deposit or nonrefundable fee requires a written lease regardless of term.

title: Giving Tenants a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: When there is a written lease, give an executed copy to each tenant who signs it; a tenant may ask for one free replacement copy during the tenancy. Give a copy of the signed move-in checklist too.

title: How to Deliver Notices
bodyText: Notices that end a tenancy or start an eviction (14-day, 10-day, 3-day and just-cause notices, 60-day non-renewal notices, rent increase notices) must be served in the statutory way: personal delivery; or leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the unit and mailing a copy; or, if neither works, posting and mailing. E-mail alone is not enough for these. Entry notices must be written. You may use e-mail for other written notices only if the tenant has agreed to conduct the transaction electronically, the tenant can print and store the message, and the tenant may withdraw that agreement for other transactions at any time; a statute requiring mail or a specific method still controls, unless that statute itself lets the parties agree otherwise.

title: Washington's Statutory Forms
bodyText: Use these statutory forms, substantially as printed: the 14-day notice to pay rent or vacate; the Rent and Fee Increase Notice; the fee-in-lieu-of-deposit disclosure; the screening adverse action notice; the eviction summons (residential); the request for storage of personal property served with a writ; the notice of default on a court payment plan; and (for tenants) the victim's qualified third-party report, whose form is optional. The Attorney General publishes translated versions of several.

title: Who the Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act covers most residential rentals. It doesn't cover: institutional residence incidental to care, detention or education; occupancy under an earnest money agreement or contract of sale by the buyer; a seller staying up to three months after closing under a qualifying written agreement; hotels and transient lodging; certain owner-condemnee, agricultural, seasonal farmworker and state-land rentals; and an employee whose right to occupy depends on employment on the premises, unless any arrangement is set up mainly to avoid the act. Mobile and manufactured home lots have their own act. A lease of a single-family dwelling for a year or more, or with a bona fide purchase option, can opt out of the act only if the tenant's attorney approves the exemption on the face of the lease; the library doesn't offer that opt-out.

title: Washington Fair Housing Classes
bodyText: Washington bars discrimination in renting because of sex, marital status, sexual orientation, race, creed, color, national origin, citizenship or immigration status, families with children status, honorably discharged veteran or military status, any sensory, mental or physical disability, or the use of a trained dog guide or service animal. That covers refusing to rent, different terms, steering, discriminatory ads or application forms, and evictions. Source of income and victim status are protected by the landlord-tenant act too. Exemptions: the act doesn't apply to sharing a dwelling unit, or renting part of one, that the owner or sublessor occupies; qualifying housing for older persons may exclude families with children. Local ordinances add more classes.

title: Citizenship and Immigration Status
bodyText: Citizenship or immigration status is a protected class in Washington housing: don't refuse to rent, set different terms, advertise preferences, or ask questions on applications that indicate a limitation based on it. Noncitizens may own and lease land. Screening criteria such as identity verification should apply equally to everyone.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: Families with children status (including pregnancy and those securing custody) is protected in Washington housing. The landlord-tenant act still contains a 90-day notice rule for a landlord planning to change to a policy of excluding children; such a policy is lawful only where an exemption applies (for example, qualifying housing for older persons or student housing), so get advice before relying on it.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies and services when needed for a person with a disability to use and enjoy the home, and allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, conditioned where reasonable on restoring the interior at move-out. Don't ask an applicant about disability beyond what the tenancy needs, and don't require waivers or hold-harmless agreements because a disabled person will live there. These two duties don't apply to an owner renting a single-family house who owns no more than three, rents without a broker and without discriminatory advertising, or to an owner-occupied building of up to four units (federal law may still apply). Separately, a tenant whose primary income is monthly government assistance paid after the due date may ask in writing to move the due date by up to five days.

title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A no-pet policy can't be applied to a disabled tenant's trained dog guide or service animal (a dog or miniature horse trained to do work for the person). You may charge the same cleaning or damage deposit every tenant pays, but no pet deposit or pet fee. You may require removal only if the animal poses an unreasonable risk of injury or harm that a reasonable attempt to fix has failed to eliminate. Other assistance animals (such as emotional support animals) are handled as reasonable accommodation requests.
