title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal
bodyText: Misrepresenting an animal as a service animal to secure the rights of disabled persons is a civil infraction in Washington when the person knew or should have known it doesn't qualify. In a place of public accommodation (which includes the public halls, elevators and washrooms of buildings with two or more units), staff may ask only whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work it is trained to perform. Enforcement is by an enforcement officer, not by the landlord.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Washington legalized adult cannabis but nothing in state law requires a landlord to allow cannabis smoking or growing at a rental: a lease may prohibit smoking cannabis and growing it on the premises. Consuming cannabis in view of the general public or in a public place is an infraction, and the medical cannabis law requires no accommodation for smoking cannabis in a public place.

title: Firearms in Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute bars or requires a residential lease rule on lawful firearm possession. The act's rules on weapons are about conduct: a tenant may not threaten others or unlawfully use a firearm or deadly weapon in a way leading to an arrest, and a tenant threatened with a weapon by another tenant or by you may end the lease in the circumstances the act describes. The state constitution protects the individual right to bear arms; how that applies between a private landlord and tenant is not settled by any section read.

title: Smoking Rules
bodyText: Washington's Smoking in Public Places law bans smoking in places open to the public and in places of employment (including areas staff must pass through), and within 25 feet of their entrances, windows and air intakes, but it excludes private residences; whether a building's lobbies, elevators and other areas open to the public count depends on the facts. A lease may ban smoking in units and common areas. In multifamily buildings the fire safety notice must say whether the building has a smoking policy and what it is.

title: Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Washington doesn't bar a lease from requiring renter's insurance. For leases entered into after December 31, 2026 you must tell tenants that your insurance doesn't cover their belongings and that they should consider renter's and flood insurance. You can't use insurance to shift your own liability: a lease term exculpating you or making the tenant indemnify you for your liability is void.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules
bodyText: Under Washington's common interest community act, an association may enforce its rules against tenants and impose fines after notice and an opportunity to be heard, and may require owners to screen tenants (at the owner's cost) but may not demand the screening report. Until January 1, 2028 that act governs only communities created on or after July 1, 2018 or that elect into it; older condominiums and HOAs stay under their own acts until then. Give tenants the association rules at move-in so they become part of the tenancy.

title: Ending a Federal Housing Contract
bodyText: If you own federally assisted housing and the assistance contract will expire or you plan to prepay the mortgage or loan, Washington requires (unless an exception applies; Section 8 certificate or voucher contracts are outside the statute, and some long-term use agreements excuse a prepayment notice) written notice at least 12 months ahead, by regular and certified mail, to each tenant household, the city or county clerk, the public housing agency and the Department of Commerce. A household that moves in after that notice must get it before being asked to sign a lease or pay any deposit. For 12 months after the notice (or until expiration or prepayment, if later) you may not evict except as the federal program allows, raise rent above the program amount, or change lease terms except as the lease permits; post the notice as the statute requires. Subsidized tenancies also have shorter rent-increase notice and form rules.

title: Government Shutdowns
bodyText: Washington has no statute protecting tenants who are federal employees or contractors from eviction during a federal government shutdown.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no express tenant-organizing right (the mobile home act has one), but retaliation for asserting rights under the act is barred. Local ordinances may protect organizing.

title: Tenant Flags and Signs
bodyText: No Washington statute gives residential tenants a right to display flags, political signs or religious items over a lease rule. The state's flag and political-sign protections bind associations' governing documents, not landlords (the older association-act versions run until January 1, 2028; RCW 64.90.510 continues them). Apply any display rule evenly and avoid rules that target protected classes.

title: Military Installations Nearby
bodyText: Washington has no lease disclosure for military installations, airports or noise zones.

title: Statement of Tenant Rights
bodyText: Washington doesn't require landlords to give tenants a state-prepared statement of rights with the lease. The 14-day pay-or-vacate notice points tenants to the Attorney General's landlord-tenant resources, and the state runs an online landlord resource center. Some cities require a local rights handout. A city or county rule requiring you to give tenants information about the property or the surrounding area takes effect only after it is listed on the state-contracted municipal research website (`edu-no-rights-responsibilities-guide-wa`).

title: Evictions for Drugs, Weapons and Gang Activity
bodyText: For drug-related activity, for imminently hazardous assaults or unlawful weapon use that led to the tenant's arrest, and for gang-related activity, the usual 30-day chance to fix a duty breach doesn't apply: you may proceed directly to an unlawful detainer action after a 3-day notice to quit for waste, nuisance or unlawful activity. You can't be held liable for bringing such an action in good faith. The ordinary show cause process applies, with differences: in a drug-activity case the tenant may not use a set-off as a defense, and an owner who in good faith brings an unlawful detainer for drug-related activity has a defense to the felony of knowingly permitting drug activity on the property. Neighbors endangered by gang activity may demand that you file and then petition the court.

title: Submetering and Utility Allocation
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no statute regulating submetering, ratio utility billing or allocation of utility costs to residential tenants. Utility commission rules do limit reselling: gas from a regulated utility may not be remetered or submetered by a customer for resale, and electricity may be resold only if the utility's tariff allows it. Utilities billed as recurring charges in the lease count as rent, so they appear on the 14-day notice and fall under the rent increase rules; put the billing method in the lease.

title: Penalties for Housing Discrimination
bodyText: A finding of an unfair practice in a rental, including refusing a disabled tenant's service animal or a reasonable accommodation, can bring actual damages, injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $10,000 for a first violation, $25,000 with one prior violation in five years, and $50,000 with two or more in seven years. Tenants may also sue in court.

title: Noncitizen and Foreign Ownership
bodyText: Washington doesn't restrict noncitizens or foreign entities from owning or leasing residential property: any noncitizen may acquire, hold and convey land. No foreign-ownership disclosure applies to residential leases.

title: Keeping Victim Information Confidential
bodyText: Tenant screening services may not disclose a person's status as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or knowingly disclose that someone ended a lease under the victim-protection statute. The third-party record a victim gives you to end a lease omits the alleged perpetrator's name. Giving you the verification doesn't waive the privilege between the victim and the third party, and no record obtained from it may be used against the victim in any proceeding without a written waiver (except the verification itself, in proceedings under the victim-protection statute). Treat the documents as confidential and use them only to process the termination.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Don't use an application form, make a record, or ask a question that indicates a limitation based on a protected class (including citizenship or immigration status, families with children status and disability; Washington's law against discrimination doesn't reach sharing or subletting part of a unit the owner or sublessor occupies), and don't publish ads indicating a preference based on source of income. With disabled applicants, ask only what the tenancy needs (for example, how many people will live there), not about the disability or aides.

title: Changing Terms During a Tenancy
bodyText: To change a month-to-month tenancy's terms: new rules take effect after 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant and at the end of the rental period's term (or sooner if the tenant agrees); any increase in rent, including a new or higher recurring fee, needs 90 days' written notice on the state form (30 days and no state form for income-based subsidized tenancies), and, unless an RCW 59.18.710 exemption applies, can't take effect in the first 12 months of the tenancy and must stay within the increase limit. Making month-to-month terms more burdensome than fixed-term terms, or the reverse, is barred, and rents for different lease types on the same unit may differ by no more than 5%.

title: Moving to Care Facilities
bodyText: Washington gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of age, illness or a move to a nursing home or assisted living. A month-to-month tenant can leave on written notice given at least 20 days before the end of a rental period; for a fixed term, consider a written early-release agreement, and remember a disability may support a reasonable accommodation request.

title: Pools and Spas at Rentals
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no pool or spa safety rule for rentals, but the state's water recreation facility rules treat a pool or spa at an apartment, condominium or rental housing unit for residents and their guests as a 'limited use pool' subject to the health rules. They don't apply to a pool or spa used only by the residents and invited guests of a single-family home, or of a duplex owned by its residents. A pool only for residents of an apartment complex, or of a group of fewer than 15 rental units (or a mobile home park), is excused from preconstruction design review, routine inspection, and permit or fee requirements; local health departments may read the size limit differently. Check with the local health department.

title: One Non-Waiver Rule Covers the Whole Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Some states put habitability in a separate part of their landlord-tenant statute with its own clause voiding any waiver of that part. Washington doesn't. Its Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) has one non-waiver rule for the whole chapter: any provision of a lease or other agreement, oral or written, that waives any section or subsection of the chapter is against public policy and unenforceable, and the rest of the agreement still stands. On top of that, a rental agreement may not provide that the tenant waives or forgoes rights or remedies under the chapter, and if you knowingly use a lease containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). An agreement made in an eviction case that makes the tenant pay more than the act allows or waives the tenant's rights under the chapter is void too. The only exception is an exemption agreement covering your repair and habitability duties and the related tenant remedies and tenant duties (RCW 59.18.060, RCW 59.18.100, RCW 59.18.110, RCW 59.18.120, RCW 59.18.130 and RCW 59.18.190), and only if it is not in a standard form lease, the parties have no substantial inequality in bargaining position, it doesn't violate the state's policy of safe and sanitary housing, and the county prosecutor, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's attorney approves it in writing; the library offers no such agreement (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). The relocation-assistance section for condemned or unlawful units carries its own non-waiver sentence for occupancy agreements. The rule reaches tenancies under chapter 59.18 RCW; it doesn't reach the living arrangements the act excludes, such as a seller who stays on for no more than three months after closing under a written rent-back where the home wasn't distressed and the seller had a lawyer or licensed broker, or a lease of a single-family home for a year or more, or with a bona fide purchase option, that the tenant's attorney has approved on its face (`edu-scope-wa`). Mobile home lot tenancies are under chapter 59.20 RCW and outside this library. Where a homeowner facing foreclosure sells the home and stays on as a tenant under a promise to convey it back, give an option or share the resale proceeds, that is a distressed home conveyance under chapter 61.34 RCW, and any waiver by the homeowner of that chapter is void; that rule dates from 2008. No 2025 or 2026 act adding a sale-leaseback non-waiver rule was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws.

title: Waiving Habitability Duties in Washington
bodyText: Your duty to keep the unit fit for human habitation, and each specific repair and maintenance duty that goes with it, can't be waived in a lease. A lease term waiving any part of the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable, and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act; knowingly using such a term exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Washington does let a landlord and tenant remove the habitability duties themselves, not only reassign who does the work, but only through a written exemption agreement that meets four conditions: it is not in a standard form lease or rental agreement; the two sides have no substantial inequality in bargaining position; the exemption doesn't violate the state's public policy of safe and sanitary housing; and the county prosecutor's office, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's own attorney approves it in writing as meeting the first three. The agreement can reach only your duties section and the repair-and-deduct, reduced-rent-value and court-ordered termination remedies, plus the tenant-duties section and the section on your notice to a tenant to remedy a nonconformance. Everything else stays: the written-notice repair deadlines, the tenant's right to end the lease after an unremedied defect, the rent escrow remedy for dangerous conditions, the rules on condemned or unlawful units and relocation assistance, retaliation, and the bar on renting a unit an agency has condemned. The safe-and-sanitary condition also limits what any exemption can give up. The library offers no exemption agreement: anything generated from a template is a standard form, and the approval must come from an official or the tenant's lawyer (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). A tenant may agree to do repairs personally in return for cash or a reasonable reduction in rent, but that agreement doesn't change your obligations under the act. Washington has no statute letting a tenant accept specified defective conditions in exchange for reduced rent, and none requiring a separate document for an agreement about heat (no such rule was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules). No published Washington case on a pre-lease "as is" acceptance was searched for; the cautious course is to fix defects rather than price them into the rent.

title: Which Habitability Duties Vary by Agreement in Washington
bodyText: A lease can't trim your habitability duties; the only way to change them is the approved exemption agreement described in `edu-habitability-waiver-wa`, which can't be in a standard form lease. Several duties do vary by their own terms, though, and a lease can affect those lawfully: (1) your repair duty is to put and keep the premises in as good condition as they should have been, by law or by the rental agreement, at the start of the tenancy (ordinary wear excepted), so a lease can promise a better condition than the statute requires but never a worse one; (2) you must keep in reasonably good working order the electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances you supply, so the lease's list of what you supply decides which appliances you maintain (`appliances-included`); (3) in a single-family residence you don't owe pest control during the tenancy (you still owe a reasonable program at the start of the tenancy, and never owe it for an infestation the tenant caused) or common-area garbage receptacles and removal; a unit sharing walls still counts as a single-family residence if it has direct access to a street and shares no heating, hot water equipment or other essential facility or service with another unit; (4) you have no repair duty, and the tenant no remedy, for a condition caused by the tenant, the tenant's family, invitee or another person under the tenant's control, or where the tenant unreasonably refuses access for repairs (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`); (5) the tenant may take on ordinary upkeep of the tenant's own space, such as cleaning, garbage disposal from the unit and yard or walkway care outside your shared-area duty (`tenant-maintenance`, `landscaping-irrigation`, `snow-removal`), and may agree to do repairs for cash or a reasonable rent reduction, but neither changes your statutory duties. Water: you must provide facilities adequate to supply heat, water and hot water as reasonably required by the tenant. Unlike some states, Washington has no exception letting the lease waive the water duty for premises without a well or utility water, and none was found anywhere in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws. Separate rules limit shutting off electricity or water for nonpayment during a heat alert (`edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`).

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be for Each Washington Remedy
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has no single "material defect" test. Your duty is to keep the premises fit for human habitation, and each duty and each tenant remedy carries its own threshold: (1) code compliance: you must substantially comply with any applicable code, statute, ordinance or regulation governing maintenance or operation that the enacting body could enforce against the premises, where the condition endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety; the other listed duties (structure, weathertightness, locks, supplied facilities and appliances, heat and water facilities and so on) carry their own standards such as reasonably good repair or working order; (2) repair deadlines after the tenant's written notice turn on the kind of defect: start within 24 hours for loss of hot or cold water, heat or electricity or a condition imminently hazardous to life, within 72 hours for loss of a refrigerator, range and oven or major plumbing fixture you supplied, and within 10 days otherwise; (3) termination by the tenant and a suit or agreed arbitration for reduced rental value follow any failure to remedy a defect in one of your duties under the act or the rental agreement after written notice, the applicable deadline and a reasonable time; (4) repair-and-deduct is available for your statutory duties except, by the Code Reviser's notes, the common-area garbage duty and the duty to designate the landlord's name and address, and the tenant's own repairs (no estimate) are limited to defects within the unit costing no more than one month's rent; (5) rent escrow requires a failure of a substantial obligation that substantially endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety, such as undersized structural members, exposure to the weather, plumbing and sanitation defects exposing occupants to illness or injury, lack of water including hot water, nonfunctional or hazardous heating or ventilation, defective or missing wiring or electrical service, defective exits, and fire risks, certified by a local government inspection; (6) a court or arbitrator may end the tenancy only for a defect so substantial that it can't feasibly be remedied in time and the tenant shouldn't remain. None of these applies to a condition the tenant, family, invitee or someone under the tenant's control caused, or where the tenant unreasonably refuses access for repairs (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`, `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`).

title: No Presumption of Repair Breach in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules presumes that you breached a habitability or repair duty from a code violation, an agency notice or the passage of time; a tenant who claims a breach must prove it. The repair remedies run on fixed periods instead: after the tenant's written notice you must start repairs within 24 hours, 72 hours or 10 days depending on the defect, with the burden on you to see the work is completed promptly (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). For the rent escrow remedy, a local government inspector certifies whether the listed dangerous conditions exist; you may appeal the certification, but the appeal doesn't stop the tenant from paying rent into escrow. The presumption the act does create runs against you on retaliation: if you evict, raise rent, reduce services or increase the tenant's obligations within 90 days after the tenant's good-faith complaint to a government authority about code conditions, or assertion of rights under the act, or within 90 days after an inspection or proceeding that resulted from it, the action is presumed retaliatory, and you must rebut it (`edu-retaliation-wa`). It works in your favor where the tenant was behind in rent or otherwise in breach when you gave a termination notice, where the tenant's complaint came within 90 days after your notice of a rent increase or other good-faith action, and where your rent-increase notice states reasonable grounds; and an eviction presumption can be rebutted by showing repairs can't practically be made while the tenant stays. Keep dated records of every repair request and what you did about it.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in a Washington Lease
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules requires a lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for human habitation. The duty applies by law whether or not the lease mentions it: you must keep the premises fit for human habitation at all times during the tenancy, and a lease can't reduce that duty (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). The library's shared maintenance clause, which says you will maintain the property as the law requires, is used for Washington as written but is optional (`landlord-maintenance`). Washington does require other statements tied to the lease: your name and address (and, if you live out of state, an in-county agent) designated on the rental agreement or by a posted notice (`landlord-disclosure-wa`); a signed fire safety and smoke detection notice given when the lease is signed (`fire-safety-notice-wa`); the flood, renter's insurance and hazard information disclosures for leases entered into after December 31, 2026 (`flood-disclosure-wa`); the Department of Health mold information at signing, which may instead be posted (`mold-disclosure-wa`); and the written deposit terms and condition checklist if you take a deposit (`security-deposit-use-wa`).

title: Liability Waivers and Indemnity Clauses in Washington Leases
bodyText: A Washington lease may not make the tenant release you from, or limit, any liability you have under law, or make the tenant indemnify you for that liability or its costs. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using a lease containing one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). The same list bars terms making the tenant waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act or give up the right to sue you or your agents or join a class action. What a lease may do: say the deposit may be kept to cover damage to the premises the tenant is responsible for (the lease must say so in writing), and hold the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, family, invitees or people under the tenant's control cause (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`). A few statutes give you protection without any lease clause: you are immune from civil liability for not giving the mold information unless the failure is knowing and intentional; you can't be held liable for bringing an eviction in good faith for drug-related activity, conduct imminently hazardous to others' safety or gang-related activity (but you remain liable for all damages if a writ of restitution is wrongfully obtained); you are held harmless for damages resulting directly from changing a lock at the request of a tenant with a court order excluding a cotenant; following the deceased-tenant property procedure relieves you of liability for that property; and you are immune from claims for damage, injury or death caused by a portable cooling device the tenant installed. The abandoned-property and writ-of-restitution storage procedures, and a police notice that drugs were seized at your property, carry no landlord immunity: they set out what you must do, and taking or keeping a tenant's belongings outside them can make you liable (`edu-abandoned-property-wa`, `edu-post-eviction-property-wa`).

title: Charging a Tenant for an Eviction in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute names an "eviction fee", but the landlord-tenant act controls what an eviction can cost the tenant, and a lease charge can't add to it. (1) Attorneys' fees: a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees except as the act authorizes and a court awards; in an eviction the court may award you reasonable fees, but not on a default judgment, not where the rent awarded is no more than the greater of two months' rent or $1,200, and, if the tenant moved to stay the writ, only if the tenant is reinstated under the hardship-stay rules (`edu-attorney-fees-wa`). (2) The judgment: possession, damages the court assesses as alleged and proved, rent due, late fees due under the lease up to $75 in total, statutory costs and any fees allowed as above. A tenant may reinstate the tenancy up to five court days after judgment (or until the date of eviction if the tenant provides a pledge of financial assistance letter from a government or nonprofit entity) by paying the rent due, court costs incurred, late fees up to $75 in total and any attorneys' fees awarded (plus $50 for each earlier post-judgment reinstatement in the previous 12 months). (3) Charges other than rent: the tenant's right to possession can't be conditioned on paying anything but rent except as the judgment rules allow; rent doesn't include late charges, damages, legal costs or other fees; you may not threaten eviction for those nonpossessory charges; and any agreement made in an eviction case that makes the tenant pay more than these rules allow, or waives the tenant's rights, is void. You must apply each payment to rent first (`application-of-payments-wa`). A fixed eviction charge in a lease has no statutory footing: it isn't rent, it can't be a condition of keeping the home, and a court awards only the damages, costs and fees the act allows. Washington has no general statute voiding penalties or advance-fixed damages in contracts outside the sale of goods and real estate earnest money (no such rule for leases of real property was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules); whether a fixed eviction charge would also fail as a penalty under the common law was not searched. The cautious course is to leave any eviction charge out of the lease and recover only what a court awards (`edu-eviction-process-wa`).

title: Tenants Cannot Waive Eviction Notices in a Washington Lease
bodyText: A Washington lease can't shorten or waive the notices the landlord-tenant act gives a tenant before the tenancy ends or an eviction starts. The default rules: you may evict, refuse to continue a tenancy or end a periodic tenancy only for a cause the act lists, each with its own written notice served the statutory way and stating the facts behind the cause, for example 14 days to pay rent or vacate in the statutory form, 10 days to cure a breach of a material lease term, 3 days to quit for waste, nuisance or unlawful activity, and 60 days before the end of a qualifying fixed term you choose not to continue (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`, `edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`, `edu-termination-notice-wa`). Any lease or other agreement, oral or written, waiving a section or subsection of the act is unenforceable, and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act; knowingly using such a term exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). So a clause in which the tenant gives up the notice to pay or vacate, the cure period or the notice before a writ is void. An agreement made in an eviction case that waives the tenant's rights under the act is void too. What the act does allow: after you have given a 90-day notice of a change to a policy excluding children or a 120-day condominium conversion notice and the change is then delayed, the tenant may waive the ordinary 20-day notice that would otherwise apply; and a fixed term may end early for owner occupancy, sale or demolition only if you and the tenant both consent in writing and the tenant gets at least 60 days to move. These are agreements made when the situation arises, not advance waivers in the lease.

title: Confession of Judgment Clauses in Washington
bodyText: A Washington lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment against the tenant on a claim arising out of the rental agreement. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using a lease containing one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). Outside leases, Washington still allows judgment by confession: a defendant may confess judgment in a pending action, or a judgment may be entered without a lawsuit on a written statement the defendant signs and verifies under oath, authorizing judgment for a specified sum and stating the facts showing the sum is justly due, which a superior court judge must find sufficient before the clerk enters it; an individual must make the confession personally. No statute makes confessions of judgment unenforceable in every contract; besides residential leases, statutes bar or limit them in lease-purchase agreements for goods, debt adjusting contracts, structured settlement transfers and some private school contracts. The state civil rules leave judgment by confession to that statute, and no court rule abolishing confessed ejectment or setting an appeal bond for it was found. Whether a separate confession signed after a rent dispute arises falls under the lease bar, or under the rule voiding agreements in an eviction case that make the tenant pay more than the act allows or waive the tenant's rights, isn't settled by statute (no published Washington case was searched for); don't use one without advice, and never as a condition of the tenancy.

title: Notice for Showings Cannot Be Waived in a Washington Lease
bodyText:
Washington sets the notice for showings by statute, so a lease can't shorten or waive it.

Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least two days' written notice before entering, stating the date and either the exact time or a window with the earliest and latest times, and a telephone number for objections or rescheduling; to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers or tenants, at least one day's notice is enough, and the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry at a specified time. You must not excessively show the unit or use access to harass the tenant, and you have no other right of access except by court order, an arbitrator or the tenant's consent. After one good-faith written notice of a violation, each further violation can cost up to $100, plus costs and attorneys' fees (`landlords-access-wa`).

A lease clause letting you show the unit on same-day or shorter notice would waive part of the entry statute, and any lease term waiving a section or subsection of the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable; a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act either, and knowingly using such a term carries statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). The library's shared showings clause, which lets the lease set a shorter notice, is therefore not used for Washington; the Washington entry clause already gives you the one-day showing notice.

What does work is the tenant's consent at the time: if the tenant agrees to a particular showing on shorter notice, you may enter by consent. Washington has no procedure for a separate signed waiver of the showing notice.

title: Deposit Protections Cannot Be Waived in Washington
bodyText: Washington's deposit rules can't be waived in a lease. They sit in the landlord-tenant act, and any lease or other agreement waiving a section or subsection of the act is unenforceable; a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act, and knowingly using such a term carries statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). The approved exemption agreement doesn't reach the deposit sections at all. So no lease can remove: the written lease and signed move-in condition checklist required before you take a deposit (`security-deposit-use-wa`); the trust account, receipt and depository notice (`deposit-depository-wa`); the bar on withholding for ordinary wear; the 30-day itemized statement with estimates or invoices and any refund, and the full-deposit penalty for missing it (up to double for an intentional refusal) (`security-deposit-return-wa`, `edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`, `edu-security-deposit-penalty-wa`); the rule that nonrefundable money can't be called a deposit; the tenant's right to pay deposits, nonrefundable fees and last month's rent in installments (`edu-deposit-installments-wa`); or the limits on holding deposits. One point is a default the parties may change: interest on the trust account belongs to you unless you and the tenant agree otherwise in writing (`edu-security-deposit-interest-wa`).

title: Casualty and Re-Renting Rules a Washington Lease Cannot Change
bodyText: Mitigation: when a tenant who is behind on rent abandons the unit, you must make a reasonable effort to re-rent, and a tenant with a fixed term owes the lesser of the rent for the rest of the term or the rent accrued while you re-rent at a fair rental plus any shortfall and your actual re-renting costs, statutory costs and reasonable attorneys' fees (a month-to-month tenant owes 30 days) (`edu-abandonment-mitigation-wa`). That rule is in the landlord-tenant act, so a lease can't waive it: any term waiving a section of the act is unenforceable, and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under it (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Don't write a clause saying you need not re-rent, or that the tenant owes all remaining rent whatever you do. Casualty: Washington has no statute written for fire or other casualty damage to a rental, and so no casualty default for a lease to waive or vary; no general statute letting an express agreement override a tenant's right to surrender a destroyed building was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. After a casualty the act's ordinary rules apply, and they can't be waived either: the repair duties and the tenant's written-notice remedies (including ending the lease after an unremedied defect, reduced rent value and court-ordered termination for a defect that can't feasibly be fixed in time), your no-duty rule for damage the tenant or the tenant's family, invitees or people under the tenant's control caused, and just-cause limits on ending the tenancy yourself (`edu-casualty-termination-wa`). The library offers no landlord casualty-termination clause for Washington, because it would add a cause for ending the tenancy that the statute doesn't list.

title: Liquidated Damages Clauses in Washington Leases (Not Offered)
bodyText:
No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules governs liquidated damages in a residential lease, either permitting an agreed damages amount for a tenant's breach or voiding damages fixed in advance. Whether a fixed sum would be enforced or struck as a penalty is left to the common law.

The landlord-tenant act does limit what a fixed charge can do: late fees can't apply to rent paid within five days of its due date (`late-fee-wa`); an eviction judgment includes late fees only up to $75 in total (`edu-eviction-penalty-clause-ban-wa`); a tenant who abandons owes the statutory measure, net of your duty to re-rent, which a lease can't replace with a larger fixed sum (`edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-wa`); and damage charges against the deposit must be documented with estimates, invoices or receipts, and undocumented damages can't be charged, reported or sent to collection (`edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`).

The library doesn't offer a general liquidated-damages clause for Washington: those limits leave little room for one, and the penalty question is unsettled. It does offer an early-termination option that lets the tenant end a fixed term early by paying one month's rent, which the tenant chooses rather than owes for a breach (`early-termination-wa`). If you want a liquidated-damages clause, add your own and take advice first.

title: Tenant Remedies When a Washington Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act gives the tenant a specific remedy for each kind of landlord breach; none can be waived in the lease. Repairs: after written notice and the statutory period to start work, the tenant may end the lease, sue or arbitrate for reduced rental value, repair and deduct within limits, or, for conditions that substantially endanger health or safety and that a local inspector certifies, pay rent into escrow; a court or arbitrator may end the tenancy for a defect that can't feasibly be fixed in time (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`, `edu-statutory-early-termination-wa`). Other breaches: unlawful entry after one written warning (up to $100 per violation, `landlords-access-wa`); a lockout or exclusion without a court order (possession or termination and actual damages) and an intentional utility shutoff (actual damages and up to $100 a day) (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`); taking or keeping the tenant's belongings (value, damages and up to $500 a day, capped at $5,000, for an intentional refusal) (`edu-landlord-lien-wa`); retaliation, with a 90-day presumption (`edu-retaliation-wa`); deposit violations (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-wa`); a removal in violation of the just-cause rules (the greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus fees) (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`); renting a condemned unit (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`); and knowingly using a prohibited lease term (`edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). A tenant threatened by you with a firearm or deadly weapon, leading to your arrest, may leave without further obligation. To use the act's remedies the tenant must be current on rent and on any utilities the lease makes the tenant pay, but that doesn't limit the tenant's suit for negligent or intentional damage or the defense in an eviction that no rent is owed. Washington has no lead, health or code statute directing a tenant to withhold rent until you comply with an eviction bar, other than the act's own rent escrow remedy, which bars an eviction for nonpayment while the tenant keeps paying the full rent into escrow (no other such rule was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules).

title: How Repair Notice Works in Washington
bodyText: The tenant's repair remedies start with a written notice. The tenant delivers it to the person you designated as landlord on the rental agreement or a posted notice, or to the person who collects the rent, and it must identify the premises, the owner's name if known and the defective condition. Your deadlines to start work (24 hours, 72 hours or 10 days, by defect) run from your receipt of it, and the tenant may send a good-faith repair estimate with it, by first-class mail or in person (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). Reduced-rent judgments run from the time of notice, and the rent escrow remedy needs its own written notice to you or to the person or place where rent is normally paid. Your duty to keep the unit fit applies at all times, not only after notice, and retaliation protection covers a tenant's good-faith complaints to a government authority and assertion of rights under the act, whether or not the tenant sent you a written repair request (`edu-retaliation-wa`). Washington has no rule that naming an oral, phone or electronic channel for repair requests in the lease gives up your right to written notice, and no rule letting the lease waive the written notice; nothing to that effect was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. You may invite repair requests by phone, email or a portal, and responding to them is good practice, but the statutory periods and remedies turn on the written notice the statute describes. A lease term narrowing it, such as accepting repair notices only through a portal or only by one person, or adding conditions before the tenant's remedies apply, would waive part of the act and is unenforceable (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). The library offers no separate repair-request clause for Washington; the notices clause and your landlord designation already tell the tenant where to send notices (`notices`, `landlord-disclosure-wa`).

title: No Ending the Tenancy Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules lets you end a tenancy, or decline a repair, because the repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. Your duty to keep the unit fit continues, and a lease can't add such a right: you may end a tenancy only for a cause the statute lists, and a lease term waiving the act is unenforceable (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-casualty-termination-wa`). What the act does provide: if completion is delayed by circumstances beyond your control, including unavailable financing, you must remedy the defect as soon as possible; a court or arbitrator (not you) may end the tenancy where a defect is so substantial it can't feasibly be remedied in the statutory time and the tenant shouldn't stay, setting a reasonable time to vacate; you may end a tenancy to demolish or substantially rehabilitate the premises on 120 days' written notice (but not before a fixed term ends unless the tenant agrees in writing and gets at least 60 days), or on at least 30 days' notice (or as much as the order allows) where a local agency has certified or condemned the unit as uninhabitable and continued occupancy would expose you to civil or criminal penalties; and a retaliation presumption against an eviction can be rebutted by showing that necessary repairs can't practically be made while the tenant stays (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Cost limits do apply to the tenant's self-help: repair-and-deduct is capped at two months' rent per repair and in any 12 months, and the tenant's own repairs at one month's rent (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). A city's unfit-dwelling ordinance may base a repair-or-demolish order on the ratio of repair cost to the building's value; that is an agency order, not a landlord's election, and if it condemns the unit you may owe relocation assistance (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`).

title: Shifting Maintenance to a Washington Tenant
bodyText: A Washington lease can't shift your statutory repair and maintenance duties to the tenant. The only way to move them is a written exemption agreement that isn't in a standard form lease, between parties of roughly equal bargaining power, consistent with safe and sanitary housing, and approved in writing by the county prosecutor, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's attorney; the library offers none (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`, `edu-habitability-waiver-wa`). Washington has no rule letting the lease shift a single listed duty on a precondition, and none letting a shift stand on adequate consideration and a conspicuous lease term alone. Two things a lease can lawfully do: (1) assign ordinary upkeep that isn't one of your statutory duties, such as yard care and snow removal for areas the tenant uses exclusively, or tenant duties the act already imposes such as keeping the unit clean and disposing of garbage from it (`tenant-maintenance`, `landscaping-irrigation`, `snow-removal`; in a single-family residence, pest control during the tenancy and garbage receptacles and removal aren't your statutory duties to begin with, `edu-habitability-modifiable-wa`); and (2) record an agreement that the tenant will do particular repairs in return for cash or a reasonable rent reduction. The second kind leaves your obligations under the act exactly where they were: if the work isn't done or is done badly, the duty and the tenant's remedies remain yours, the repair work must meet applicable codes, and you may recover actual damages from a tenant whose negligent repairs damage the property. The library doesn't offer a tenant-repair-for-rent clause for Washington: the price must be negotiated for the specific work, it shifts no duty, and a template version risks reading as a waiver of your duties, which would be unenforceable. If you want one, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: Smoke Drift Between Units in Washington
bodyText:
No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules addresses tobacco smoke drifting between units, or lets a lease make the tenant accept drifting smoke or give up claims about it.

Don't use a smoke-drift waiver. As to claims against you, it would be a lease term releasing or limiting your liability under law, or waiving the tenant's right to sue you, and those terms are unenforceable and carry statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent if knowingly used (`edu-exculpatory-clauses-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`); no statute authorizes a waiver of the tenant's claims against other residents either.

What works instead: a lease may ban smoking, including vaping and cannabis, in units and common areas (`smoking-policy`), and in any building other than a single-family residence the fire safety notice given at signing must say whether the building has a smoking policy and what it is (`fire-safety-notice-wa`).

The state smoke-free law bans smoking in public places (the parts of a building used by and open to the public, such as lobbies, elevators and reception areas) and places of employment (areas under an employer's control that employees must pass through, including common areas), and within 25 feet of their entrances, opening windows and air intakes; a private residence is neither (`edu-smoking-wa`).

It doesn't name apartment hallways: whether an enclosed hallway counts as a place of employment because your staff must pass through it, or as a public place, depends on the facts, and no statute or held rule settles it, so the cautious course is to keep common areas smoke-free.

Vaping is banned statewide in elevators (and in schools, child care facilities and near schools), and local governments may regulate it in other indoor public places; using cannabis in view of the general public or in a public place is a civil infraction (`edu-cannabis-wa`).

title: Binding Arbitration Clauses in Washington Leases (Not Offered)
bodyText: The library doesn't offer a binding arbitration clause for Washington. Washington's arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds for revoking any contract; it has no exclusion for consumer, adhesion or tort claims and no notice-format rule, and an agreement made before a dispute can't take away a party's right to a lawyer. The landlord-tenant act, though, limits what a lease may say. A rental agreement may not provide that you and the tenant have agreed to a particular arbitrator when the lease is signed, or that the tenant agrees to arbitrate disputes unless you pay the entire cost of the arbitration and the agreement is notarized; nor may it make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the act, or give up the right to bring, join or take part in a lawsuit against you or your agents, including a class action (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). A prohibited term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing one, the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). The act's own arbitration sections let a landlord and tenant agree in writing to arbitrate controversies under the act, except a dispute over whether a no-heat, no-water, no-electricity, imminently hazardous or major-appliance defect exists before the tenant has started a remedy, and except where a court action has been started that substantially affects the dispute, including any eviction (unlawful detainer) case; the arbitrator is one agreed on when the dispute arises, the hearing is held within 10 days, and the written decision within 5 days after the hearing is final and binding. Mediation by agreement is also allowed. The library's rule is to offer an arbitration clause only where state law allows one and no statute penalizes putting a prohibited term in a lease; Washington has such a penalty, and the shared clause would itself be a prohibited term here (it names an arbitrator at signing and has the landlord pay only fees above the court filing cost, without notarization). If you want arbitration, add your own clause and take advice first; at the least it must have you pay the entire cost, be notarized, leave the arbitrator to be chosen when a dispute arises, keep every right and remedy under the act (including class actions), and leave eviction cases and the act's other exceptions in court. You can also simply agree to arbitrate after a dispute arises.

title: Deposit Return After a Victim Ends the Lease in Washington
bodyText: Washington gives the deposit no special clock when a tenant ends the lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking under RCW 59.18.575 (the termination right itself is in `edu-dv-lease-termination-wa`). What the statute changes is forfeiture: whatever the lease says about forfeiting the deposit for early termination, that tenant is entitled to the return of the full deposit, subject to the good-faith rule (RCW 59.18.020) and the ordinary deposit statute (RCW 59.18.280). So you may still make lawful, documented deductions (damage beyond wear resulting from ordinary use, rent or other charges owing), and you must give the full and specific statement, the documentation and any refund within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement and the tenant's vacating (`security-deposit-return-wa`); missing the deadline costs you the full deposit (`edu-security-deposit-penalty-wa`). The same 30-day statement and refund apply where the tenant leaves first because the landlord or the landlord's employee committed sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment (RCW 59.18.575(3)(b)). Where the tenant instead changed the locks and the lease ends on the ninetieth day after the tenant's notice (RCW 59.18.575(4)(b)), the 30 days run from that ending and the tenant's vacating. If you seek reimbursement for damages from the state landlord mitigation program for a tenant who terminated this way, you may not keep any part of that tenant's deposit (RCW 59.18.575(2)(b)(ii)). Co-tenants: other tenants on the same agreement stay bound unless they are themselves victim household members (RCW 59.18.575(2)(c)). No statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (session laws of 2025 and 2026 included) says whether the deposit clock waits until every occupant has left, or how one deposit is divided between a victim who leaves and co-tenants who stay, and no published Washington case deciding it was searched for. Cautious course: within 30 days after the victim moves out, give the victim a written statement of the deposit and either refund what is due to the victim or explain in writing why it is still held; get a written agreement signed by the victim and the remaining tenants on how the deposit is to be split, and take legal advice before holding back the victim's money. Don't give the remaining tenants the victim's new address without the victim's consent.

title: Documents a Victim Gives You in Washington
bodyText: Washington's victim-protection sections ask for different documents, so match the document to the right you are being asked to honour (the rights themselves are in `edu-dv-lease-termination-wa`, `edu-dv-lockchange-wa` and `edu-dv-eviction-protection-wa`). 1. Ending the lease (RCW 59.18.575(1)): the tenant must notify you in writing that the tenant or a household member was a victim of a crime of domestic violence, sexual assault, unlawful harassment or stalking, and make available a copy of either (a) a valid protection order: a domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking or antiharassment protection order under chapter 7.105 RCW, or a valid order for protection under chapter 26.26A or chapter 26.26B RCW, the former chapters 7.90 and 26.50 RCW, RCW 9A.46.040, RCW 9A.46.050, RCW 10.99.040(2) or (3), RCW 26.09.050 or former RCW 10.14.080 (see topic `dv-protection-order-chapter-moved` for what this list leaves out); or (b) a written record of the report the tenant or household member made to a qualified third party, signed and dated by that person. Qualified third parties are, acting in their official capacity, law enforcement officers, health professionals regulated under chapter 18.120 RCW, court employees, licensed mental health professionals or other licensed counselors, trained advocates of crime victim/witness programs, and members of the clergy (RCW 59.18.570(5)). The record must state that the person reported being a victim, the time, date and place of the act, a brief description, and that the person named the alleged perpetrator, but it must not include the perpetrator's name; the statute gives a form the third party may use. The time limit runs from the incident, not from the date of the document: the request to terminate must be made within 90 days of the act, event or circumstance that gave rise to the order or report. Once a qualifying copy is made available, the tenant may terminate; the statute lets you ask for nothing more. 2. Leaving first because the landlord (including your employees) committed sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment (RCW 59.18.575(3)): the tenant may move out first and then deliver the order or record by mail, fax or personal delivery by a third party within seven days of moving out. This subsection opens by overriding any other provision of the section and states no 90-day limit of its own; whether the 90-day limit still applies is not settled by statute, so don't refuse the termination for lateness alone without advice. On your written request the third party must tell you the alleged perpetrator's name within seven days, but only if that person meets the statute's definition of landlord. 3. Changing locks because of the landlord's conduct (RCW 59.18.575(4)(a)): written notice of the lock change and the same order or record, delivered the same ways within seven days of changing or adding the locks. 4. Replacing a lock to exclude a co-tenant (RCW 59.18.585): a copy of a court order granting the tenant possession to the exclusion of one or more cotenants; the statute sets no time limit. 5. Not ending, not renewing or refusing to rent because of victim status (RCW 59.18.580(2)) needs no document at all; the bar applies to domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking (unlawful harassment is not named there). In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, the federal protections have their own documentation rules (a certification form, a third-party statement, an agency or court record, or at your discretion the tenant's own statement), which are separate from these Washington rules. Keep every document confidential (`edu-victim-confidentiality-wa`).

title: Protection Order Citations in Washington Tenant Law
bodyText: Washington moved its civil protection orders into one chapter, chapter 7.105 RCW, effective July 1, 2022, and the victim-protection sections of the landlord-tenant act were updated to match. Use these citations in any lease, notice or form that refers to protection orders. Which orders qualify for a victim's lease termination (RCW 59.18.575(1)(a)(i)): a domestic violence protection order, sexual assault protection order, stalking protection order or antiharassment protection order under chapter 7.105 RCW; or a valid order for protection under chapter 26.26A or chapter 26.26B RCW, the former chapters 7.90 and 26.50 RCW, RCW 9A.46.040, RCW 9A.46.050, RCW 10.99.040(2) or (3), RCW 26.09.050, or former RCW 10.14.080. So the older chapters still appear, by name, as former chapters. What the list does not name: chapter 7.105 RCW also provides vulnerable adult protection orders and extreme risk protection orders (RCW 7.105.100(1)(d)-(e)), and RCW 7.105.550(2) keeps valid the protection orders issued before July 1, 2022 under chapter 74.34 RCW and the former chapters 7.90, 7.92, 7.94, 10.14 and 26.50 RCW. Orders under chapter 74.34 RCW and the former chapters 7.92 and 7.94 RCW are not on the landlord-tenant list, and neither are out-of-state, tribal or military protection orders, which Washington treats as valid foreign protection orders (RCW 26.52.020). Whether such an order counts is not settled by statute, and no published Washington case deciding it was searched for. Cautious course: accept any valid court order protecting the tenant or household member, and remember the tenant can always qualify instead with a qualified third party's signed record (`edu-dv-qualifying-documents-wa`); take advice before refusing a termination over the type of order. Definitions: domestic violence and unlawful harassment take their meanings from RCW 7.105.010 (unlawful harassment also includes asking a tenant or household member for sexual favors in return for a change in or performance of lease terms), sexual assault from RCW 70.125.030 and stalking from RCW 9A.46.110 (RCW 59.18.570). The lock-change sections name no chapter: the key exception speaks of a valid protection, antiharassment or other protective order (RCW 59.18.575(4)(b)(i)), and the co-tenant lock change of a court order granting exclusive possession (RCW 59.18.585). One printing slip: the definition of landlord in RCW 59.18.570(4) refers to RCW 59.18.030 with a letter l in place of the digit 1; read it as RCW 59.18.030. No other section of chapters 59.18, 59.12 or 59.20 RCW still cites the pre-2022 chapters. The rights themselves are in `edu-dv-lease-termination-wa`, `edu-dv-lockchange-wa` and `edu-dv-eviction-protection-wa`.

title: Carpet Cleaning Charges in Washington
bodyText: You may not take carpet cleaning out of a Washington tenant's deposit unless you document wear to the carpet beyond wear resulting from ordinary use of the premises (RCW 59.18.280(1)(c)(ii)). This applies to every deposit taken under a residential lease covered by chapter 59.18 RCW. So a lease term that automatically charges a fixed carpet-cleaning amount against the deposit at move-out, or that makes the tenant pay for professional carpet cleaning whatever the carpet's condition, can't be enforced against the deposit: it would waive RCW 59.18.280(1)(c)(ii), and any lease provision waiving a section of the chapter is unenforceable (RCW 59.18.230(1)(a)). A lease providing that the tenant agrees to waive rights under the chapter is a prohibited term, and knowingly using one exposes you to the tenant's actual damages, statutory damages of up to two times the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (RCW 59.18.230(2)(a), (3)). Nor may you bill the tenant separately, send to collections or report to a screening service any charge for wear resulting from ordinary use or not backed by the required documentation (RCW 59.18.280(3)(b)). What you can do: (1) record the carpets' condition and cleanliness in the signed move-in checklist, which must cover carpets and other flooring (RCW 59.18.260(2)(b); `edu-condition-checklist-wa`); (2) at move-out, document any stains, burns or soiling beyond ordinary use (photographs help) and deduct only the reasonable, documented cost of cleaning or repairing it, with copies of estimates or invoices, or for your own staff's work the materials receipt and the time and hourly rate, in the 30-day statement (RCW 59.18.280(1)(b); `edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`); for an item damaged only in part, deduct no more than the cost of the damaged portion (RCW 59.18.280(1)(c)(iv)). Alternatively, you may charge a nonrefundable cleaning fee at the start of the tenancy if the written lease clearly states that it is nonrefundable; it is not a deposit and the tenant may ask to pay it in installments (RCW 59.18.285, RCW 59.18.610; `nonrefundable-fees-wa`). If you collect one, the library's deposit clause (`security-deposit-use-wa`) does not charge the tenant for normal cleaning as well. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) lets a landlord require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, or sets an age or condition schedule for carpet; the library therefore offers no professional-cleaning clause. If you want one, have it reviewed first, and never apply it to the deposit without documented excess wear.

title: Preset Deposit Charges in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) lets a lease pre-set the amounts you will deduct from a deposit for cleaning, repair or replacement. Washington instead ties every damage deduction to documents. With the 30-day statement you must include copies of estimates received or invoices paid that reasonably substantiate the damage charges; where you or your employee do the work, a copy of the bill, invoice or receipt for materials (or, for stock on hand, a vendor price list or other vendor document), and a statement of the time spent and the reasonable hourly rate charged (RCW 59.18.280(1)(b); `security-deposit-return-wa`, `edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`). And you may not withhold for wear resulting from ordinary use, for carpet cleaning without documented excess wear (`edu-carpet-cleaning-wa`), for items whose condition the move-in checklist did not reasonably document, or more than the cost of repairing or replacing the damaged portion of a partly damaged item (RCW 59.18.280(1)(c)). A schedule in the lease that fixes what you will charge regardless of the actual, documented cost would let you keep more than the statute allows, and a lease term that waives part of the chapter is unenforceable (RCW 59.18.230(1)(a)). What the lease must contain is the terms and conditions under which the deposit may be withheld, including that it may be used for damage the tenant is responsible for (RCW 59.18.260(1)); the library's deposit clause does this (`security-deposit-use-wa`). The refund is due under the terms and conditions of the rental agreement (RCW 59.18.280(1)(a)), but those terms work only within the statute's limits, which apply to any deposit. Charges unrelated to damage, such as rent or other charges owing, are outside the checklist and documentation requirements (RCW 59.18.280(4)), but they must be charges the lease or the law already lawfully imposes. If you want a set cleaning charge, the lawful route is a nonrefundable cleaning fee stated as nonrefundable in the written lease (RCW 59.18.285; `nonrefundable-fees-wa`); a tenant who paid one may not be charged for normal cleaning (RCW 59.18.130(10)). Nothing in the statute stops you telling a tenant your usual hourly rate, but the library offers no price-list clause: each deduction must still rest on the documents above and be no more than the actual, reasonable cost, and a list in the lease is easily read as a pre-set charge. A landlord who wants one should have it reviewed first.

title: No Surrender Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds in Washington
bodyText: In Washington, returning the deposit does not depend on the tenant giving you advance notice of surrender or a forwarding address. Within 30 days after the rental agreement ends and the tenant vacates (or within 30 days after you learn the tenant abandoned the unit), you must give the full and specific statement, the documentation and any refund; you comply by handing them to the tenant or mailing them first-class to the tenant's last known address within the 30 days (RCW 59.18.280(1)(a); `security-deposit-return-wa`). No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) lets a lease make advance notice of surrender, a move-out notice or a forwarding address a condition of the refund. A lease term that does so would waive part of RCW 59.18.280 and is unenforceable (RCW 59.18.230(1)(a)); a rental agreement providing that the tenant waives rights or remedies under the chapter is a prohibited term, with damages of up to two times the monthly rent if you knowingly use it (RCW 59.18.230(2)(a), (3)). The library therefore offers no surrender-notice condition. Notice to end the tenancy is a separate rule: a month-to-month or other periodic tenant ends the tenancy by written notice of at least 20 days before the end of a rental period (RCW 59.18.200(1)(a)). If a tenant leaves without ending the tenancy properly, any rent the tenant still owes, for example under the abandonment rule (RCW 59.18.310(1)), may be withheld from the deposit as rent owing and listed in the statement (RCW 59.18.280(4)); the deposit itself can't be forfeited for lack of notice. Ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out (the library's return clause does), and if none is given, mail to the last known address. The same 30-day statement and refund apply when a tenant ends the tenancy because of an unrepaired defect (RCW 59.18.090(1)), another tenant's threatening behavior (RCW 59.18.352), or as a victim (`edu-dv-deposit-timing-wa`), and after a tenant's death the statement and refund go to the tenant representative (RCW 59.18.595).

title: Deposit-Setting Standards in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no rule requiring a landlord who uses differing standards to set deposit amounts to post those standards or hand them to applicants before signing, whatever the number of units. No statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) requires it; city ordinances were not searched, so check any local deposit rules where the property is. The Washington rules that do touch how you set a deposit: (1) if screening leads you to approve an applicant only on condition of an increased deposit, that is an adverse action, and you must give the applicant a written adverse action notice stating the reasons in the statutory format, which lists 'Residency requires an increased deposit' (RCW 59.18.257(1)(c)) as a condition; the screening criteria themselves must be disclosed in writing or posted before you obtain any information (RCW 59.18.257(1); `edu-tenant-screening-wa`); (2) you may not set a deposit differently because of a protected characteristic, which would discriminate in the terms or conditions of a rental (RCW 49.60.222(1)(b); `edu-fair-housing-wa`), and for a tenant with a disability who uses a dog guide or service animal you may enforce your standard cleaning or damage deposit only if you enforce it equally on all tenants, and may not add a pet deposit (WAC 162-38-100(4)-(5)); (3) if you offer a fee in lieu of a deposit, you must offer it to every approved applicant without regard to income, credit score or the other listed factors (RCW 59.18.670(1)(c); `fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). Washington sets no cap on the deposit amount under chapter 59.18 RCW (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-wa`), but a holding deposit is capped at 25 percent of the first month's rent (RCW 59.18.253(3); `edu-holding-deposit-wa`), the tenant may ask to pay deposits in installments (RCW 59.18.610; `edu-deposit-installments-wa`), and no deposit may be taken without a written lease stating the withholding terms and a signed move-in checklist (RCW 59.18.260). Good practice, not a statutory duty: write down the standards you use to set deposits, apply them consistently, and keep the record with your screening criteria.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no expedited deposit procedure. The deposit statute sets an outer limit: within 30 days after the rental agreement ends and the tenant vacates (or after you learn of an abandonment) you must give the full and specific statement, the documentation and any refund (RCW 59.18.280(1)(a); `security-deposit-return-wa`). Nothing stops you doing it sooner, and no tenant request is needed to do so. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) authorizes an administrative or processing fee for handling the deposit early or at all, unlike Virginia's statute. The library therefore offers no expedited-processing fee clause. Whether such a fee could lawfully be charged is not settled by statute; the statement and refund are your own duty under RCW 59.18.280, deductions are limited to what that section and the lease lawfully allow, and a lease term that waives part of the chapter is unenforceable (RCW 59.18.230(1)(a)). If you want one, take advice first and never take it out of the deposit without the tenant's separate written agreement. Disputes over the deposit go to court or, if agreed, arbitration; in the tenant's action to recover the deposit the prevailing party recovers the cost of suit or arbitration including a reasonable attorneys' fee (RCW 59.18.280(2); `edu-security-deposit-penalty-wa`). The district court's small claims department hears claims for money of up to $10,000 brought by a natural person, or $5,000 in other cases (RCW 12.40.010). Faster disposition after a tenant's death has its own procedure: the statement and any refund go to the tenant representative after the representative removes the property (RCW 59.18.595; `edu-tenant-death-wa`).

title: Nonrefundable Fees: No Separate Notice in Washington
bodyText:
For an ordinary nonrefundable fee (a cleaning fee, for example), Washington requires no separate notice, separate document or initials. What it requires is that the rental agreement be in writing and clearly specify that the fee is nonrefundable (RCW 59.18.285); the library's clause lists each fee, its amount and purpose, and says it is nonrefundable (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`).

Two consequences follow from RCW 59.18.285: if you collect a nonrefundable fee without a written rental agreement, you are liable to the tenant for the amount of the fees collected; and if the written agreement does not specify that the fee is nonrefundable, the fee is treated as a refundable deposit, with the checklist, trust-account and 30-day statement rules that go with it (RCW 59.18.260, RCW 59.18.270, RCW 59.18.280).

Money that is nonrefundable may never be called a deposit or part of a deposit, so don't use the words "nonrefundable deposit".

The one Washington rule that does call for a separate step is the fee in lieu of a security deposit: it may be entirely or partially nonrefundable only if that is disclosed in the lease and separately acknowledged by the tenant, and the statutory disclosure form must be given with the lease and any renewal that includes the option (RCW 59.18.670(1)(f)(iii), (2)(a); `fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`).

Related: a fee to hold a unit after you offer it needs a receipt and a written statement of the conditions under which you may keep it, given immediately on payment (RCW 59.18.253(2); `edu-holding-deposit-wa`); on written request the tenant may pay nonrefundable fees in installments (RCW 59.18.610; `edu-deposit-installments-wa`); and a tenant who paid a nonrefundable cleaning fee may not be charged for normal cleaning at move-out (RCW 59.18.130(10)).

Apart from the fee in lieu of a deposit, no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) requires a separate notice, separate signature or initials for a nonrefundable fee.

title: Inspection Notices and Deposit Penalties in Washington
bodyText: Washington does not require you to offer a move-out inspection, to tell the tenant of a right to attend one, or to give notice of one, so there is no penalty or deposit forfeiture for leaving such a notice out. No statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles (2025 and 2026 session laws included) creates one. The inspection-related penalties Washington does have: (1) The move-in checklist. You may collect no deposit unless the rental agreement is in writing and you give the tenant, at the start of the tenancy, a written checklist or statement of the unit's condition and cleanliness, signed and dated by both of you, with a copy to the tenant (and one free replacement copy on request). Collect a deposit without the checklist and you are liable to the tenant for the amount of the deposit, and the prevailing party may recover court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees (RCW 59.18.260(2)-(5); `edu-condition-checklist-wa`). At move-out you also can't deduct for repair or replacement of fixtures, equipment, appliances or furnishings whose condition the checklist did not reasonably document (RCW 59.18.280(1)(c)(iii)). (2) The move-out statement. Miss the 30-day statement, documentation and refund and you owe the full deposit, lose your claims and defenses in the tenant's suit, and risk up to twice the deposit for an intentional refusal (RCW 59.18.280(2); `edu-security-deposit-penalty-wa`). (3) Entering to inspect during the tenancy. Give at least two days' written notice stating the date and exact time or the earliest and latest times, and a telephone number for objections or rescheduling, except in an emergency or where impracticable; a landlord who keeps violating the access rules after one good-faith written notice of the violation is liable for up to $100 for each later violation, plus costs and reasonable attorneys' fees to the prevailing party (RCW 59.18.150(6), (8); `landlords-access-wa`). For a city rental-inspection program, your written notice must also give the inspector's company or name and tell the tenant of the right to see the inspector's identification (RCW 59.18.125(7)(a); `edu-rental-inspection-wa`). (4) The state landlord mitigation program pays damage claims only if the unit was inspected at the start of the tenancy by both you and the tenant and a detailed written move-in inspection report was prepared and signed by both (RCW 43.31.605(2)(a)). Good practice, not a statutory duty: invite the tenant to a walk-through before move-out, photograph the condition, and never let the walk-through delay the 30-day statement.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules has a general rule barring a residential landlord from charging a fee for a service, amenity or utility the tenant does not actually receive. Several specific rules reach the same ground, and they apply to every tenancy under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) Screening: you may charge an applicant for the costs you incurred in obtaining a tenant screening report only if you first gave the written or posted screening notice; if you screen yourself you may charge only your actual costs, no more than the customary charge of a screening service in the area; and if you say you accept a comprehensive reusable screening report, you may not charge the applicant for pulling your own report (`edu-application-fees-wa`). (2) You may not charge any fee or deposit for putting someone on a waiting list. (3) If a tenant paid a nonrefundable cleaning fee, you may not also charge for normal cleaning at move-out; a nonrefundable fee must be written into the lease as nonrefundable or it is treated as a refundable deposit (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`). (4) You may not charge any fee for the use, inspection or installation of a tenant's portable cooling device (you may charge rent for a unit you supply, and damages) (`portable-cooling-device-wa`). (5) A recurring service or amenity charge identified in the lease for use and occupancy is rent, so it goes on the rent increase notice and counts toward the statewide increase limit (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`); a one-time fee is not rent and the tenant's right to stay can't be conditioned on paying it. Beyond these, a charge for something you did not provide is tested under the Consumer Protection Act's general ban on unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce (`edu-consumer-protection-act-wa`); whether a particular fee crosses that line is a question for case law. Cautious course: charge a service, amenity or utility fee only for something the tenant actually gets, describe each one in the lease, and stop or credit the fee for any period you do not provide it. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Cap on Late Fees in Washington Apart From the Eviction Limit
bodyText: This is a pointer: the rules on late fees are in `late-fee-wa` (the clause) and `edu-late-fee-wa`.
