In short, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) Washington sets no dollar or percentage cap on the late fee itself. What it does limit: (1) you may not charge a late fee for rent paid within five days after its due date, and a lease term agreeing to one is a prohibited term (knowing use exposes you to actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees); once rent is more than five days late, the fee may run from the first day after the due date; (2) in a nonpayment eviction, the judgment, and the amount a tenant pays to be reinstated, may include late fees only if they are due under the lease and total no more than $75; (3) late fees were barred on rent that came due between March 1, 2020 and six months after the eviction moratorium ended (a closed period). Two other Washington late-fee figures do not reach dwelling tenancies: mobile home lot agreements entered into or renewed on or after May 7, 2025 carry percentage caps (2%, then 3%, then 5% of total rent per month for consecutive past-due months) under chapter 59.20 RCW, which is outside this library; and the self-service storage statute deems $20 or 20% of monthly rent reasonable for a storage unit, but that chapter forbids residential use of a storage facility and has no dwelling counterpart. Because no statute caps the fee, a late fee is also open to challenge in court as an unenforceable penalty if it is far out of line with your actual loss. Cautious course: set a flat fee you could justify as a reasonable estimate of your cost of late payment, never charge it in the first five days, and expect a court to allow no more than $75 of it in an eviction judgment.

title: Washington Money Limits for Rentals
bodyText: A summary of the money figures Washington sets for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW); each has its own row. WHAT YOU MAY CHARGE: (1) Holding fee or deposit to secure a unit: no more than 25% of the first month's rent, credited to rent or the deposit if the applicant moves in (`edu-holding-deposit-wa`). (2) Screening: only the cost of the screening report, or if you screen yourself your actual costs up to what a local screening service customarily charges, and only after the screening notice; no waiting-list fee (`edu-application-fees-wa`). (3) Rent increases: none in the first 12 months of a tenancy, and in any 12-month period no more than 7% plus the Seattle-area CPI, or 10%, whichever is less, unless an exemption applies; rent for the same unit may differ by no more than 5% between lease types (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`, `edu-lease-type-parity-wa`). (4) Late fees: none for rent paid within five days of its due date; no cap on the amount otherwise, but an eviction judgment or reinstatement may include no more than $75 in late fees, and a tenant reinstated after judgment pays $50 more for each earlier post-judgment reinstatement in the past 12 months (`edu-late-fee-limit-wa`, `edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). (5) Fee in lieu of a security deposit: no more than the cost of obtaining and administering the insurance it buys (`fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). (6) Installments of deposits, nonrefundable fees and last month's rent: no fee, interest or other cost for choosing installments (`edu-deposit-installments-wa`). (7) A dishonored check: a reasonable handling fee; if it stays unpaid 15 days after the statutory notice of dishonor, 12% interest and collection costs of up to $40 or the check amount, whichever is less, unless the instrument provides otherwise; in a court action on the check, reasonable attorneys' fees plus three times the check amount or $300, whichever is less (`edu-returned-payments-wa`). (8) Interest: 12% a year applies to a loan or forbearance where no other rate is agreed in writing (`edu-unpaid-damages-interest-wa`). (9) Attorneys' fees in an eviction: none after a default judgment, and none where the rent awarded is no more than two months' rent or $1,200, whichever is greater (`edu-attorney-fees-wa`). (10) Storage after an eviction: sale proceeds applied to drayage and storage may not exceed the actual or reasonable costs, whichever is less. NO STATE CAP: the security deposit (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-wa`), pet deposits, fees and pet rent (`edu-pet-fees-wa`), and the size of a late fee or other lease fee. Some cities set their own limits; check local ordinances. WHAT A VIOLATION CAN COST YOU (the main statutory awards): a prohibited lease term knowingly used, up to twice the monthly rent; keeping a tenant's belongings after a written demand, up to $500 a day capped at $5,000 if intentional; an unlawful holding fee, up to twice the fee; a screening-notice violation, up to $100; intentionally refusing the deposit statement or refund, up to twice the deposit; a utility shutoff, up to $100 a day; repeated entry violations after written notice, up to $100 each; refusing installments, one month's rent; a source-of-income violation, up to 4.5 times the monthly rent; a wrongful eviction, the greater of damages or three times the monthly rent; a fee-in-lieu violation, up to twice the monthly rent; an unlawful rent increase, the excess plus up to three months of the unlawful amount, and Attorney General penalties of up to $7,500 per violation; knowingly renting a condemned unit, the greater of three months' rent or treble damages, and relocation assistance of the greater of $2,000 or three months' rent. Most of these also carry attorneys' fees. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) have their own caps and are outside this library.

title: Listing Fees in a Washington Lease
bodyText: Washington has no statute that requires a lease to carry a single list of every fee, and none that requires a labelled all-in monthly total in the lease. What it does require, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) An obligation binds the tenant only if it does not violate the act or other law and was brought to the tenant's attention at the time of initial occupancy, so put every fee you intend to charge in the lease (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). (2) A new rule, including a new fee, takes effect only after 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant, and then only at the end of the lease term or sooner if the tenant agrees; a rent increase is never a rule (`edu-term-change-notice-wa`). (3) A nonrefundable fee needs a written lease that clearly says the fee is nonrefundable, or it is treated as a refundable deposit (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`); list upfront amounts in `due-at-signing-wa`. (4) Recurring charges identified in the lease for use and occupancy, such as utilities, parking or pet rent, are rent: they go on the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice, which itemizes rent, utilities and other recurring charges and states a total amount due, and any increase needs 90 days' notice on the state form, which states the new total of rent and other recurring charges, and counts toward the increase limit (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). (5) You may not make the payment terms or other material conditions more burdensome for a month-to-month agreement than for a longer or shorter one, or the reverse (`edu-lease-type-parity-wa`). (6) Payments go to rent first, before late fees, damages or other fees (`application-of-payments-wa`). No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules caps your markup on a service a third party bills (gas and electricity resale is limited by the utility commission rules in `edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`), bars a fee for maintaining common areas, or sets a charge for accepting a partial payment. Cautious course: list each fee in the lease with its amount, what it is for and when it is due, mark nonrefundable fees as nonrefundable, and treat any recurring fee as rent. Local ordinances may require more; check them.

title: Passing Government Fines to a Tenant in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules generally bars you from passing a government fine to a tenant, and none makes a tenant liable to you for a fine or a nuisance-abatement cost by default (there is no rule like Colorado's that makes the occupant liable "unless the lease provides otherwise"). The rules that do bear on it, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) The tenant must comply with the obligations that municipal, county and state codes impose on tenants, and must not damage the premises or let family, invitees or anyone under the tenant's control do so; you have no repair duty, and the tenant has no remedy, for a defective condition caused by the conduct of the tenant, the tenant's family, an invitee or another person acting under the tenant's control (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`, `edu-tenant-statutory-duties-wa`). (2) Some fines fall on the tenant directly: a tenant who fails to maintain the smoke detection device, including batteries, faces a fine of up to $200 (`edu-alarm-duties-wa`). (3) Clean buildings standard: if you own a covered building (for a multifamily building, generally one whose multifamily, nonresidential, hotel, motel and dormitory floor area exceeds 20,000 gross square feet, excluding parking), penalties for failing to document compliance may not be passed along to tenants, so long as tenants give access to utility usage data and physical spaces and respond to your needs in meeting the standard. (4) An association may fine a tenant and the unit owner after notice and an opportunity to be heard; the shared `hoa-compliance` clause covers that (`edu-hoa-wa`). (5) A lease may not make the tenant agree to the exculpation or limitation of any liability of the landlord arising under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its costs. A fine imposed on you as owner is a liability arising under law, so a lease clause that simply makes the tenant reimburse every fine risks being a prohibited term (knowing use exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent); whether a reimbursement clause limited to fines the tenant's own breach caused escapes that bar is a question only case law could settle, and none was searched. For that reason the library offers no fine-reimbursement clause for Washington. You may still recover, as damages, a loss the tenant's breach of a statutory or lease duty actually caused; it is not rent, can't condition the tenant's right to stay, and comes out of a deposit only with the itemized statement. If you want a clause of your own, have a lawyer draft it to the tenant's breach and to the persons listed in (1).

title: Passing Local Government Fees Through to Tenants in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules authorizes or bars passing a local government fee, such as a rental registration, business licence or inspection fee, through to a tenant of a dwelling under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW). How the charge is set up decides which rules apply: (1) A recurring or periodic charge identified in the lease for use and occupancy is rent. A yearly or monthly registration-fee reimbursement written into the lease is therefore rent: it goes on the 14-day notice, can't be raised during the first 12 months or before a fixed term ends, needs 90 days' notice on the state form to increase, and counts toward the statewide increase limit (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). A clause letting you bill a new or higher fee on short notice during the tenancy would get around those rules, so the library offers none. (2) A one-time charge is not rent: it binds the tenant only if it was in the lease at move-in (or added as a new rule after 30 days' written notice, effective at the end of the term or sooner if the tenant agrees), and the tenant's right to stay can't be conditioned on paying it (`edu-required-fees-wa`). (3) If you own a building covered by the state clean buildings standard (for multifamily, generally over 20,000 gross square feet), penalties for failing to document compliance may not be passed along to tenants who cooperate (`edu-governmental-fines-wa`). Simplest course: build any recurring government fee into the rent you set at the start of the tenancy. Local registration and inspection programs are in `edu-rental-inspection-wa` and `edu-no-landlord-registration-wa`; check your city's ordinance, which may itself bar or limit a pass-through. Mobile home communities, where the state registration assessment may be partly charged to tenants, are under chapter 59.20 RCW and outside this library.

title: Charging for a Disabled Smoke or CO Alarm in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no statute or rule that sets or authorizes a fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm; no such provision was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles (including the state fire marshal's smoke detector rules and the building codes), the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. What applies instead: (1) Duties. You install smoke detection devices in every rental dwelling unit and make sure they work before each new occupancy; the tenant maintains them, including batteries, as the manufacturer specifies, and maintains any carbon monoxide alarm the same way (`edu-alarm-duties-wa`). The tenant also may not damage, impair or remove any part of the dwelling or its equipment, or let family, invitees or anyone under the tenant's control do so. (2) Who pays for repair or replacement. The state fire marshal's rule says the actual costs of maintenance, repair or replacement of smoke detection devices are as agreed beforehand by the occupant and owner; the required fire safety notice in the lease (`fire-safety-notice-wa`) records that choice. (3) Damage. If the tenant, the tenant's family, an invitee or another person acting under the tenant's control removes, disables or damages a detector, you may recover the reasonable cost of repair or replacement under `tenant-caused-damage-wa`; it is not rent, can't condition the tenant's right to stay, and comes out of a deposit only with the itemized statement and documentation. (4) Penalties fall on the person, not through the lease: an owner or tenant who fails to comply with the smoke detector statute faces a fine of up to $200, and willfully tampering with a private fire alarm apparatus is a misdemeanor (whether that criminal statute reaches a single smoke alarm in a unit is for the courts). A fixed tampering fee is not offered: no statute authorizes one, a pre-set charge for breach could be challenged as a penalty, and deposit deductions must rest on actual, documented cost. If you want one, have a lawyer draft it.

title: Collection Fees and Collection Agency Charges in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules authorizes a landlord to charge a residential tenant a collection fee, or to pass on a collection agency's charges, for unpaid rent or other money owed under a lease. The library offers no collection-fee clause for Washington, for these reasons: (1) A lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorneys' fees except as the landlord-tenant act authorizes and a court awards (`edu-attorney-fees-wa`). (2) A licensed collection agency may collect, beyond the principal of a claim, only allowable interest, collection costs or handling fees expressly authorized by statute and, in a lawsuit, attorneys' fees and taxable court costs. Contingent collection fees set by contract are allowed only on a commercial claim (one not primarily for personal, family or household purposes), capped at 35%; a residential tenancy debt is for household purposes, so an agency cannot add a contractual collection fee to it. The agency also may not suggest that fees have been or may be added when the law does not allow them. One statute does authorize charges: on a dishonored check assigned to a collection agency, a reasonable handling fee and, 33 days after the statutory notice of dishonor, 12% interest and a cost of collection of $40 or the check amount, whichever is less (`edu-returned-payments-wa`). (3) You may not submit for collection by any third-party agency damages for ordinary wear, or damages not documented the way the deposit statement requires (`edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`); for tenancies whose rental agreements began on or after July 23, 2023, a suit for more than the deposit must be filed within three years after the tenancy ends or the tenant abandons; and a tenant who paid a fee in lieu of a deposit has extra collection protections (`fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). (4) The tenant's right to stay can't be conditioned on paying anything but rent (apart from the reinstatement amounts in a nonpayment eviction), and you may not threaten eviction for nonpossessory charges (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). (5) From January 1, 2027, a default judgment in a suit to collect a consumer debt (not an eviction or other action for possession) requires a complaint that itemizes the outstanding balance and any fees or costs and carries a statutory consumer notice; on our reading a post-move-out suit for unpaid rent or damages is a consumer debt suit. If you collect your own debt in your own name you are not a collection agency, but collecting it under another name that suggests a third party is collecting makes you one. A collection-fee clause is not barred by name, so you may add one of your own with a lawyer's advice, but expect it to be limited by the rules above.

title: Fees for Serving Notices or Filing an Eviction in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules authorizes a lease charge for serving a notice (such as a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice, a 10-day comply-or-vacate notice or a termination notice) or for preparing or filing an eviction, and the library offers no such clause for Washington. The reasons, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) The 14-day notice may demand only rent, utilities and other recurring charges identified in the lease; a notice-service fee is not rent, so the tenant's right to stay can't be conditioned on it, and you may not threaten eviction over it (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`, `edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). (2) In a nonpayment eviction the judgment may include the rent due, late fees due under the lease up to $75 in total, statutory costs and any attorneys' fees the court awards; a tenant reinstated before or within five court days after judgment pays the rent, court costs incurred to that point, those late fees and any awarded attorneys' fees (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). Court costs, such as filing fees and the fee for serving the summons, are awarded by the court to the prevailing party under the general costs statute, not by the lease. (3) A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees except as the landlord-tenant act authorizes and a court awards, and the court may not award them after a default or where the rent awarded is two months' rent or $1,200 or less, whichever is greater (`edu-attorney-fees-wa`). A fee for a notice or an eviction filing would work as a way around these limits. (4) Any agreement made in an eviction case that requires the tenant to pay amounts beyond these limits is void. Because no statute fixes a charge for breach, a pre-set fee could also be challenged in court as an unenforceable penalty. A notice-service fee is not barred by name, so you may add a clause of your own with a lawyer's advice, but it can't be collected through the notice or the eviction judgment beyond the amounts above. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no statute that, like Colorado's, expressly bars a late fee on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays; none was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. Four rules still decide most cases: (1) Due-date change for tenants on monthly assistance. When late fees can be charged after rent is due, a tenant may propose in writing moving the rent due date to a different day of the month, and you must agree if the tenant shows that his or her primary source of income is a regular, monthly source of governmental assistance that arrives after the due date in the lease; the new date can be no more than five days after the old one. This is separate from any request for a reasonable accommodation (`edu-rent-due-date-change-wa`). (2) Housing Choice Vouchers. Under the federal voucher rules the family is not responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, the housing agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and you may not end the tenancy during the lease term for the agency's nonpayment; so a late fee may be charged only on the family's own share, and only if your lease and the HUD tenancy addendum allow it (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`). Other subsidy programs have their own rules; follow the program contract. (3) Source of income. You may not make any distinction in the price, terms, conditions, fees or privileges of a tenancy because a tenant's income comes from a subsidy, housing assistance, public assistance or similar program, so a late-fee policy that treats assisted tenants worse is barred (`edu-source-of-income-wa`). (4) Rental assistance pledges. Before a 14-day pay-or-vacate notice expires you must accept a pledge of emergency rental assistance from a government or nonprofit for the full rent owed, and in a nonpayment eviction the tenant can be reinstated with assistance funds; late fees in a judgment or reinstatement are capped at $75 (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). The general late-fee rules (no fee in the first five days) are in `edu-late-fee-wa`.

title: Passing Property Tax Increases to Tenants in Washington
bodyText: For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), no Washington statute authorizes a lease clause that passes property tax or insurance increases to the tenant during the term, and the rent rules stand in the way of one; the library offers no such clause for Washington. A share of taxes or insurance that the lease makes the tenant pay on a regular schedule is, on our reading, rent: rent means the recurring and periodic charges identified in the rental agreement for the use and occupancy of the premises. An increase in rent can't take effect before the end of the lease term (for most tenancies), needs at least 90 days' written notice on the state form, is barred during the first 12 months of a tenancy, and counts toward the statewide limit of 7% plus CPI or 10%, whichever is less, unless an exemption applies (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). A clause that raises the tenant's payment mid-term when taxes rise would waive those rules, which makes it unenforceable, and knowingly using a lease with a prohibited term can cost statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent. (For a subsidized tenancy whose rent is based on the tenant's income, 30 days' notice applies and an increase may take effect sooner than the end of the term only by mutual consent.) What you can do: set the rent for each new term with your expected tax and insurance costs in mind, and raise it at renewal within the limit and with proper notice. No Washington rule like Massachusetts' or New Hampshire's lets you deduct a tax share from the deposit. If your lease makes you responsible for property taxes and the tenant ends up paying them, the tenant may recover the amount from you with 10% interest or deduct it from rent. Mobile home lot agreements, which may carry a pro rata property-tax escalation clause, are under chapter 59.20 RCW and outside this library.

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilled Utility Charges in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules caps what a residential landlord may charge a tenant for utilities the landlord buys and rebills, sets rules for a utility allowance with a tenant-paid overage, or limits an administrative fee on utility billing. What does apply, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) Utility charges identified in the lease as recurring charges are rent: they go on the 14-day notice, and an increase needs 90 days' notice on the state form and counts toward the statewide limit (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). An allowance with a monthly overage the tenant repays is, on our reading, rent too, and whether a fluctuating overage is an increase in rent each month is unsettled; the library therefore offers no allowance-and-overage clause for Washington (cautious course: set the billing method and any fixed charge in the lease at the start and do not change it during the term). (2) Utility commission rules limit reselling: gas from a regulated utility may never be remetered or submetered by a customer for resale, electricity may be resold only if the utility's tariff allows it, and an electric utility may refuse to serve a master meter in a multi-unit building where tenants control much of their own use and individual meters are cost-effective (`edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`). The commission does not regulate a landlord that supplies water only to its own tenants as part of renting. (3) You may never intentionally cause a tenant's water, heat, electricity or gas to be shut off except briefly for repairs, and landlord-billed electric or water service carries heat-alert protections (`edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`). (4) Where a city or town utility serves the rental through one account for several units, bills you at an address other than the rental, or has been told a tenant lives there, and you fail to pay for the electricity or water, a tenant who puts service in his or her own name may deduct the reasonable charges paid from rent. Local ordinances may limit rebilling or fees; check them. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No State Incentive for Renting to Veterans in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no state program that pays landlords an incentive, guarantee or bonus for renting to veterans or servicemembers; none was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws (including the 2025 and 2026 budgets) or the saved court rules. The state's general landlord program, the landlord mitigation program run by the Department of Commerce, reimburses landlords for certain damages, unpaid judgments and installment defaults, but it is not tied to veterans (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). Local programs and federal veterans housing programs administered through housing agencies may exist; check with them. Rules that bear on renting to veterans and servicemembers: (1) Fair housing law makes it an unfair practice to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of honorably discharged veteran or military status (`edu-fair-housing-wa`). Whether offering only veterans a rent concession counts as discrimination against other applicants is not settled by statute and no case was searched; if you offer one, get advice and keep it consistent with fair housing law (`edu-rent-concession-wa`). (2) You may not refuse to rent or set different terms because the rent will be paid with veterans benefits or another source of income (`edu-source-of-income-wa`). (3) Servicemembers have their own termination rights under state and federal law (`edu-servicemember-rights-wa`).

title: Collecting Rent Apart From the Repair Duty in Washington
bodyText: This topic is about receiving rent (the uniform act's rule that no lease, assignment, deed, trust deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the landlord's duty to maintain), not about rent receipts, which are in `edu-rent-receipts-wa`. Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) left that uniform-act rule out: no such provision was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. Other Washington rules cover most of the same ground: (1) Your repair and habitability duties can't be waived in a lease or any other agreement; the only exception is a written exemption agreement that may not appear in a standard form lease and needs, among other conditions, written approval by the county prosecutor, the Attorney General's consumer protection division or the tenant's attorney (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). (2) "Landlord" includes the owner, lessor or sublessor and anyone designated as the owner's representative, such as an agent, resident manager or property manager, so whoever collects rent in that role is acting as landlord (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). (3) A lender holding an assignment of rents under a deed of trust may not demand or collect rent from a tenant of a single-family home, or of a unit in a building with fewer than five residential units, without first giving the tenant a court order or your written consent; a tenant who paid the lender under such an order or consent has a defense to a nonpayment eviction. (4) A sale doesn't end the tenancy, and deposits move to the new landlord (`edu-sale-or-management-change-wa`). Whether a lender, receiver or buyer of the rent stream that collects rent takes on the landlord's repair duties is not settled by statute. Cautious course: keep the repair duty with whoever collects the rent, and don't sign or draft an agreement that separates them without advice.

title: Rent Escalation Clauses in Washington
bodyText: This is a pointer: Washington's rent increase rules are in `edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa` and `edu-term-change-notice-wa`, and they leave no room for an escalation clause in a lease under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW). An increase in rent, including a scheduled step-up or an index-based adjustment written into the lease, can't take effect before the current term ends, needs at least 90 days' written notice on the state form, is barred during the first 12 months of the tenancy, and is capped at 7% plus CPI or 10% (whichever is less) in any 12-month period unless an exemption applies; rent includes recurring fees. So the library offers no mid-term or scheduled rent increase clause for Washington; set the rent for each term at the start and raise it, if at all, at renewal with proper notice. (Income-based subsidized tenancies use 30 days' notice and may change sooner only by mutual consent.) How the other states' questions come out in Washington: retaliation protection doesn't depend on a lease clause. A rent increase within 90 days after a tenant's good-faith complaint to a government agency or assertion of rights is presumed retaliatory, but no presumption arises if your increase notice states reasonable grounds, and a complaint made within 90 days after your notice of an increase is presumed not to be in good faith (`edu-retaliation-wa`). Your notice period is fixed by statute, not measured against the notice the lease asks of the tenant. Mobile home lot agreements, which may carry certain escalation clauses, are under chapter 59.20 RCW and outside this library.

title: No Rent Deposit Needed to Defend an Eviction in Washington
bodyText: In a Washington eviction under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), a tenant does not have to pay rent into court, or into the court registry, to defend, and does not have to bring a counterclaim: at the show-cause hearing the tenant may answer orally or in writing and assert any legal or equitable defense or set-off arising out of the tenancy (except that no set-off is allowed where the eviction is for drug-related activity). No statute or rule in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved state and local court rules requires a rent deposit as the price of a defense, or of a continuance. Paying into court comes up only as the tenant's option: (1) If you get a writ of restitution before final judgment in a nonpayment case (which requires you to post a bond the court sets), the tenant may stay the writ within three days after it is served by paying into court or to you, as the court directs, all rent found due and then the monthly rent each month until final judgment. (2) In a nonpayment case the tenant may pay into court or to you the rent due, court costs incurred at the time, late fees due under the lease up to $75 and any awarded attorneys' fees, before judgment or within five court days after it (longer with a rental assistance pledge letter), and the tenancy is reinstated (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). (3) A tenant using the rent escrow remedy for a certified dangerous condition pays rent to an escrow, not to court; while the tenant keeps paying the full rent into escrow on time you may not start a nonpayment eviction, and in your action to release the funds the tenant's counterclaim is limited to diminished rental value for the conditions in the tenant's notice. A tenant who files for bankruptcy after a judgment for possession may have to deposit rent with the bankruptcy court to keep the automatic stay.

title: When Washington Stops You Collecting Full Rent
bodyText: Rent is due at the times and in the amounts the lease sets, without any demand, but before you can evict for nonpayment you must serve the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`). Washington has no general statute barring you from demanding rent for a unit in poor repair, but under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) these rules stop or reduce what you may collect: (1) Condemned or unlawful units: once a code agency notifies you that a unit is condemned or unlawful to occupy, you may not enter into a rental agreement for it until the conditions are corrected; knowingly doing so costs the greater of three months' rent or up to treble damages, and a tenant who leaves or must vacate gets back all prepaid rent and deposits; from the agency's first notice of violations until relocation assistance is paid or the conditions are fixed, you may not raise the rent or otherwise materially increase the tenant's obligations (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). (2) Court-ordered reduction: if a court or arbitrator finds you failed to carry out a repair duty after notice and a reasonable time, it may set the diminished rental value, award the tenant the rent paid above it, and the tenant owes no more than the diminished rent until the defect is fixed or the court decides otherwise (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). (3) Rent escrow: where a government inspector certifies a condition that endangers the tenant's health or safety and the tenant pays rent into escrow as the statute allows, you may not start a nonpayment eviction while the full rent keeps going into escrow. (4) Repair and deduct, and a city utility the tenant had to put in his or her own name, let the tenant subtract the cost from rent within the statutory limits. (5) A lender holding an assignment of rents may not collect rent from a tenant of a small residential property without a court order or your written consent (`edu-no-rent-receipt-anti-waiver-wa`). (6) No rent increase in the first 12 months, before a fixed term ends, without 90 days' notice, or above the limit (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`); you may not report a tenant to a screening service for not paying the unlawful part of an increase. In the other direction, a tenant must be current in rent (and agreed utilities) before using the act's repair remedies, though the tenant can always argue in an eviction that no rent is owed. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in Washington
bodyText: You may not lock a tenant out, change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or shut off utilities to collect unpaid rent in Washington, and a lease clause allowing it (even one with advance notice and 24-hour key access, as some states permit) is barred. It is unlawful for a landlord to remove or exclude a tenant from the premises except under a court order. A tenant locked out may recover possession or end the lease, and recover actual damages, with costs and attorneys' fees to the prevailing party. Intentionally causing a tenant's water, heat, electricity or gas to be cut off costs actual damages plus up to $100 a day. The common-law right of distress for rent is abolished, any lease term creating a lien on the tenant's belongings or authorizing distress is void, and keeping a tenant's belongings without specific written consent, after a written demand for their return, can cost up to $500 a day (capped at $5,000) if intentional (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`, `edu-landlord-lien-wa`). A lease clause that waives these rules is unenforceable, and knowingly using one exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`). The only lawful route is the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice and an unlawful detainer action; the sheriff executes the writ of restitution (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`, `edu-eviction-process-wa`). No Washington statute in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules authorizes a lockout for delinquent rent.

title: No Property Tax Statement for Renters in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no renter's property tax credit and no rule requiring you to tell tenants what share of their rent goes to property taxes, whether yearly, on a rent change, or on request; nor does any state agency require you to certify the rent a tenant paid for a tax credit. No such provision was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules. Related rules: if your rental receives a property tax exemption, such as the multifamily housing exemption or the accessory dwelling unit exemption for low-income rentals, you report to the city or county under that program, not to the tenant; and if the lease makes you responsible for property taxes and the tenant ends up paying them, the tenant may recover the amount from you with 10% interest or deduct it from rent (`edu-tax-escalation-wa`). Passing tax increases to a tenant during the term is not allowed. No disclosure is needed in the lease. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Recording a Residential Lease in Washington
bodyText: Washington doesn't require you to record or register a residential lease with any state or county office, and nothing in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) makes a tenant's rights depend on recording. A lease needs no acknowledgment, witnesses or seals to be valid, but to record a lease or a memorandum of lease with the county recording officer, both your signature and the tenant's must be acknowledged before a notary. Recording protects a long lease: the recording act treats a lease for more than two years as a conveyance, and an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later buyer or mortgagee of the same property who acts in good faith, pays value and records first. A lease for two years or less is outside the recording act. Washington has no rule like Nebraska's for unrecorded leases to relatives. Whether a tenant's possession by itself warns a later buyer or lender of an unrecorded lease is a case-law question; no Washington case was searched, so if you sign a lease for more than two years and want it to bind a later buyer or lender, record it or a memorandum of it. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a residential lease to be recorded or registered. Cities may run rental registration or business license programs tied to inspections (`edu-no-landlord-registration-wa`, `edu-rental-inspection-wa`); state law limits how a city requires inspection certificates but doesn't preempt local registration itself, so check your city's code.

title: What a Washington Notice Ending a Tenancy Must Say
bodyText: Washington's cause requirement covers tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (not the arrangements the act excludes or an attorney-approved single-family lease under RCW 59.18.415; see `edu-scope-wa`): you may not evict, refuse to continue a tenancy or end a periodic tenancy except for a cause listed in RCW 59.18.650(2), apart from the two narrow end-of-term options (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Every written notice you give for a listed cause must be served the way eviction notices are served (RCW 59.12.040) and must identify the facts and circumstances known and available to you when you issue it that support the cause, specifically enough for the tenant to respond and prepare a defense. You may add facts later only if they were unknown or unavailable when you issued the notice. A notice ending a tenancy after four or more cured violations must also state the reason and supporting facts and include all the earlier notices. The end-of-term options need their own written notice at least 60 days before the term ends, served the same way. Washington doesn't require the lease, an addendum or a separate notice to tell the tenant whether the tenancy is covered by or exempt from the cause requirement: no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires one, so the library adds no such clause. If you remove a tenant in violation of the rule, you owe the greater of the tenant's economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus attorneys' fees and costs. If the tenant has a federal housing choice voucher, federal rules separately limit termination during the lease term to serious or repeated lease violations, violations of law tied to the tenant's occupancy, or other good cause (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`). Cities may add their own cause and notice rules; no state statute preempts them, so check local ordinances (for example Seattle, Tacoma and Spokane).

title: No State Landlord-Tenant Rights Guide Required in Washington
bodyText: Washington doesn't require you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires it, and the state has no statement of tenant rights for the lease either (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-wa`). Three related rules: First, if a licensed real estate broker handles the rental, the broker (not you as the landlord) must give each party the state's brokerage pamphlet and get an acknowledgment of receipt: a party the broker serves gets it before signing a services agreement, and an unrepresented party before signing an offer or as soon as reasonably practical. The pamphlet explains brokers' duties to landlords and tenants; it isn't a guide to landlord-tenant law. Second, mobile home community landlords must post the Attorney General's notice summarizing tenant rights in common areas; mobile home lot tenancies are under chapter 59.20 RCW and outside this library. Third, some cities require landlords to hand tenants a local rights guide. A city or county ordinance, resolution or policy requiring landlords to give tenants information about the property or the surrounding area takes effect only after a summary and a link are posted on the state-contracted municipal research website, and one adopted before June 9, 2016 stopped being in effect if it wasn't posted within 90 days of that date. The statute doesn't say whether a general rights handout counts as information about the property or the surrounding area, and no case was searched, so follow your city's handout rule and check that website's list for your jurisdiction.

title: Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones and Unrelated Occupants in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute limits renting out a home in a single-family zone or makes owner occupancy a condition of renting it; no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws does. State law instead restricts local rules that would limit who may live in a rental: Cities, towns, code cities and counties may not regulate or limit the number of unrelated persons who may occupy a household or dwelling unit. They may still apply occupant limits on group living arrangements regulated under state law, occupant limits on short-term rentals (stays of fewer than 30 consecutive nights under chapter 64.37 RCW), lawful limits on occupant load per square foot, and generally applicable health and safety provisions in the building code or a city or county ordinance. Condominium, homeowners' and other community associations are under the same limit. So any occupancy limit in your lease must rest on a lawful occupancy standard, not on whether the occupants are related (for familial status, see `edu-children-occupancy-wa`). In the urban growth areas of counties and cities planning under the Growth Management Act, a city or county may not require the owner of a lot with an accessory dwelling unit to live in it or in another unit on the lot. The state's administrative lot-split process sets no owner-occupancy or minimum-rental-term condition; if a lot split would require demolishing or altering existing housing that would displace a renter, the applicant must recommend a displacement mitigation strategy, which may include relocation assistance. Beyond these rules (and the state limits on regulating the amount of rent and on rental inspection programs), zoning of rental use, short-term rental rules and rental licensing are local, and no state statute preempts them; check your city's or county's code.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit in Washington
bodyText:
A rental of an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) is an ordinary tenancy under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act; Washington's ADU statutes govern what cities and counties may allow and require, not what your lease says.

What reaches renting: In urban growth areas of counties and cities planning under the Growth Management Act, a city or county may not require the owner of a lot with an ADU to live in the ADU or another unit on the lot, so you may rent both the house and the ADU. These limits apply in those areas once the local rules are updated, and where a city or county hasn't adopted them in time, the state rules override conflicting local development regulations. Cities and counties may still restrict ADUs as short-term rentals (stays of fewer than 30 consecutive nights) and apply the health, safety, building code and environmental rules that apply to the house. No state law sets a minimum rental term for an ADU.

Condominium, homeowners' and other community association documents created after July 23, 2023 for property in an urban growth area may not restrict building, developing or using an ADU beyond what the city or county could, except for rules protecting public health and safety or waters from on-site wastewater; older association documents are not changed by these rules.

Outside urban growth areas, a county that allows detached ADUs under RCW 36.70A.685 (in force June 11, 2026) must limit each parcel to one ADU and apply conditions such as metered water and a shared driveway; county ADU ordinances adopted before that date and other lawful methods are not affected.

If you live in a single-family home and rent out no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU, those tenancies are exempt from the state rent increase limit unless the owner is a real estate investment trust, a corporation or an LLC with a corporate member; claim the exemption with supporting facts in the increase notice (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`).

In a county of 1,500,000 or more people, or in a city or county within a county of 900,000 to 1,500,000 people that passes a resolution, the local legislative authority may exempt from property tax an ADU rented to a low-income household; to qualify you file a lease of at least 12 months stating the rent, keep the rent at no more than 30% of the tenant's monthly income and don't rent to an immediate family member (rule effective until January 1, 2034).

The library offers an optional clause describing the ADU, the shared areas and who lives in the main house (`accessory-dwelling-unit-term-co`). Local ADU, short-term rental and rental licensing rules vary; check your city's or county's code.

title: Local Health Board Rules and Rentals in Washington
bodyText: Washington doesn't require you to give tenants copies of local health district rules on request or to refer them to the health district; no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws does. Local health still reaches your rental: each county or district board of health supervises matters of public health in its area and may enact local rules to preserve and improve public health and provide for abating nuisances that harm it, and the local health officer enforces state public health statutes and local health rules and abates health nuisances. No state statute preempts local health rules for rental housing. Your duty to keep the premises in substantial compliance with any applicable code, statute, ordinance or regulation governing their maintenance or operation, where a condition endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety, can therefore include local health rules (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). If you believe a tenant contaminated a vacated or abandoned unit with hazardous chemicals, you must contact the local health officer, who may order the unit unfit for use (`edu-meth-contamination-wa`), and you may not rent a unit a government agency has declared condemned or unlawful to occupy (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). A tenant may complain to a government authority about a code violation that may endanger health or safety, and you may not retaliate for a good-faith, lawful complaint (`edu-retaliation-wa`). Check your county or district health department's rules for rentals, such as rules on sewage systems, water, solid waste or contaminated property.

title: Washington Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Lease Disclosure
bodyText: Washington adds no lead notice, certificate or packet to the lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal disclosure applies, and the library's shared lead clause carries it (`lead-based-paint`, `edu-lead-based-paint-wa`): before the tenant is bound by the lease you must give the EPA-approved lead pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and hand over available records and reports, with the lead warning statement and signed certifications in or attached to the lease. The federal rule doesn't apply to leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension, housing a certified inspector found free of lead-based paint, renewals where everything was disclosed before and you have no new information, or housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or units with no separate bedroom, unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there. Washington's own lead law reaches renovation work, not leases. The Department of Commerce runs a state renovation, repair and painting program (chapter 70A.420 RCW, rewritten by a 2025 act effective July 27, 2025): renovation in pre-1978 housing must be done by certified renovation firms using certified renovators, or workers trained by them, under the department's work practice standards. No more than 60 days before renovating a unit, the firm doing the work must give the owner the EPA renovation pamphlet and, where the owner doesn't live in the unit, an adult occupant too, getting a signed acknowledgment (or a written certification of delivery when the occupant won't or can't sign) or mailing it at least seven days before the work; the tenant's acknowledgment is in the language of the lease or the pamphlet. For work in common areas of multiunit pre-1978 housing, the firm must give each affected unit written notice or post signs where occupants will see them. Emergency renovations are excused from these notice rules. If you or your own staff do painted-surface work in a pre-1978 rental, get advice on whether the program treats you as a firm performing renovation for compensation; the rules don't say, and no ruling was searched. Local governments may add lead rules; no state statute preempts them, and a local rule requiring you to give tenants information about the property takes effect only after it is listed on the state-contracted municipal research website (RCW 64.06.080).

title: Unfit-Dwelling Orders, Code Liens and Receivers in Washington
bodyText: Washington lets each city, town and county adopt its own unfit-dwelling ordinance (chapter 35.80 RCW); the state sets the framework and the local ordinance supplies the standards and procedures. Under such an ordinance, an improvement board or officer who finds after a preliminary investigation that a dwelling is unfit for human habitation serves a complaint on everyone with an interest shown in the county auditor's records, posts it on the property and files it with the auditor, where it works like a lis pendens. A hearing follows 10 to 30 days after service. After the hearing, the board or officer may order you, within a set time, to repair, alter or improve the dwelling or to vacate and close it, or to remove or demolish it, and posts the order on the property. You have 30 days from service and posting to appeal to the local appeals commission, which must decide within 60 days, and 30 days after the commission's order to petition the superior court. If you don't comply with a final order, the city or county may do the work itself. The cost is assessed against the property, entered on the tax rolls, collected like delinquent taxes and is a lien equal in rank to state, county and city taxes. The cost of vacating and closing includes relocation assistance a local government advanced to your tenants that you haven't repaid, plus penalties and interest (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). Inspectors may enter when they have reasonable grounds to believe a building is unfit, with the least inconvenience to the people living there, and must get a court order if entry is refused. Tenants learn of the case from the posted complaint and order; the statute requires service only on interests shown in the auditor's records. Washington has no statute providing a receivership for substandard rental housing. A superior court may appoint a general receiver under RCW 7.60.025 in listed cases or where needed to secure ample justice, and generally only if a receiver is reasonably necessary and other remedies are unavailable or inadequate. A tenant facing a dangerous condition can use the local-government inspection and rent escrow remedy (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`), and a unit declared condemned or unlawful to occupy can't be rented until fixed. Chapter 35.80 RCW doesn't preempt local codes: its powers are in addition to cities' other powers, including nuisance abatement, so check your local housing code.

title: Code Variances and Waivers Need No Tenant Notice in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no rule requiring you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a health, housing or building code variance, waiver or exception that applies to your rental. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires one. The state-level waivers that exist are granted to the property, not disclosed to tenants: for example, a local health officer may waive specific state board of health requirements for an on-site sewage system with flows under 3,500 gallons a day, after a site-by-site review, if the waiver is consistent with the state rules' standards and intent. Building code changes run the other way: a city or county may amend the state building code locally, but not below its minimum performance standards, and an amendment affecting single-family or multifamily residential buildings takes effect only if the State Building Code Council approves it. Housing maintenance and unfit-dwelling standards are set by local ordinance (`edu-substandard-property-receivership-wa`), and your duty to keep the premises in substantial compliance with applicable codes where a condition endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety still applies (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). If a city or county requires you to tell tenants about a variance, that is a local requirement to give tenants information about the property, which takes effect only after it is listed on the state-contracted municipal research website (RCW 64.06.080); check your local code.

title: When Washington Makes You State a Certificate of Occupancy Date
bodyText: Washington doesn't require you to give a tenant a copy of the certificate of occupancy, or to state in the lease whether the unit has one or what occupancy it allows; no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws does. A certificate of occupancy matters in three other places: First, the state rent increase limit doesn't apply to a unit whose first certificate of occupancy was issued 12 or fewer years before the date of the increase notice. If you raise rent above the limit on that ground, the notice must state the date the first certificate was issued and you must include facts or attach documents supporting the exemption (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`); this rule expires July 1, 2040. Second, a city's rental inspection program can't require an inspection certificate for a property that received a certificate of occupancy within the last four years and has had no reported code violations in that time (`edu-rental-inspection-wa`). Third, when a building is converted to condominiums or another common interest community, the public offering statement must include a city or county housing code inspection report unless a final certificate of occupancy was issued within the preceding 24 months. The building code's own rule that a building needs a certificate of occupancy before it is used sits in the model codes the state adopts by reference, which weren't searched. A unit a government agency has declared condemned or unlawful to occupy can't be rented until the conditions are fixed (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). Local codes may require more; check your city's or county's code.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice or Lease Font Rule in Washington
bodyText: Washington requires no special notice because the rental is a single-family home, and no notice at the top of the first page or in larger type about whether the lease must be notarized or signed by a licensed agent. Washington law has no presumption that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized or agent-signed, so there is nothing of that kind to disclose; no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws provides one. A residential lease needs no notarization to be valid. The one notarization rule in a lease concerns arbitration: a lease may not require the tenant to arbitrate disputes unless you pay the entire cost of the arbitration and the agreement is notarized (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Washington also has no general font-size or first-page placement rule for leases (`edu-no-plain-language-rule-wa`). What Washington does have is a police removal route for people who were never tenants: an owner's sworn declaration in the statutory form lets an officer with probable cause of criminal trespass remove someone who hasn't been a tenant, or an owner on title, in the last 12 months, but the officer must give occupants a reasonable chance to show they are tenants or guests, and the route can't be used against anyone entitled to occupy under a rental agreement or that person's guests (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-wa`). So give every tenant who signs a lease an executed copy, which you must do anyway and which is the tenant's simplest proof of the right to be there (`edu-lease-copy-wa`).

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid Utility Bill Becomes a Lien on Your Washington Rental
bodyText: If a city or town, a county, a water-sewer district or an irrigation district supplies water, sewer, garbage or electric service to your rental, a tenant's unpaid bill can become a lien on your property, whatever the lease says about who pays. A city or town that owns its waterworks or electric plant has a lien on the premises for up to four months of charges (not for charges more than four months past due, except where a governor's emergency declaration prevented collection), and it may enforce that lien only by cutting off service; if you dispute the account and tender the amount you believe is due before the shutoff, the city must sue and win a judgment before it can refuse service. Code cities have the same lien. City sewer charges are a lien ranking ahead of everything except general taxes and local and special assessments: it covers six months of delinquent charges without any recording (a city may extend that to one year by ordinance), more if the city records a lien notice, and the city may enforce it by shutting off its water service. A city's garbage ordinance may make unpaid collection charges a lien on the property, filed with the county auditor. County sewer, water and stormwater charges and water-sewer district and irrigation district charges are also liens on the property served. Your protection is notice, not the lease: tell the city or town, water-sewer district or irrigation district in writing that the property is a residential rental, ask to be notified of a tenant's delinquency and give a complete, accurate mailing address. If it then fails to notify you, it has no lien on the premises for that tenant's delinquent charges (and a city or town can't collect the tenant's electric charges from you); even when it does notify you, a city or town can't collect from you electric charges more than four months past due, unless you failed to tell it within 14 days after an account-holder tenant's tenancy ended and the tenant moved out (`edu-utility-landlord-account-wa`). County systems have no such notice rule. A lease clause making the tenant pay the utilities (`utilities-responsibility`) binds the tenant, not the utility, so keep the tenant's duty to pay and to reimburse you clear in the lease and act quickly on any delinquency notice. When you sell, you as seller must clear these unrecorded city, sewer and county utility liens at closing unless the buyer agrees otherwise in writing. No statute was found giving a public utility district a lien on the premises for unpaid service charges, and no Washington statute exempts an owner outright from a tenant's utility debt. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Splitting Unmetered Utility Bills Among Washington Tenants
bodyText: Washington has no statute on how you split among tenants a utility bill that isn't separately metered: nothing in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires, permits or bars ratio billing or another allocation formula, and nothing makes a lease term charging tenants for unmetered utilities unenforceable as such (`edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`). The limits come from other rules. Utility charges the lease identifies as recurring and periodic charges are rent: they go on the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice (the statutory form has its own line for utilities), a tenant must be current on the utilities the tenant agreed to pay before using the landlord-tenant act's remedies, and a new or changed recurring charge falls under the rent increase rules (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). How a bill that varies from month to month fits the increase rules is not settled by the statutes (no case law searched), so the cautious course is to state the allocation method in the lease and give the rent increase notice before adding a charge or changing the method. Utility commission rules limit resale by customers of regulated utilities: gas may never be remetered or submetered by a customer for resale, electricity may be resold only if the utility's tariff allows it, and a regulated electric utility may refuse to serve a new master meter in a building with more than one dwelling unit when the occupants control a significant part of their own electricity use and individual meters would be cost-effective. Providing water only to your own tenants as part of renting does not make you a commission-regulated water company. A gas master meter system that resells gas to tenants by meter or through rent is regulated as a gas pipeline (see the topic `electric-submetering-disclosure`). City, town and county utilities and public utility districts are not under the commission's rules, so check your local utility's own terms before you master-meter or allocate.

title: Interrupting Submetered or Master-Metered Electricity in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no separate set of rules for interrupting electricity you resupply to tenants through a submeter or a master meter (`edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`); the general rules apply to it. You may not intentionally cause any of a tenant's utility services, including electricity, to be cut off, except for an interruption for a reasonable time to make necessary repairs; a violation costs the tenant's actual damages plus up to $100 for each day or part of a day without service, and fees (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`). The heat-alert limits on a landlord's disconnection of electric or water service for nonpayment are explained in `edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`; they don't authorize a nonpayment shutoff, so don't disconnect without advice. You are not responsible for an interruption in electrical service caused by a tenant's portable cooling device, unless you caused it. When the utility itself may cut service to your master-metered building or your account: a commission-regulated electric, gas or water utility must make reasonable efforts to tell the occupants about the pending disconnection, and if a service user who is not the customer of record asks, it must allow at least five more days for the tenants to arrange continued service; electric and gas utilities must also give the disconnection notices to the service user when the billing address differs from the service address. A city or town electric or water utility must try to give seven calendar days' written notice at the service address, must serve a tenant who asks on ordinary terms without collecting your arrears, and a tenant who puts the service in their own name may deduct the charges from rent (`edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`). No city or town, public utility district, water-sewer district, irrigation district, electric cooperative or mutual, or commission-regulated electric or water company may cut off a residential user, expressly including tenants of metered apartment buildings, for nonpayment on a day with a National Weather Service heat-related alert. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Duty to Disclose Past Utility Bills to Washington Tenants
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires you to give a prospective residential tenant past utility bills, heating or cooling costs, or energy-use data for the unit, or to attach a utility cost disclosure to the lease. The one energy-disclosure duty found is for nonresidential buildings: the owner or operator of a nonresidential building must give a prospective buyer, lessee or lender the building's ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager benchmarking data and ratings for the most recent continuously occupied twelve months; it doesn't reach a residential lease. The lease should still say which utilities you provide and which the tenant pays (`utilities-paid-by-landlord`, `utilities-responsibility`), and any recurring utility charge you bill is rent (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). If you choose to share cost information, give a building average or your own bills rather than a former tenant's individual electric bills: a person who obtained an electric customer's usage or billing information for a commercial purpose may not pass it on without that customer's consent. A tenant who holds the account can see their own usage on the regulated utility's website. City ordinances (for example energy-disclosure ordinances) may add duties where your property is located.

title: Getting Notice of a Tenant's Pending Utility Shutoff in Washington
bodyText:
How you get word of a tenant's pending utility shutoff depends on who supplies the service.

City or town utilities, water-sewer districts and irrigation districts: you don't need the tenant's permission. Notify the utility in writing that the property is a residential rental (for districts, a rental property), ask to be told of a tenant's delinquency and give a complete, accurate mailing address; it must then notify you at the same time and in the same manner it notifies the tenant, or by mail, and it must tell the tenant it is sending you duplicate bills or delinquency notices. If it fails to notify you after your request, it loses its lien on the premises for that tenant's charges (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-wa`, `edu-utility-landlord-account-wa`).

Electric and gas companies regulated by the Utilities and Transportation Commission: the customer, usually the tenant, may designate a third party, such as you, to receive disconnection notices and notices of other matters affecting the service, and the utility must offer every customer that option; once it issues a disconnection notice to the designated third party, it must wait at least five business days past the original disconnection date before disconnecting. The utility will need the tenant's written consent before it discloses account information to you.

Commission-regulated water companies have no third-party designation rule, and no statute was found giving an owner a right to delinquency notices from a public utility district or a county sewer or water system; ask those utilities about their own policies.

If you want the tenant to name you as a notice contact, use the optional authorization clause `utility-shutoff-notice-authorization-co`; it binds the tenant only, can't oblige any utility to notify you, and never lets you cut off service yourself (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`).

title: Reselling Electricity or Gas to Washington Tenants
bodyText: No Washington statute or rule in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires you to give tenants a written disclosure when you submeter or resell electricity, or sets terms for doing it (`edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`). Reselling can, however, bring you under utility regulation. Electricity: if a utility regulated by the Utilities and Transportation Commission serves the building, you may resell electricity only if that utility's tariff specifically allows it. The state's definition of an electrical company reaches any person operating electric plant used to furnish electricity for hire; whether a landlord who resells through submeters falls within it isn't settled by the text (no case law was searched), so get the utility's written confirmation and legal advice before you submeter. Gas: a customer of a regulated gas utility may never remeter or submeter gas for resale. Separately, if your property runs a gas master meter system, meaning you buy metered gas and distribute it through your own piping to tenants who pay for it by meter or through rent, you are a gas pipeline company under the state pipeline safety law: you must design, construct, operate and maintain the system so that it is safe, follow the commission's gas pipeline safety rules, and pay the annual pipeline safety fee. Water: providing water only to your own tenants as part of renting does not make you a commission-regulated water company. City utilities and public utility districts aren't under the commission's rules; check their terms. Any utility charge the lease bills as a recurring charge is rent (`edu-utility-apportionment-wa`).

title: Energy Savings Charges on Washington Rental Utility Bills
bodyText:
Since June 11, 2026, the Utilities and Transportation Commission must allow a regulated electric or natural gas company to invest in energy conservation and efficiency for single-family and multifamily rental housing instead of requiring the owner to pay for the measures, with priority for low-income customers, vulnerable populations and highly impacted communities.

The investment is secured through the meter and recovered through the regular bill paid by the tenant, including any later tenant, or by the owner (under a site-specific services agreement when the owner pays the bill). It appears on the bill as an "energy savings charge" line item and is collected like any other energy charge until the utility's authorized return is fully recovered.

If you authorize such work, you must notify the tenant living there at least 30 days before the work starts that you have authorized it, with a description of the work and its expected benefits; the utility must give you the information you need. The statute doesn't say the notice must be written, but give it in writing so you can prove it. It also doesn't expressly require you to tell a new tenant that the charge is on the bill, but a tenant who will pay it should know before signing: use the optional clause `meter-conservation-charge-wa`. No commission rule implementing the program was found in the held WAC Title 480, so Check the utility's tariff.

City and town utilities, public utility districts and irrigation districts may finance conservation for owners of structures, repaid as additions to the utility bill over no more than 240 months; those statutes don't say whose bill carries the payments when a tenant holds the account, so the cautious course is to pay or reimburse those payments yourself and say so in the lease. No Washington rule on surcharges or monthly statements for water you submeter was found.

title: Energy Benchmarking and Tenant Usage Data in Washington
bodyText:
If you own a multifamily residential building in Washington with more than 20,000 gross square feet (not counting a parking garage), it is a tier 2 covered building under the state's Clean Buildings law: you must benchmark its energy use, develop energy management and operations and maintenance plans, and report compliance to the Department of Commerce by July 1, 2027 and every five years after.

A multifamily residential building here means one with sleeping units or more than five dwelling units whose occupants are primarily permanent.

You don't need your tenants' consent to get benchmarking data: for a covered building with tenants, an electric or gas utility must give you, on request, aggregated monthly energy consumption data without requiring prior consent from tenants, and what it gives you must not contain personally identifiable information or customer-specific billing information about tenants. Commerce penalties for failing to report may not be passed along to tenants, so long as tenants are providing access to utility usage data and physical spaces and are responsive to your compliance needs.

Outside benchmarking, a tenant's own account and usage data is protected. A regulated utility may give it to you only with the tenant's written consent (paper or electronic), which the tenant may revoke subject to agreements the tenant has made with you; and anyone who obtains an electric customer's usage or billing information for a commercial purpose must tell the customer first and get written or electronic permission, and may not pass it on without consent (benchmarking programs authorized by law are exempt).

If you want unit-level data for an audit, a rebate or utility allocation, use the optional authorization clause `energy-data-release-wy`, which lets the tenant withdraw consent without breaching the lease. Commerce's implementing rules are in chapter 194-50 WAC; check them for details and deadlines.

title: Transferring Utilities to the Tenant's Name in Washington
bodyText: You may require in the lease that the tenant open accounts in the tenant's own name for the utilities the tenant pays (`utilities-responsibility`); no Washington statute regulates that transfer. What you may not do is cut off a utility that is still in your name to force the transfer: intentionally causing termination of a tenant's water, heat, electricity, gas or other utility service, except for an interruption for a reasonable time to make necessary repairs, is unlawful and costs the tenant's actual damages plus up to $100 for each day or part of a day without service, and fees (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`). Asking the utility to close an account in your name while the tenant still depends on the service would cause that termination too. So the library does not offer a clause letting you shut off or close landlord-name utilities when a tenant fails to transfer them. A plain transfer deadline with reimbursement of what the utility actually billed is lawful, but the library declines it for now: recurring and periodic utility charges identified in the lease are rent in Washington (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`), so how a reimbursement is labeled and collected needs care; you may add your own clause with legal advice. Two related rules: when a city or town utility account is in the tenant's name, notify the city in writing within 14 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant moves out (`edu-utility-landlord-account-wa`); and if you fail to pay a city or town for electric or water service, a tenant who has the service placed in the tenant's own name may deduct the reasonable charges paid from rent, and you may not retaliate. No Washington statute or rule in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws was found that lets a court order a utility account transferred in a protection order, or lets a deployed servicemember suspend utilities.

title: Utility Deposits and Utility Deductions in Washington
bodyText: Washington's deposit statute has no list of permitted deductions.
