Any money a tenant pays you as a deposit or as security for the tenant's obligations is a deposit under the landlord-tenant act, including one you call a utility deposit: you need a written lease stating the terms and conditions under which it may be withheld and a signed move-in checklist before you collect it, you must hold it in a trust account in a Washington financial institution or licensed escrow agent, give a written receipt and tell the tenant where it is held, and within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant vacates give a full and specific statement of the basis for keeping any of it with any refund due (`security-deposit-return-wa`, `edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`). You may deduct unpaid utility charges the tenant owes you only if the lease's withholding terms cover them; the library's deposit clause covers "Rent and other charges Tenant owes under this Lease" (`security-deposit-use-wa`). The statute's checklist and invoice documentation rules don't apply when you withhold for rent or other charges owing rather than damage, but itemize the utility charges and periods in the statement anyway. Recurring utility charges identified in the lease are rent (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). Deposits the tenant pays a utility are separate and are between the tenant and the utility. A commission-regulated electric or gas utility may require a residential deposit only in listed cases, one of which is an applicant who doesn't own and isn't buying the premises; the deposit can't exceed two-twelfths of estimated annual billings for monthly billing (three-twelfths for bimonthly), earns interest, and must be refunded or credited after twelve months of satisfactory payment or when service ends, less amounts owed to the utility. Commission-regulated water companies have similar rules. City or town utilities, water-sewer districts and irrigation districts may also require deposits before serving; failing to take one doesn't affect their liens (`edu-municipal-utility-lien-wa`).

title: Which Building and Fire Codes Apply to Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington has one state building code, in force in every city and county. The State Building Code Act (chapter 19.27 RCW) adopts by reference the International Building Code, the International Residential Code, the International Mechanical Code, the International Fire Code and the Uniform Plumbing Code, and the State Building Code Council adopts and amends them by rule on a three-year cycle. The council's current rules adopt the 2021 editions of the International Building, Residential and Fire Codes, effective statewide on March 15, 2024 (chapters 51-50, 51-51 and 51-54A WAC). Cities and counties enforce the code, and each county administers and enforces the International Fire Code in its unincorporated areas. A city or county may amend the code but may not go below the state minimum, and a local amendment that affects single-family or multifamily residential buildings takes effect only once the council approves it. The model codes themselves aren't in the sources searched for this library, only Washington's amendments to them, so confirm the code text, and any local amendment, with your building or fire code official. For an existing rental the starting point is that a building's legal occupancy may continue without change, except where the existing building code or the fire code specifically requires otherwise or the code official finds it necessary to fix an unsafe building; lack of compliance with the current code is not by itself what makes a building unsafe. Some fire-code rules do reach existing buildings: for example, existing Group R occupancies must have carbon monoxide alarms (`edu-alarm-duties-wa`). Separate statutes put duties directly on owners: smoke detection devices in every rental unit and the signed fire safety notice (`edu-alarm-duties-wa`, `fire-safety-notice-wa`); if the building has fire dampers, smoke dampers, combination fire and smoke dampers or a smoke control system, testing and inspection by a certified inspector (dampers within 12 months of installation and then at least every four years; smoke control systems every six to twelve months), keeping the full reports on the property, and fixing any deficiency within 120 days of the inspection, on pain of civil infractions and per-square-foot penalties; and, if the building has an elevator or other conveyance, a posted state operating permit, annual state inspection and the owner's responsibility (a lessee who controls the conveyance counts as an owner) for its safe operation, proper maintenance and periodic tests. Under the landlord-tenant act you must keep the premises in substantial compliance with any applicable code, statute, ordinance or regulation governing their maintenance or operation where the condition endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety, and keep shared areas safe from defects increasing the hazards of fire or accident (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires an old fire-escape or tenement-house retrofit of existing residential buildings, and the International Property Maintenance Code is not one of the codes the state adopts statewide (a city or county may have its own housing or maintenance code; local codes weren't searched). Acts of 2025 and 2026 direct the council to study scissor stairs and minimally sized elevators in apartment buildings of up to six stories and 24 units for the 2027 code update; they don't change what an existing building must have today.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Washington Rentals: New Buildings, No General Retrofit, Licensed Work
bodyText: New buildings: Washington's fire and building codes require an automatic sprinkler system throughout every new building with a Group R fire area (apartment houses, boarding houses, congregate living and similar residential buildings), with a narrow exception only for small, single-story recreational Group R-1 structures; a lighter NFPA 13R system is allowed in Group R buildings up to four stories and 60 feet high. Townhouses built under the residential code need sprinklers unless the townhouse building has no more than four townhouse units, and an addition or alteration to an existing townhouse unit without sprinklers doesn't trigger them. Washington did not adopt the model residential code's sprinkler requirement for new one- and two-family dwellings; a city or county may require sprinklers in new one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses by adopting Appendix AWV, after notifying the State Building Code Council. Existing buildings: no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires an existing apartment building or rental house to be retrofitted with sprinklers. Washington's own amendments to the fire code's existing-building chapter add a sprinkler requirement only for nightclubs, and a building's legal occupancy may otherwise continue without change unless the existing building code or the fire code specifically requires otherwise or the code official finds the building unsafe (`edu-fire-code-standard-wa`). The model fire code's retroactive provisions are adopted by reference and weren't in the sources searched, and local codes weren't searched, so ask your fire code official whether any retroactive requirement applies to your building. If the building has sprinklers: keep the system in reasonably good working order as a facility you supplied (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`), and use a state-licensed fire protection sprinkler system contractor to install, inspect, maintain or service it. The statute exempts an owner who occupies a single-family residence and does their own installation there, and the State Fire Marshal's rule says builders and contractors are not to use that exemption for single-family homes they plan to sell, lease or rent; the rule also exempts a full-time employee or owner of a facility whom the local fire code authority accepts as qualified to do sprinkler work in that facility, and that work must still meet every applicable standard, code and local ordinance. Keep copies of the contractor's material and test certificates for at least five years. An owner who has actual knowledge that an unlicensed contractor is installing or maintaining the system illegally can be criminally liable. Since June 11, 2026 a fire code official can ask the contractor to show its license, stop unlicensed work and decide whether work done by an unlicensed contractor must be removed and replaced. The fire safety notice tells each new tenant whether the building has a sprinkler system, except in a single-family residence (`fire-safety-notice-wa`).

title: Telling Tenants Whether the Building Has Sprinklers
bodyText: Washington requires this disclosure, and the library's fire safety notice clause already carries it (`fire-safety-notice-wa`). At the time the lease is signed, give each new tenant the written fire safety and protection notice, signed by you or your authorized agent and by the tenant, with copies to both. Except in a single-family residence the notice must say whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, together with the other listed items: whether the smoke detection device is hard-wired or battery operated, whether there is a fire alarm system, the smoking policy, and whether there are emergency notification, relocation and evacuation plans (with copies of any that exist). In a multifamily residential building you may give the information as a checklist instead, and the checklist must include a diagram of the emergency evacuation routes. No Washington statute requires any further sprinkler disclosure to tenants, such as the system's inspection or test history. Grants and tax credits: no Washington grant, loan or tax credit for adding sprinklers to existing rental housing was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws. A person who installs a residential fire sprinkler system in a single-family home doesn't have to pay the fire operations portion of a local impact fee. A property tax exemption for sprinklers installed in nightclubs, whose benefit went to a lessee who had paid for the system, closed to new applications after December 31, 2009.

title: Which Code Edition Binds a Washington Rental
bodyText: Washington's building code statute adopts the model codes by name without fixing an edition: the International Building, Residential, Mechanical and Fire Codes and the Uniform Plumbing Code are adopted by reference, and the State Building Code Council must review each new edition and act on it within 30 months of its publication, on a three-year adoption cycle. So the edition that binds you is the one the council's rules adopt, not the newest one in print. The rules in the sources searched adopt the 2021 editions, effective statewide on March 15, 2024; statutes passed since 2024 direct the council to make changes for the 2024 International Building Code cycle and for the 2027 code update, so confirm with your building official which edition is in force when you build or alter. Which edition applies to your building: a valid and fully complete building permit application is considered under the building permit ordinance in effect when it is filed. A building that already exists may keep its legal occupancy without change, except where the existing building code or the fire code specifically requires otherwise or the code official finds the building unsafe, and not meeting the current edition does not by itself make a building unsafe (`edu-fire-code-standard-wa`). Additions, alterations and repairs follow the existing-building rules, and newly built elements must meet the current code. Some Washington rules freeze a definition at a named edition or date, so read the citation rather than the current edition: a nightclub is an A-2 occupancy under the 2006 International Building Code; the fire and smoke damper testing law uses the fire code's definition of a combination fire and smoke damper as it stood on January 1, 2020; the local permit exemption for small Group R-3 work refers to the 1988 Uniform Building Code; the accessibility statute's coverage turns on occupancy groups in the 1994 Uniform Building Code and exempts apartment houses with ten or fewer units and buildings with no more than two dwelling units; and the residential code fixes liquefied petroleum gas installations to the 2011 edition of NFPA 58 and the 2012 edition of NFPA 54, while the mechanical code uses the 2020 and 2021 editions of the same standards. Other rules roll forward: the sprinkler contractor law defines NFPA 13-D and NFPA 13-R as whatever standard the National Fire Protection Association currently uses. A lease can't lower the standard: your duty to keep the premises in substantial compliance with applicable codes where a violation endangers health or safety can't be waived in a standard lease (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`).

title: Lighting Shared Areas of a Washington Rental
bodyText: Washington has no statute written specifically about lighting the shared areas of a rental. Two general rules cover it. Under the landlord-tenant act you must keep any shared or common areas reasonably clean, sanitary and safe from defects increasing the hazards of fire or accident, and keep the electrical facilities you supply in reasonably good working order (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`); an unlit stairway or hallway may well be such a defect (no Washington case on the point was searched for), so the cautious course is to keep shared areas lit and replace failed lights promptly. The building code sets the lighting itself. In buildings under the residential code (houses, duplexes and townhouses), Washington's amendments require every interior stairway to have an artificial light source, powered from the building wiring, that lights the treads and landings to at least one foot-candle, with a wall switch at each floor level where the stairway has six or more risers unless the lighting has remote, central or automatic control, and every exterior stairway to have a light at the top landing, also powered from the building wiring. In apartment buildings and other buildings under the International Building Code and International Fire Code, means of egress lighting is set by the model codes' Section 1008, which Washington adopts by reference while deleting only the exit discharge subsection; that model-code text isn't in the sources searched, so confirm the requirement with your building or fire code official, and check any local housing code (local codes weren't searched). Shared-area lights on a tenant's meter: no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles (including the Utilities and Transportation Commission's electric, gas and water rules) or the 2025-2026 session laws addresses lights or outlets in shared areas wired to a tenant's electric service, either to allow or to forbid charging the tenant for that power. The arrangement appears lawful if the lease says so plainly, but the library doesn't offer a Washington clause for it, because your duty to keep the shared areas safe stays with you even if the tenant's service is cut off, and moving the shared lighting to your own service avoids the problem. If you want such a clause, have a lawyer draft it for your building.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators in Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act doesn't require you to supply a stove, oven or refrigerator. If you do supply them, they are appliances you must keep in reasonably good working order (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`), and the tenant must use and operate them properly. After a tenant's written notice that a refrigerator or a range and oven you supplied can't be used, you must start repairs within 72 hours, and the tenant has remedies if you don't (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`); there is no repair duty for damage the tenant, the tenant's family, invitees or others under the tenant's control caused. Describe the appliances' condition in the move-in checklist: you can't withhold deposit money for repairing or replacing an appliance whose condition wasn't reasonably documented there. The building code is where cooking and refrigeration can be required. A dwelling unit is defined as having permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking and sanitation, and under Washington's amendment to the International Building Code a newly built efficiency dwelling unit (one where living, sleeping, eating and cooking are all in a single room), other than an accessible, Type A or Type B unit, must be provided with a kitchen sink, a cooking appliance and a refrigerator, each with at least 30 inches of clear working space in front. A city or county housing code may require more (local codes weren't searched). If an unused refrigerator, icebox or deep freeze locker of 1.5 cubic feet or more is left on property you control, take the door off or remove part of the latch: an owner, lessee or manager who knowingly lets one remain on the premises without doing so commits a misdemeanor.

title: No Steam Radiator Cover Rule in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord to put covers or guards on steam radiators or other hot heating surfaces, on request or otherwise, or to give a radiator-cover notice or lease rider. What does apply: you must provide facilities adequate to supply heat as reasonably required and keep supplied heating facilities in reasonably good working order, with repairs starting within 24 hours of the tenant's notice of a loss of heat (`edu-heating-wa`, `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`), and keep the unit fit for habitation. If the building is heated by a boiler, the state boiler law applies to apartment houses of six or more families: a low-pressure steam heating boiler (15 pounds per square inch or less) or hot water heating boiler (30 pounds per square inch or less) there must be inspected every two years, with no more than 26 months between inspections, and operated only under a valid inspection certificate posted under glass in the boiler room; those boilers in private residences and in apartment houses of fewer than six families are exempt from the inspection and certificate requirements, and boilers in a city whose own enforced boiler ordinance is at least as strict are outside the state law. The cautious course with exposed steam radiators, especially where young children live, is to offer covers anyway and note any you install in the move-in checklist; a city housing code may have its own rule (local codes weren't searched).

title: No Periodic Balcony or Deck Inspection Rule in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord to have balconies, decks, walkways, stairs or other exterior elevated elements periodically inspected, or to report on them. What does apply: you must keep the structural components of the premises in reasonably good repair so as to be usable, keep shared areas safe from defects increasing the hazards of fire or accident, and keep the premises in substantial compliance with applicable codes where a violation endangers the tenant's health or safety (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). The building code sets construction standards for new decks, balconies and guards (for example guards at least 36 inches high on open-sided porches, balconies and decks more than 30 inches above grade in houses, and generally 42 inches in other buildings), and repairs and alterations must follow the code's existing-building rules. The only required inspection that reaches balconies and decks is a one-time inspection at construction: a multiunit residential building (generally more than two attached dwelling units, with exclusions including small buildings of 12 or fewer units of limited height) whose construction permit issued on or after August 1, 2005 must have its building enclosure, which includes balcony support columns and decks that keep out water, inspected by a qualified inspector during initial construction and during any rehabilitative construction costing more than 5% of the building's assessed value. A building whose units are all under one ownership and covered by a recorded covenant barring condominium sales for at least five years, as many rental apartment buildings are, is excluded. The cautious course is to have balconies, decks, railings and exterior stairs checked for rot, corrosion and loose guards at turnover and at regular intervals, repair promptly, and keep the records; a city may have its own inspection program (local codes weren't searched).

title: No Window-Guard Duty for Washington Rentals; Code Fall Protection on Replacement Windows
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord to install window guards or stops, to install them on request where children live, to give a window-guard notice, or to disclose release mechanisms on security bars. Window fall protection comes only from the building code. In houses, duplexes and townhouses built under the residential code, fall protection is required by the model code's Section R312.2 (adopted by reference; its text isn't in the sources searched), and Washington's amendment applies it when you replace an existing window, sash and glass, other than replacing only the glazing: the replacement must have window fall protection, with any window opening control device or fall protection device placed at the height the code requires or as low as can be installed in the existing opening. Apartment buildings under the International Building Code follow its window-opening rules, also adopted by reference and not in the sources searched. Security bars: no Washington statute bans or regulates bars or grilles on residential windows as such, but every sleeping room and basement covered by the residential code must keep an operable emergency escape and rescue opening, and anything over that opening must not defeat it; check bars, grilles and security screens against the code with your building official. You may limit a tenant's window-mounted portable cooling device if the window is a necessary egress and the device would interfere with it, if it would interfere with locking a window accessible from outside, or if it can't be secured so it won't fall out (`portable-cooling-device-wa`). The cautious course where young children live is to offer window stops or guards that don't block an escape opening; a city housing code may have its own rule (local codes weren't searched).

title: Wells Serving Washington Rentals: When the Drinking Water Rules Apply
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord to test a private well or give tenants well-test results, and the seller disclosure statement asks a seller about the water source, its year-round adequacy, problems, treatment and water rights, not about test results. So a well serving only one single-family rental has no state testing rule. A well that serves more than that is different: under the Department of Health's drinking water rules any system providing water for human consumption through pipes is a public water system unless it serves only one single-family residence (or four or fewer connections all serving residences on the same farm), each dwelling unit, including each apartment, counts as a residential service connection, and you, as the owner or operator, are the system's purveyor. Group A: a community water system serves 15 or more service connections used by year-round residents for 180 or more days a year, or regularly serves at least 25 year-round residents (an apartment complex is one of the rule's examples). Its purveyor must meet chapter 246-290 WAC, including routine water quality monitoring, maximum contaminant levels and follow-up, written public notice to users of violations and other listed situations, recordkeeping, and an annual consumer confidence report to customers, delivered by July 1 each year under the rules that take effect January 1, 2027. Group B: a system with fewer than 15 service connections and fewer than 25 people a day (or 25 or more for fewer than 60 days a year) falls under chapter 246-291 WAC, except that a Group B system with only one or two service connections (for example a well serving a duplex) is outside that chapter unless the local board of health has adopted rules for such systems or the department decides it's needed to protect health. A Group B purveyor must provide potable water to its consumers; take, analyze and report water samples when the department or local health officer requires; and notify the department, the health officer and every consumer in writing within 24 hours of a lab result showing E. coli or nitrate at or above 10 mg/L, or of circumstances posing a threat of acute contamination such as a flood, saying what is wrong, what is being done, what consumers should do, including using another source of water, and when it should be fixed. A new or expanding Group B system needs design approval based on source-water tests, and before serving a connection the purveyor must record on the customer's property title the system's details, including whether and how often it will monitor and how consumers will learn the results; one built before 2014 must notify consumers if arsenic exceeds 0.010 mg/L. A landlord whose building takes all its water from a city or other public water system, has no source or treatment of its own and doesn't sell water directly to any person is not subject to these rules. The rules don't say whether billing tenants separately for water is selling it directly, so if you do, ask the Department of Health or your local health jurisdiction. In every case you must provide facilities adequate to supply water as reasonably required and keep the plumbing working (`edu-heating-wa`, `edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). The cautious course for a rental on a private well is to test for coliform bacteria and nitrate at least at each turnover and share the results with the tenant; local health rules may require more (local rules weren't searched).

title: Elevators, Boilers, Laundries and Other Facilities You Supply in Washington
bodyText: Washington's landlord-tenant act has one general rule for every facility you supply rather than a list: keep all electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances you supply in reasonably good working order, keep shared areas reasonably clean, sanitary and safe from defects increasing the hazards of fire or accident, and, except in a single-family residence, provide and maintain garbage receptacles in common areas and arrange regular removal (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). A facility you supply, such as a laundry room, garage, storage area, gym or playground, is measured against that standard, and these duties can't be waived in a standard lease. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws puts a separate duty on a landlord for automatic garage door openers or similar equipment. Some facilities carry their own state rules. Elevators, escalators, dumbwaiters, wheelchair and stairway chair lifts and other conveyances need a state operating permit posted near the conveyance and an annual state inspection, and once the permit issues the owner (which includes a lessee or anyone else in control of the conveyance) is responsible for its safe operation, proper maintenance and periodic tests and must fix violations within 90 days of written inspection results; a conveyance in a single-family dwelling is inspected only when work is done or on the owner's request. Heating boilers in apartment houses of six or more families need inspection and a posted inspection certificate (`edu-no-steam-radiator-cover-rule-wa`). Fire dampers, smoke dampers and smoke control systems must be tested on a fixed schedule with reports kept on site (`edu-fire-code-standard-wa`), and sprinkler work must be done by a licensed contractor (`edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-wa`). A pool or spa for residents and their guests is a limited use pool under the state health rules (`edu-pool-rules-wa`), and a well serving more than one single-family residence is a public water system (`edu-private-well-testing-wa`). An unused refrigerator or freezer left on the property must have its door or latch removed (`edu-stove-refrigerator-wa`). Shared areas of a building occupied by two or more tenants, or by the owner and one or more tenants (halls, elevators, washrooms, garbage areas, recreation facilities, laundry or work areas and open space), are places of public accommodation under the Washington Law Against Discrimination, so their rules and access must not discriminate. A city or county may have further rules (local codes weren't searched).

title: Asbestos in Washington Rentals: No Tenant Disclosure, but Inspect Before Work
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to tell a tenant about asbestos, to put an asbestos disclosure in a lease, or to test a rental for asbestos before renting it. The seller disclosure statement that asks about asbestos does not reach a lease: the seller disclosure chapter does not apply to the transfer of an interest less than fee simple (a lease), except a buyer's interest under a real estate contract. What Washington does regulate is asbestos work. If you, as the owner of a building or your agent, allow or authorize construction, renovation, remodeling, maintenance, repair or demolition that has a reasonable possibility of disturbing or releasing asbestos into the air, you must first have a good faith inspection done by an accredited inspector (or be reasonably certain asbestos will not be disturbed, or assume it will be and take the maximum precautions federal and state rules require), keep a written report or statement of assumption, and give a copy to every contractor before they bid or apply for the work. Starting work without the inspection report or statement, or without the additional written description of the project the asbestos project rules require, carries a mandatory fine of at least $250 for each violation, each day counting separately, and the work must stop until the requirements are met. Only certified asbestos workers under the on-site supervision of a certified asbestos supervisor may remove or encapsulate asbestos, and a project needs prior written notice to the Department of Labor and Industries unless it involves less than 48 square feet of surface area or less than 10 linear feet of pipe, unless the pipe's surface area is greater than 48 square feet (even an exempt project must keep its reports, statements and written descriptions for the department; an emergency project is reported within three working days after it starts). The owner exemption covers only individuals working on their own single-family residence no part of which is used for any commercial purpose; whether a home you rent out is used for a commercial purpose is not settled by the statute, and no Washington case was searched, so the cautious course is to treat a rental as covered. The statute's copies of the report go to contractors, the department and representatives of exposed employees, not to tenants. Your general duties still apply: keep the premises in substantial compliance with the codes that govern their maintenance where a condition endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety, and enter for repairs only with two days' written notice except in an emergency (`landlords-access-wa`). Not covered by this row: the asbestos rules of regional clean air agencies and the Department of Labor and Industries' worker-safety rules (neither is in the corpus), and city or county ordinances. A city or county rule requiring landlords to give tenants information about a property takes effect only once a summary and link are posted on the state's municipal research website, which lists those requirements by jurisdiction; check it for your area. Cautious course: before any repair or renovation that could disturb old building materials (ceilings, flooring, pipe or duct insulation), get the good faith inspection, use certified workers for any asbestos removal, and tell tenants in advance about work in or near their unit.

title: Pest Control and Pesticide Notices in Washington Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute, and no regulation in the held WAC titles, requires you to give tenants notice before pest control treatment inside a rental, or sets a waiting period, a pesticide disclosure or a re-entry rule written for tenants. The pest control duties themselves are in `edu-pest-control-wa`, and the optional cooperation clause is `pest-cooperation-wa`. Treating inside a unit is an entry: except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give the tenant at least two days' written notice stating the date and time or time window and a telephone number for objections, and enter only at reasonable times (`landlords-access-wa`). Outdoor treatments carry the state's posting rules, which bind the certified pesticide applicator, not you as landlord. A certified applicator making a landscape application (any registered pesticide applied to the exterior landscape around residential property or commercial property such as apartments) must, at the time of the application, place a marker at the usual point of entry to residential property, or, at apartments and other commercial property, a marker in a conspicuous location at or near each site treated. The owner or tenant removes the marker on the schedule set by Department of Agriculture rule. The landscape rules do not cover commercial applicators making structural (building) applications, or private applicators. If a tenant is on the Department of Agriculture's list of pesticide-sensitive individuals and lives in an apartment or condominium, an applicator making a landscape application to that person's notification area must notify the person at least two hours before the scheduled application, or ask the manager or the owner's representative to notify them; the statute does not itself put the duty on you, but if an applicator asks you to pass the notice on, do it promptly. Anyone may ask the applicator in writing for the names and safety data sheets of the pesticides used on a landscape. Not covered: the Department of Agriculture's pesticide rules (chapter 16-228 WAC) are not in the corpus, and city or county ordinances (a local rule requiring landlords to give tenants information about a property takes effect only after it is posted on the state's municipal research website, which lists such rules by jurisdiction). Cautious course: give tenants the two-day entry notice for any indoor treatment, include the product name and any preparation or re-entry instructions from the pest control operator, and have outdoor applications done by a certified applicator who posts the markers.

title: Contaminated Property and Environmental Covenants in Washington Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws makes you tell a prospective tenant that a rental is contaminated, sits on or near a cleanup site, or is subject to a recorded environmental covenant, and none requires a contamination statement in a lease. The seller disclosure statement's environmental questions do not reach a lease, because that chapter does not apply to an interest less than fee simple (other than a buyer's interest under a real estate contract). Three rules still reach a rental. (1) Drug-lab contamination (chapter 64.44 RCW, `edu-meth-contamination-wa`): if you believe a tenant contaminated a unit that is now vacated or abandoned, you must contact the local health officer; the officer posts a warning, and an order declaring the property unfit is served on all occupants, posted, and filed with the county auditor. Entering or removing property found unfit is a misdemeanor except for officials, authorized contractors and owners doing approved decontamination, and anyone the officer or a court allows. Reuse needs a certified contractor's decontamination under an approved work plan, retesting and a recorded release for reuse, at your cost. A unit you have been told is condemned or unlawful to occupy may not be rented until the conditions are fixed (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). (2) Environmental covenants (chapter 64.70 RCW): when the Department of Ecology or another agency approves a cleanup that leaves activity or use limits on land, the covenant is recorded, runs with the land, and may restrict uses zoning would allow. A copy must be given, by the persons and in the manner the agency requires (or by the grantor if the agency names no one), to each person in possession of the property when the covenant is executed, which includes a tenant then in possession. Later tenants get no copy by statute. Ecology keeps a public registry of covenants. (3) A city or county may require landlords to give tenants information about a property or its surroundings, but only once the requirement is posted on the state's municipal research website, which lists such rules by jurisdiction. The library offers no Washington contamination or covenant clause: each covenant's limits are site-specific and set by the agency, so a template could not state them. If your property carries a recorded environmental covenant, you may add your own clause or rule stating its use limits (for example no digging, gardening or wells) with legal advice; a rule must be brought to the tenant's attention at the start of the tenancy, or adopted later on 30 days' written notice and effective only at the end of the lease term or sooner by agreement, to bind the tenant (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). Cautious course: check Ecology's covenant registry and the county records before renting a property with an industrial or cleanup history, tell applicants about any use limits that affect them, and never rent a unit under a health officer's unfit order.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no defective drywall disclosure. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to tell a tenant (or a buyer) about defective, corrosive or imported drywall, or to put a drywall statement in a lease; the word drywall appears only in building-code, setback and public-works wage provisions. Your ordinary duties cover the condition: keep the premises fit for human habitation, keep the walls and other structural components in reasonably good repair, and keep the electrical, plumbing, heating and other facilities and appliances you supply in reasonably good working order, and the tenant's repair remedies apply if you don't after written notice (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`, `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). Cautious course: if you know of drywall that is damaging wiring, plumbing or appliances or causing odors, fix it, and answer applicants' questions truthfully; this library offers no drywall clause.

title: No Proposition 65-Style Chemical Warning for Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord to post or give a warning that a rental may expose tenants to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and none requires such a statement in a lease. Washington's chemical laws (for example the safer products and cosmetics chapters) regulate manufacturers and products, not rental housing. The hazard disclosures Washington does require of landlords are the fire safety notice (`fire-safety-notice-wa`), the mold information (`mold-disclosure-wa`), the flood disclosure for leases entered into after December 31, 2026 (`flood-disclosure-wa`) and the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing (`lead-based-paint`). Don't copy California's warning sign into a Washington lease: it states nothing Washington law requires and can mislead tenants about the property.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures in Washington
bodyText: This topic bundles three California-style disclosures. Washington has none of them as a lease disclosure, but it has rules on two of the subjects. (1) Former ordnance or military sites: no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to tell a tenant about former military ordnance or munitions sites near a rental (see also `edu-no-military-zone-disclosure-wa`). (2) Planned demolition: there is no duty to tell an applicant that you have applied for a demolition permit. Once a tenancy exists, demolition, substantial rehabilitation or a change of use is a just cause only after written notice at least 120 days before the tenancy ends (not in a city or county that has a relocation assistance program under the state enabling law and otherwise gives 120 days' notice), and it cannot end a fixed term early unless you and the tenant agree in writing and the tenant gets at least 60 days to vacate (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). In a city or county that requires relocation assistance for low-income tenants displaced by demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use, a person who moves in after you apply for the necessary permit is not entitled to that assistance only if, before taking possession, they received your written notice specifically describing the activity or condition that may displace them and advising them that they are not eligible for relocation assistance. If you rent a unit after applying for such a permit in one of those jurisdictions, give that written notice before move-in; the library offers no fixed text because the local program sets the details. (3) Shared utility meters: no Washington statute requires you to disclose that a meter serving the unit also serves other areas; the utility rules and the lack of a submetering statute are in `edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`. Recurring utility charges stated in the lease are rent. A city or county may add local disclosure duties, but only once they are posted on the state's municipal research website, which lists them by jurisdiction.

title: Inspection Findings and Condemnation Orders: Washington Bars Renting Rather Than Requiring Disclosure
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to give an applicant or tenant a list of outstanding code violations, inspection findings or condemnation orders, or to put them in the lease. Washington instead bars renting the unit. (1) Once a building, housing or other code agency has notified you that a dwelling is condemned or unlawful to occupy because of code violations, you may not enter into a rental agreement for it until the conditions are corrected; if you knowingly do, the tenant recovers the greater of three months' rent or up to treble damages, plus costs and attorneys' fees, and gets back all deposits and prepaid rent if the tenant leaves or the agency orders them out. Relocation assistance and the freeze on evictions, reduced services and rent increases after an agency's first notice are in `edu-condemned-premises-wa`. (2) A city or county with a rental inspection program may tell you that until a certificate of inspection is provided it is unlawful to rent the unit or let a tenant keep occupying it (`edu-rental-inspection-wa`); if you inspect only a sample of units, every unit gets written notice of how to ask for repairs. (3) Orders declaring a dwelling unfit under a city or county unfit-dwelling ordinance, and health officer orders for drug-lab contamination, are posted on the property and filed with the county auditor, so they are public (`edu-hazardous-contamination-disclosure-wa`). (4) The Department of Labor and Industries may post a prohibited lease notice on a manufactured home offered for lease that has alterations hazardous to life, safety or health; you may not lease or offer it while the notice is posted, and it stays until the violations are corrected, inspected and approved and the fees are paid. (5) A unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable, where continued habitation would expose you to civil or criminal penalties, is a just cause on 30 days' written notice (or as much as the order allows) (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Answer applicants' questions truthfully; a city or county may add disclosure duties once they are posted on the state's municipal research website. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Washington Rentals: Federal Disclosure and State Renovation Rules
bodyText: Washington has no lead-safe certificate for rentals: no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to register a pre-1978 rental, have it periodically certified lead-safe, or attach a state lead certificate to the lease, and the 2025 amendments to the state lead program added none. What applies instead: (1) The federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978 (other than housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities, or a 0-bedroom dwelling, unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there): before the tenant is obligated under the lease you give the EPA pamphlet, disclose known lead-based paint and hazards and provide available records, and the lease must include, as an attachment or within the lease, the federal Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure, the list of records and the signed acknowledgments; keep a copy for at least 3 years from the start of the lease. The library's tagged federal clause is `lead-based-paint` (`edu-lead-based-paint-wa`). Leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension, and renewals where you already disclosed everything and have nothing new, are exempt. (2) The only certificate the federal rule recognizes is optional: a lease of pre-1978 housing that a certified inspector has found to be lead-based paint free is exempt from the federal disclosure. In Washington lead inspectors are certified by the Department of Commerce. (3) The state renovation, repair and painting program: renovation for compensation that disturbs painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing must be done by a firm certified by the Department of Commerce, directed by a certified renovator, following the state work practices; no more than 60 days before work in a unit you do not occupy, the firm must give you and an adult occupant the pamphlet "The Lead-Safe Certified Guide to Renovate Right" and get a written acknowledgment (in the language of the lease) or a certificate of mailing, and for common areas it must notify each affected unit in writing or post signs. Exceptions include components a certified inspector, risk assessor or renovator has determined are lead-free, and emergency renovations for the notice rules. The rules do not say whether work you or your employees do on your own rental counts as renovation "for compensation"; no Washington case was searched, so the cautious course is to use a certified firm or certified renovator for any work that disturbs paint in a pre-1978 rental.

title: No Shoreline or Public Access Disclosure for Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington has no shoreline or public-access disclosure for leases. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to tell a tenant about public rights-of-way to the shore, public tidelands, beach access or shoreline master program limits, and the Shoreline Management Act (chapter 90.58 RCW) puts no duty on landlords or tenants; it regulates development on shorelines through local shoreline master programs and permits. Related rules: for leases entered into after December 31, 2026 you must disclose that the property may be in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding, that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, and that hazard information is available from the county (`flood-disclosure-wa`). The state leases its own aquatic lands and tidelands under its own leasing chapters, which do not reach a residential lease of upland property. The seller disclosure statement does not apply to a lease. If your rental includes a dock, beach or waterfront area, say in the lease or your rules what the tenant may use, and get advice on any shoreline permit before building or altering a structure there. A city or county may add its own disclosure duty once it is posted on the state's municipal research website.

title: Key Control, Smart Locks and Biometric Data in Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington has no key-control policy mandate: no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a written key-control policy, a key log, rekeying between tenants, or background checks of staff who hold keys, for any size of complex. What the law does require: provide reasonably adequate locks and furnish keys to the tenant, and maintain and safeguard with reasonable care any master key or duplicate keys to the unit (`edu-security-devices-wa`). Holding a key gives no extra right of entry: you may enter only as the entry statute allows (two days' written notice, one day for showings, or an emergency or abandonment) (`landlords-access-wa`). Two lock rules override any lease term: a tenant who is, or whose household member is, a victim of sexual assault, stalking or unlawful harassment by the landlord may change or add locks at the tenant's expense, giving you written notice and the supporting document within seven days; and a tenant with a court order granting possession to the exclusion of a cotenant may ask you to replace or rekey a lock at the tenant's expense, and you must do it and must not give the new key to the excluded person (`edu-dv-lockchange-wa`). From January 1, 2027, if your building uses a smart access system (an app, card, fob or biometric entry, but not a keypad code), you must offer a tenant who asks a key that uses no biometrics and no phone app, give tenants a plain-language data policy at lease signing or within five days of installation, and collect only the listed data (`edu-smart-access-wa`). Biometric entry also brings two general privacy laws. The biometric identifiers chapter (chapter 19.375 RCW) reaches you as a person who enrolls biometric identifiers, but its notice-and-consent and disclosure limits apply only to enrollment or disclosure for a commercial purpose (selling or disclosing for marketing unrelated to the original transaction), and it expressly needs no notice or consent for a security purpose, so using fingerprints or face scans only to open doors is outside its consent rule; selling or sharing them for marketing is not, and the Attorney General enforces it. The consumer health data chapter (chapter 19.373 RCW) counts biometric data as consumer health data and requires a published privacy policy, opt-in consent before collection (unless necessary to provide a service the consumer requested), separate consent before sharing, and reasonable security, with Consumer Protection Act remedies; whether a landlord's door-access biometrics fall under it, or under its security exemption, is not settled by the statute and no Washington case was searched. Cautious course: don't make biometrics the only way in, get each user's separate written opt-in consent before enrolling them, publish a privacy policy, never sell or share the data, and delete it when the tenancy ends. The library offers no key-control clause for Washington; the tagged `keys` clause covers key receipts, return and replacement.

title: Recycling and Organics Notices for Washington Rentals: Local Option Only
bodyText: No statewide Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires every landlord to tell tenants where and how to recycle, or to put recycling terms in the lease. Washington leaves it to cities and counties, and gives you a general garbage duty. (1) Garbage: except in a single-family residence, you must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles in common areas for ashes, rubbish and garbage and arrange for reasonable and regular removal (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`); the tenant must properly dispose of rubbish, garbage and other organic or flammable waste from the unit at reasonable and regular intervals. (2) Local multifamily rules (since July 27, 2025): a city or county may require owners or operators of new or existing multifamily residential buildings to do any combination of: provide space to put organics and recycling containers next to the garbage containers, or, if that is not possible, post signs telling residents where they are; label organics containers with signs and colors that distinguish organics, recycling and garbage; and give residents waste-sorting educational material every year. Check your city or county's solid waste code. (3) Local collection: a city's solid waste or recycling ordinance may require property owners and occupants to use its collection system and make unpaid charges a lien on the property; local solid waste plans submitted after July 1, 2026 must phase in organics collection from multifamily residences, including all newly built or substantially remodeled multifamily buildings, with waivers possible for existing buildings without enough space. The business organics mandate does not apply to a multifamily residential entity. (4) New buildings: the state building code requires space for recycling, compost and solid waste storage in new buildings other than Group R-3 and U occupancies (for example, detached one- and two-family homes), available to occupants and haulers. The library offers no recycling clause for Washington, because what must be said depends on the local ordinance; if your city or county requires signs or annual material, you can add your building's recycling and organics instructions to your rules or the lease. A rule adopted after move-in takes effect only after 30 days' written notice and at the end of the lease term or sooner by agreement (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`).

title: No Waterbed Rule for Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington has no waterbed rule for rentals. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to allow a waterbed or other liquid-filled furniture, lets you charge a special waterbed deposit or fee, or sets an insurance amount for one. The library's Washington common-area clause already says the tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your prior written consent (`common-area-use-wa`), so no separate waterbed clause is offered. If you consent on conditions, the general rules apply: any money held as security for the waterbed is a deposit, which requires a written lease stating when it may be withheld, a signed move-in condition checklist, and the itemized statement and refund within 30 days after the tenancy ends; a nonrefundable charge must be stated in a written lease as nonrefundable or it is treated as a refundable deposit (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`). You may require the tenant to insure the item, but not use insurance or the lease to release yourself from your own liability (`edu-renters-insurance-wa`). Damage the waterbed causes is tenant-caused damage the tenant pays for (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`). A request to use a particular bed as a disability accommodation is decided under fair housing rules, not a lease ban.

title: Candidates, Canvassers and Political Signs at Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington gives candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators and canvassers no right to come onto your rental property. No statute in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Washington Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a residential landlord under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) to let them into a building, a hallway or a common room, to knock on tenants' doors, to keep a voter-registration area, or to host tenants' political meetings. (In the election code "canvassing" means examining and counting ballots, not door-to-door campaigning.) So access by outsiders is yours to control by rule. A rule binds the tenant only if it is reasonable, doesn't violate the act or other law, and was brought to the tenant's attention at initial occupancy; a new rule needs 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant and takes effect at the end of the term, or sooner if the tenant agrees (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). Write any no-solicitation rule so it applies evenly to non-residents and doesn't reach the tenant's own political activity or a visitor the tenant invites into the unit (`guest-policy`). Three limits apply. First, retaliation: while the tenant complies with the act, you may not evict, raise rent, cut services or add obligations to punish a good-faith complaint to a government authority about a code violation that may endanger health or safety, or the tenant's assertion of rights under chapter 59.18 RCW (`edu-retaliation-wa`). Organizing and political activity are not themselves on that list (`edu-no-tenant-organizing-rule-wa`), but don't adopt or enforce an access rule in response to a complaint. Second, signs: any person who removes or defaces lawfully placed political advertising, including yard signs, without authorization commits a misdemeanor, each sign a separate violation. No Washington statute says whether a lease rule makes a tenant's sign unlawfully placed, and no published Washington case deciding it was searched for, so enforce a sign rule by written notice to the tenant rather than by taking the sign down yourself. In a condominium or homeowners association, the association can't ban candidate or ballot-issue signs (and, under the older homeowners' association act until January 1, 2028, political yard signs before an election), but that limit binds the association, not you (`edu-no-display-rule-wa`). Third, the boundary: in a mobile home park under chapter 59.20 RCW the landlord may not stop candidates for public office from meeting tenants in their homes or bar tenants' political caucuses in open community halls, but lot tenancies are outside this library. Check local law before enforcing a blanket ban.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays at Washington Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute gives a residential tenant a right to display a religious or cultural item (a doorpost item, a wreath, a prayer flag, a home shrine or holiday decorations) over your lease rules, and none limits a landlord's display rules as such; the search covered the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Washington Constitution and the 2025-2026 session laws. What limits your rule is the Washington Law Against Discrimination. It is an unfair practice for any person, because of creed, national origin, race or another protected class, to discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the facilities or services provided with it, or to expel a person from occupancy, and the Human Rights Commission's rules say creed discrimination includes religious discrimination under the federal Fair Housing Amendments Act. The federal Fair Housing Act likewise bars religious discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of renting (`edu-fair-housing-wa`). So a rule that lets some displays stay but bans those of one faith or culture, or is enforced that way, is the risk. The same act keeps your right to post and enforce reasonable rules of conduct and safety for all tenants and their guests. Keep any display rule content-neutral (size, placement, fire safety, blocked doors and exits, damage to doors and walls), bring it to the tenant's attention at move-in or adopt it on 30 days' written notice effective at the end of the term (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`), apply it to everyone, and consider allowing small door or doorframe items that cause no damage. Don't remove or damage a tenant's religious item yourself: maliciously and intentionally damaging another person's property because of that person's perceived religion is a hate crime offense, and a lease dispute is enforced by notice, not self-help. Condominiums and HOAs: Washington's association statutes protect flags and political signs, not religious items, and they bind the association, not you as landlord. Until January 1, 2028, two regimes run side by side. A homeowners' association under chapter 64.38 RCW may not bar an owner's or resident's outdoor display of the United States flag or a flagpole for it, or political yard signs before an election (subject to reasonable rules on placement and manner); an association under chapter 64.90 RCW (a community created on or after July 1, 2018, or one that elected in) may not bar the United States or Washington state flag or a flagpole for it, or signs about candidates or ballot issues, on or within a unit or limited common element, subject to reasonable rules. Older condominiums under chapters 64.32 and 64.34 RCW have no flag or sign statute. From January 1, 2028, chapter 64.90 RCW applies to all common interest communities and its flag and sign rules reach every association (`edu-no-display-rule-wa`, `edu-hoa-wa`). The Law Against Discrimination doesn't apply to sharing a dwelling unit, or renting or subletting part of one, that the owner or sublessor will occupy.

title: EV Charging Rules That Reach Washington Rentals
bodyText: Washington gives a residential tenant no right to install an EV charger and puts no EV duty on a landlord in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (`edu-no-ev-charging-rule-wa`). The rules that do reach you come from building, utility, weights-and-measures and condominium law. New construction: the state building code requires EV charging infrastructure in new buildings and accessory structures with on-site parking, including parking lots and garages. For apartment buildings (Group R, more than two units, no private garages) the current table requires EV charging stations at 10% of parking spaces, EV-ready spaces (a 40-amp, 208/240-volt circuit ending at an outlet or charger) at 25%, and EV-capable spaces (raceway and panel capacity) at 10%; a building of no more than two dwelling units, or a unit with a private garage, needs one EV-ready space per unit. On-site parking with fewer than 10 spaces is exempt for residential buildings, as is a site with no utility power or dwelling units without garages or other on-site parking. New dwelling units under the residential code with an attached private garage or carport need one dedicated 40-amp 208/240-volt circuit per unit. These rules govern construction and permits; they don't require you to add chargers to an existing building, and the current versions took effect March 15, 2024. Any charger must be installed under the state electrical law (chapter 19.28 RCW) and the National Electrical Code. Billing for electricity: if your power comes from a utility the utilities commission regulates, its rules say a customer may not resell electricity unless the utility's tariff specifically allows it, so check your utility's tariff before charging tenants by the kilowatt-hour (`edu-no-submetering-statute-wa`). A charger that measures and bills electricity used for commercial purposes falls under the state weights and measures law (an annual registration fee per charger port, and Department of Agriculture rules on electricity sold as vehicle fuel for equipment placed in service from January 1, 2024). If you open a charger to the public, the price-disclosure, payment-method, reporting and signage rules for publicly available chargers apply; a charger reserved only for residents or tenants is generally not publicly available, but whether an apartment building fits the statute's exemption for chargers reserved for residents of a private residence or common interest community is not settled by the statute. The utilities commission doesn't regulate the rates of an entity that offers battery charging to the public for hire unless it is otherwise a regulated electrical company. No Washington tax aimed at electricity sold through EV chargers was found. Condominiums and HOAs: the association may not unreasonably restrict a unit owner from installing a charger in the unit or the owner's designated parking space, but may require an application, a licensed electrical contractor, insurance naming the association (not in an association of single-family homes, site condominiums or a planned development whose units are not immediately adjacent), registration within 30 days and payment for the electricity; that right belongs to the unit owner (you, if you own the unit), not to your tenant. If you agree to a tenant's charger, put the terms in a written agreement with advice: the library doesn't offer a Washington installation clause (see the notes), and you may not make a tenant indemnify you for your own liability (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`).

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking at Washington Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute governs EV chargers in parking shared by tenants of a rental: nothing gives a tenant a right to install one in a shared lot or garage, to reserve the space in front of it, or to use a charger you provide, and nothing sets a fee or damage rule for one. The search covered the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Washington Constitution and the 2025-2026 session laws. So a shared charger is your amenity, run on terms you set in the lease or your written parking rules (`parking-vehicle-rules`, `assigned-parking-space`, `common-area-use-wa`); a rule adopted mid-tenancy needs 30 days' written notice and takes effect at the end of the term unless the tenant agrees (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). Rules that can still apply: if you build new parking, the building code sets EV charging, EV-ready and EV-capable percentages, including for accessible spaces (`edu-ev-charging-requirements-wa`); if you bill tenants for the power, check your utility's tariff on resale and the weights and measures law; and if you open the charger to the public, the publicly available charger rules apply, including signage, and parking in a publicly available charger space without being plugged in is a $124 parking infraction. A charger you designate only for your tenants is generally not publicly available, so the infraction usually won't reach it, but equipment in a lot or garage that any member of the public can drive into is treated as publicly available, and whether the exemption for chargers reserved for residents reaches an apartment building is not settled by the statute (`edu-ev-charging-requirements-wa`). In a condominium or HOA under chapter 64.90 RCW, the association may install chargers in the common elements for all unit owners and must then set terms of use, and may let a unit owner install one in the owner's designated parking space without reallocating common elements; those rights run to unit owners, not to your tenant. If a tenant installs a charger in a shared area with your written consent, charge the tenant for damage only on the fault basis the landlord-tenant act uses (the tenant, family, invitees or others under the tenant's control; `tenant-caused-damage-wa`), not for damage you or your contractor cause, and don't try to bind a later tenant of the space through this lease.

title: A Tenant's EV Charger When a Washington Tenancy Ends
bodyText: No Washington statute says who owns, or who must remove, an EV charger a tenant installed when a residential tenancy ends; the search covered the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Washington Constitution and the 2025-2026 session laws. Unlike some states, Washington has no tenant-EV statute making the charger the tenant's property or letting the tenant sell it to you. Under the library lease, a charger is an alteration that needs your written consent, and an approved alteration stays part of the property at the end of the term unless you require its removal (`no-alterations`). So settle ownership, removal and restoration in writing before the charger goes in. Whether a charger bolted to the building becomes part of the real property under the common law of fixtures is a question only case law could settle, and no published Washington case was searched. At move-out the ordinary rules apply: the tenant must not intentionally or negligently damage or remove any part of the structure, its facilities or equipment; you may deduct from the deposit only for damage beyond ordinary wear that the tenant, family, invitees or others under the tenant's control caused, documented against the move-in checklist (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`, `edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`); and a charger or other personal property left behind is handled under the abandoned-property rules (`edu-abandoned-property-wa`, `surrender-end-of-term-wa`). Two boundaries: in a condominium or HOA, the unit owner (you, if you own the unit) may remove a charger installed at the owner's cost if it comes out without damaging others' property, and the association need not buy it; and on a mobile home lot, improvements a tenant bought and installed stay the tenant's property even if affixed, but lot tenancies are outside this library.

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no statute about tenant portals as such, but several rules decide what a portal can and can't do. Rent: you must accept a personal check (except for nine months after a tenant's check to you bounced or hit a closed account), a cashier's check or a money order, and you must let the tenant pay by mail unless you provide an accessible on-site place to pay. A lease may not require rent to be paid by electronic means only; if you knowingly use a lease with that term, the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees. So a portal can be an added way to pay, never the only one (`acceptable-payment-methods-wa`). Give a receipt for cash you accept and a written receipt for other payments on request. A recurring portal or technology charge in the lease is part of rent and falls under the rent-increase rules (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`); no Washington statute names a per-payment convenience fee. Electronic signatures and notices: Washington's electronic-transactions act applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse later electronic transactions; that right can't be waived in the lease. A written notice sent through the portal counts only if the tenant can print or store it. Where a statute requires a particular delivery method, that method still controls: notices that end a tenancy or start an eviction must be served personally, or left with a person of suitable age and discretion and mailed, or posted, delivered to a resident and mailed, so posting them to a portal is not service (`edu-notice-delivery-wa`, `electronic-signatures`, `notices`). Your website: if you keep a website that advertises rentals or serves as a source of information for current or prospective tenants, its home page must say whether you accept a comprehensive reusable tenant screening report. Apps that open doors: from January 1, 2027, if the portal or its app is part of a smart access system, a tenant who asks must get an alternative key that needs no phone app and no biometrics, and the system may collect only the data the statute lists, including log-ins for the online tools that manage building accounts (`edu-smart-access-wa`). If the portal stores tenants' log-ins, bank or health information, or biometric data, Washington's breach-notice, disposal and consumer health data laws can apply to you (topic `tenant-confidential-information`).

title: Protecting Tenant and Applicant Information in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no general statute that stops a landlord from sharing what it knows about a tenant or applicant; the search covered the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Washington Constitution and the 2025-2026 session laws. Several specific laws limit what you may collect, how you must protect and dispose of it, and when you must report a breach. Medical information: you may not ask about, consider or require disclosure of a tenant's or applicant's medical records or history unless it is necessary to evaluate a reasonable accommodation or modification request; a violation can cost up to two and one-half times the monthly rent plus costs and attorneys' fees. Victims: screening companies may not report that someone is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and the records a victim gives you to end a lease are protected (`edu-victim-confidentiality-wa`). Screening reports: a condominium or homeowners association may make an owner screen tenants but may not require the screening report or a tenant's background information to be given to the association (`edu-hoa-wa`). Knowingly and willfully getting a consumer report under false pretenses is a crime. The state credit-reporting act puts no re-disclosure limit on a landlord that receives a report; treat it as confidential anyway (`edu-tenant-screening-wa`). Breach notice: if you do business in Washington and own or license personal information (a name with a Social Security, driver's license, passport or account number and access code, full date of birth, health insurance number, medical information or biometric data; or a user name or e-mail with its password), you must notify each Washington resident whose unsecured information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorized person, in plain language and within 30 days after discovery (later only if law enforcement asks for a delay or the time is needed to determine the scope of the breach and restore the system), unless the breach is not reasonably likely to put them at risk of harm; if more than 500 residents are notified, tell the attorney general within 30 days too. Disposal: when you get rid of records, take all reasonable steps to destroy personal financial and health information and government-issued identification numbers (shred or erase them). Screening reports and anything taken from them have a federal disposal rule too: dispose of them by reasonable measures that protect against unauthorized access, such as shredding or burning paper and destroying or erasing electronic files so they can't practicably be read or reconstructed. A tenant hurt by a negligent failure can recover $200 or actual damages, and up to $600 or triple damages (capped at $10,000) if it was willful, plus attorneys' fees. Biometrics: Washington's biometric identifier law does reach a landlord, since it covers any individual or business, but its notice-and-consent duty applies only to enrolling a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose (selling or disclosing it for marketing unrelated goods or services); using fingerprints or face scans to secure a building is a security purpose it expressly excludes, and only the attorney general enforces it. The consumer health data law (chapter 19.373 RCW) is broader: it treats biometric data, and health information such as the details behind an accommodation request, as consumer health data. Any legal entity doing business in Washington that decides why and how such data is collected must keep a consumer health data privacy policy linked on its home page, collect the data only with consent or as necessary to provide what the tenant asked for, get separate consent before sharing it, honor access and deletion requests, limit staff access and keep reasonable security; violations are enforceable under the Consumer Protection Act. The statute doesn't say whether an individual owner of a few units is such an entity, and no case was searched, so collect biometric or health data only when the tenant's own request needs it, share it only with consent, and keep a written policy if you collect it. From January 1, 2027, smart access systems carry their own data and privacy-policy rules (`edu-smart-access-wa`). In the other direction, a lease entered into or renewed on or after July 27, 2025 may not require the tenant to sign a nondisclosure agreement about the lease or the offer (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`).

title: What You Can Recover When a Washington Tenancy Ends for Breach
bodyText: This row gathers what you can recover when a Washington tenancy under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) ends for the tenant's breach; the details sit in the rows named. Possession: you recover possession only through an unlawful detainer case in superior court, never by lockout or utility shutoff (`edu-eviction-process-wa`, `edu-self-help-eviction-wa`), and only for a cause the just-cause statute lists (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Judgment: if you win, the judgment restores possession and, where the case is for nonpayment or for breach of a lease condition, declares the tenancy forfeited. In the same judgment the court assesses the damages the unlawful detainer caused you that you plead and prove, any rent found due in a nonpayment case, and late fees only if the lease provides for them and they total no more than $75. It may award statutory costs, and attorneys' fees only as the act allows: none after a default, and none where the rent awarded is no more than two months' rent or $1,200, whichever is greater. The double-damages rule of the general unlawful detainer statute does not apply to these tenancies. In a nonpayment case the tenant can still pay and be reinstated before judgment or within five court days after it, or until the date of eviction if the tenant gives a pledge of financial assistance letter from a government or nonprofit entity; you must accept a pledge of emergency rental assistance that meets the statute's conditions and suspend the court action for 14 court days after giving the payment information; and the court may stay the writ on a payment plan (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). If you served the summons only by posting and mailing, the court can restore possession but cannot enter a money judgment until it has jurisdiction over the tenant. Money owed other than rent: the tenant's right to possession may not be conditioned on paying anything other than rent (apart from the reinstatement amounts), so collect late fees, damages and other charges by other lawful means, such as a separate suit or the deposit accounting (`edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`). Holdover and abandonment: a tenant who stays after the tenancy has lawfully ended owes you the damages you sustain, and you recover possession through the court (`holdover-wa`, `edu-holdover-rate-wa`). A tenant who defaults in rent and abandons owes the statutory measure (for a month-to-month tenancy, 30 days' rent; for a longer term, the lesser of the rent for the rest of the term or the re-renting measure), and you must make a reasonable effort to mitigate (`edu-abandonment-mitigation-wa`).
