Rent acceleration: no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws authorizes or regulates a lease clause making the rest of the term's rent due at once on default. Where the tenant abandons, the statute sets its own lesser-of measure, and a lease term that waives any section of the act is unenforceable, so the library offers no acceleration clause. Which court for money alone: you don't need to evict to sue for rent. A claim on the lease for money only, up to $100,000 per claimant, can be brought in district court, and the small claims department hears money claims up to $10,000 brought by a natural person and $5,000 in other cases (for example, a landlord company); the claim must be verified by the real claimant, and an assignee such as a collection agency can't use small claims. A case that involves the right to possession of the property goes to superior court as an unlawful detainer. A lease may make the tenant pay your attorneys' fees only as the act authorizes and a court awards, and any one-sided fee clause works both ways. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Naming Someone in the Lease to Accept Eviction Papers in Washington
bodyText: Some states let a lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. Washington has no statute or court rule that provides for this, and the library offers no such clause. For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), every notice that ends a tenancy or starts an eviction (the 14-day, 10-day, 3-day and just-cause notices) must be served the statutory way on the tenant: by personal delivery; or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the unit and mailing a copy; or, if neither works, by posting, delivering to a resident if one can be found, and mailing (`edu-notice-delivery-wa`, `edu-termination-notice-wa`). The eviction summons must be served the way a summons is served in any other civil case: on the tenant personally, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual home with a resident of suitable age and discretion, and if you can't serve personally after at least three attempts over not less than two days and at different times of the day, by posting at the unit and mailing by both regular and certified mail, each at least nine days before the return date, which limits the court to restoring possession (`edu-eviction-process-wa`). Those methods all run to the tenant or the tenant's home, and a lease term that waives any section of the act is unenforceable, so a clause sending notices to someone else could leave you with notices a court won't accept. The civil rules do accept, as proof that a summons was served, the written acceptance of the defendant or the defendant's agent or attorney; a tenant who has a lawyer or a person actually authorized to accept service can accept in writing at the time. Whether a person named in a lease signed at move-in counts as that agent is not settled by any statute or rule read, and no Washington case was searched; don't rely on one. Address confidentiality participants: a person certified in the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program (victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, trafficking or stalking, and some others) has designated the Secretary of State as their agent for service of process and receipt of mail. The statutes read don't say how that fits with serving eviction papers at the rental itself; if you know your tenant is a participant, take advice, and the cautious course is to serve at the unit by the statutory methods and also send a copy through the Secretary of State. Don't confuse this with your own agent: if you live outside Washington, the lease or a posted notice must name a person in the county who can accept notices and process for you (`landlord-disclosure-wa`). You may add your own clause naming a person to receive courtesy copies, with advice, but it can't replace statutory service on the tenant.

title: No Possession Bonds in Washington Leases: Court Bonds Only
bodyText: Some states let a landlord take a bond, often with a confessed judgment, that secures the tenant's surrender of possession at the end of the term. Washington has no such bond. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws provides for a possession bond in a residential lease, and for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) a lease may not authorize any person to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement; such a term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing it the tenant may recover actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Possession at the end of a tenancy is recovered only through an unlawful detainer case (`edu-eviction-process-wa`). The bonds Washington does have are court bonds inside that case. (1) If the court orders a writ of restitution at the show cause hearing but sends other issues to trial, no writ issues before final judgment until you file a bond in the amount the court sets, with a surety the clerk approves, conditioned that you will prosecute the case without delay and pay the tenant's costs and damages if the writ was wrongfully obtained. (2) In a nonpayment case, the tenant can stay a writ issued before final judgment, within three days after it is served, by paying into court or to you, as the court directs, all rent found due and then the monthly rent while the case is pending; this is a payment, not a bond. (3) If the writ rests on a finding of drug-related activity at the premises, neither the tenant nor anyone in possession may post a bond to keep possession. (4) The sheriff may not require a bond to serve or execute the writ. (5) A tenant who appeals and wants the case stayed meanwhile must file a bond with two or more sureties approved by the judge, conditioned to obey the court's order and to pay the rent and damages that accrue while the appeal is pending; chapter 59.18 RCW has no appeal-bond section of its own and doesn't exclude this one, so expect it to apply. The general unlawful detainer statute's own pre-judgment writ bond and tenant's bond to stay the writ do not apply to residential tenancies, and neither does the small-rent eviction chapter's bond to recall a writ. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction in Washington
bodyText: Washington's version of redemption is reinstatement in a nonpayment eviction (the full rules, including the court's payment-plan stay, are in `edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`; the notice is in `edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`). For tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) During the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice the tenant keeps the tenancy by paying the total on the notice, and any payment must first be applied to that total. (2) After you file, the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or anyone else interested in keeping the tenancy alive may pay into court or to you the rent due, court costs incurred so far, late fees due under the lease up to $75 in total and any attorneys' fees awarded, at any time before judgment or within five court days after it; the judgment is then satisfied, the tenant is restored to the tenancy, and you must file a satisfaction of judgment. A tenant reinstated after judgment in the previous 12 months pays an extra $50 for each such reinstatement. Execution on a nonpayment judgment waits those five court days; if the full amount isn't paid by then, the judgment can be enforced for money and possession. (3) If the tenant provides a pledge-of-financial-assistance letter from a government or nonprofit entity, the window runs until the date of eviction. You must accept a pledge of emergency rental assistance that covers the full rent if it comes before the pay-or-vacate notice expires, and after expiry if it will cover the rent due (including current rent) and the other reinstatement amounts; you then suspend the court case for 14 court days after giving the program your payment information, and accepting the pledge doesn't bind you to conditions beyond giving the payment information and documentation the program needs. Rental assistance and other benefits are a protected source of income, so don't refuse or treat differently money paid by a charity or agency (`edu-source-of-income-wa`). A lease can't require rent to be paid only electronically, and the statutory 14-day notice tells the tenant that payment may be made as the lease provides or by nonelectronic means, including cashier's checks, money orders and other certified funds. (4) Partial payments: no Washington statute prescribes reservation wording for accepting part of the rent before judgment, and a payment of less than the reinstatement amount doesn't reinstate the tenancy. Whether accepting part payment after serving a notice waives that notice is a question no statute read answers and no Washington case was searched for; take advice before accepting it, and record in writing what the payment does. After a writ of restitution issues, accepting a payment that only partly satisfies the judgment doesn't invalidate the writ unless you and the tenant sign a written agreement, and the eviction isn't stopped unless the sheriff gets a copy. (5) Any agreement in the eviction case that makes the tenant pay more than these limits or waives the tenant's reinstatement rights is void. How Washington's older relief-against-forfeiture statute adds to these rules is covered under the `forfeiture-redemption` topic. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Relief Against Forfeiture After an Eviction Judgment in Washington
bodyText: When you win an unlawful detainer case for unpaid rent or for breach of a lease condition, the judgment declares the tenancy forfeited. Washington gives the tenant three separate ways back, and they stack. (1) Reinstatement as of right in a nonpayment case: paying the rent due, court costs, late fees up to $75, any awarded attorneys' fees and $50 for each post-judgment reinstatement in the last 12 months, before judgment or within five court days after it (until the eviction date with a government or nonprofit pledge letter), satisfies the judgment and restores the tenancy (`edu-redemption-wa`). (2) A discretionary stay of the writ in a nonpayment case, on a payment plan of up to 90 days, sought before the writ is executed; a tenant served three or more pay-or-vacate notices in the prior 12 months generally can't use it (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`). (3) Relief against forfeiture under the general unlawful detainer statute: within 30 days after the judgment declaring the forfeiture, the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or anyone interested in continuing the tenancy may file a verified petition setting out the facts, served on you with notice, and you may appear and contest it. The court may then relieve the tenant of the forfeiture and restore the tenancy, but only on condition that the rent due is first paid in full, or the broken lease conditions are first fully performed so far as practicable. How (3) fits with (1) and (2) for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): the act says which sections of the general statute don't apply to residential tenancies (the double-damages judgment and three bond and pleading sections), and the relief-against-forfeiture section is not among them; the act also sends residential evictions through the general unlawful detainer chapter. So expect a court to treat relief against forfeiture as available to your tenants, as an additional, discretionary route that (unlike (1) and (2)) also reaches forfeitures for breach of a lease condition, and that can be sought after the five court days have run, up to 30 days after judgment. Its condition is full payment or performance, not a payment plan. Whether the act's limits on what a reinstating tenant must pay, or its three-notice bar, also limit this route is not settled by any statute read, and no Washington case was searched. What to do: for 30 days after the judgment, check the court file for a petition before re-letting the unit or disposing of the matter, since a granted petition restores the tenancy. Before suit, a tenant served with a 10-day notice to comply can save the tenancy by curing within the 10 days (`edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-wa`). Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Late Benefit Payments and Nonpayment Evictions in Washington
bodyText: Some states give a tenant a defense or an automatic continuance in a nonpayment eviction when a Social Security or other benefit payment arrives late. Washington has no such statutory defense: no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws, and no held court rule, requires a continuance, dismissal or reinstatement because a benefit check was late. What Washington does have, for tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW): (1) A due-date change. Where late fees can be charged after rent falls due, a tenant may propose in writing to move the rent due date, and you must agree if the tenant shows that their primary source of income is a regular, monthly source of government assistance that doesn't arrive until after the lease's due date; the new date may be no more than five days after the old one. This doesn't limit the tenant's right to ask for a reasonable accommodation. (2) Source-of-income protection. You may not evict, refuse to rent to, or set different terms for a tenant because their income is Social Security, SSI, public assistance, veterans benefits, a housing voucher, emergency rental assistance or another benefit program; a violation exposes you to liability of up to four and one-half times the monthly rent, plus costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-source-of-income-wa`). (3) Court discretion and assistance. After a nonpayment judgment, the court may stay the writ on a payment plan and must weigh, among other things, whether the nonpayment was caused by exigent circumstances beyond the tenant's control that are not likely to recur; you must accept a qualifying emergency rental assistance pledge, and the court stays the writ as needed for a tenant relying on one (`edu-eviction-hardship-stay-wa`, `edu-redemption-wa`). (4) Federal voucher rule. In a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, the housing agency's failure to pay it is not a lease violation, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy for the agency's nonpayment (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`). What to do: if a tenant tells you a benefit payment is late, consider the due-date change and a written payment arrangement before serving a 14-day notice, and never serve one for the voucher share. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Cold-Weather Limits on Evictions or Move-Outs in Washington
bodyText: Some states limit evictions or move-outs in cold weather, or require a tenant to give a cold-weather notice before vacating so pipes don't freeze. Washington has neither. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws, and no held state or local court rule, bars filing an eviction, entering a judgment or executing a writ of restitution in winter or in cold weather, and none requires a tenant to notify you before leaving a unit empty in freezing weather. The seasonal protections Washington does have run between a utility and its customer: from November 15 to March 15, a city utility, public utility district or commission-regulated electric or gas utility may not cut off residential space heating to a low-income customer who notifies it, applies for assistance and keeps to a payment plan, and utilities may not cut off residential service for nonpayment on a day with a National Weather Service heat-related alert. Those rules bind utilities, not you. As a landlord you may never intentionally cause a tenant's heat, water, electricity or gas to be cut off except briefly for repairs (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`, `edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`), and your duty to keep heating facilities working is in `edu-heating-wa`. Protecting an empty unit in winter: you may enter without consent only in an emergency (a burst or freezing pipe can be one) or after abandonment; otherwise give at least two days' written notice (`landlords-access-wa`). The library doesn't offer a Washington clause requiring tenants to keep the heat on or to report absences in winter; you may add your own with advice, but it can't give you entry rights beyond the statute, and any charge for freeze damage should reach only damage caused by the tenant, family, invitees or others under the tenant's control. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Forms and Work During a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Two rules found in other states have no Washington counterpart. First, no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a warning on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you hand a tenant to sign, or says that extra terms in such a form bind the tenant only with a warning. A tenant's notice under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) just has to be in writing and given at least 20 days before the end of a rental period (or before a fixed term ends); no form is prescribed (`edu-termination-notice-wa`). But the act defines a rental agreement as every agreement that establishes or modifies the terms of the use and occupancy of the unit, so a term in a move-out form the tenant signs is treated like a lease term: anything that waives a right under the act is unenforceable, the act's list of prohibited terms applies (for example, agreeing to pay your attorneys' fees beyond what the act allows, or waiving claims against you), and knowingly using a prohibited term exposes you to actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Keep a move-out form to the facts (the move-out date and a forwarding address) and handle the deposit through the statutory statement. Your own notices have fixed contents: each notice ending a tenancy must state the date by which the tenant must vacate or comply, and a just-cause notice must state the facts supporting the cause with enough detail for the tenant to prepare a defense; the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice follows the statutory form, and don't add demands for late fees or other non-rent charges as a condition of staying (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`, `edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Second, Washington has no statute specifically barring alterations that make a unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate is pending. Your duty to keep the premises fit for human habitation runs at all times during the tenancy, so it continues until the tenant actually leaves; you may not exclude the tenant or cut off utilities to hurry a move-out, and removing a tenant other than as the just-cause statute allows makes you liable for the greater of the tenant's damages or three months' rent, plus fees (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`). Demolition, substantial rehabilitation or a change of use needs 120 days' notice. The cautious course is to schedule work that affects an occupied unit after it is vacated, or to get the tenant's written agreement first. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Minors as Tenants and as Eviction Defendants in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no eviction-specific rule about minors: no statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws, and no held state or local court rule, bars or requires naming a minor in an unlawful detainer case. The general rules decide it. Who to name: in an unlawful detainer, no one other than the tenant, and any subtenant in actual occupation when you file, needs to be made a defendant, and anyone who moves in under the tenant after you file is bound by the judgment; a tenant's minor children who live there as occupants are not tenants and don't need to be named. Age and capacity: everyone is an adult at 18 for all purposes, including making contracts and suing and being sued without a guardian, so an 18-, 19- or 20-year-old can sign a lease and be bound like any adult. A person under 18 who marries a person of full age is treated as of full age. A minor's contract binds the minor, but the minor may disaffirm it within a reasonable time after turning 18 by returning the money and property still held from it, unless the minor's own misrepresentation of age, or doing business as an adult, gave you good reason to think the minor could contract. A minor emancipated by court decree has an adult's power to make nonvoidable contracts, set up a separate residence and sue and be sued in their own name. Suing a minor who is a tenant: a minor defendant must appear through a guardian, and the court appoints a guardian ad litem if there is none (the minor may apply within 30 days after service if 14 or older; otherwise you, a relative or a friend may apply); a summons against a minor under 14 is served on the minor personally and also on a parent, guardian or the person caring for the minor; and no default judgment may be entered against a minor who isn't represented by a general guardian or guardian ad litem. What to do: name the adult tenants; if a lease signer is under 18 and not emancipated or married to an adult, take advice before relying on the lease or suing on it. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: When a Washington Tenant Files Bankruptcy
bodyText: A tenant's bankruptcy is governed by federal law; Washington adds almost nothing. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws, and no held court rule, says whether a writ of restitution is executed after the sheriff or you learn that the tenant has filed bankruptcy. The one state rule is about money: if the sheriff learns before levying under a writ of execution or attachment that the defendant is a debtor in a bankruptcy case, the sheriff must tell you (or your attorney) in writing and isn't bound to levy. Federal law: (1) The automatic stay. Filing a petition generally stops the start or continuation of a court case against the tenant, any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate, and any act to collect rent or other claims that arose before the filing. (2) Judgment already entered. If you obtained a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay doesn't stop you from continuing the eviction, unless the tenant, with the petition, certifies that state law lets the tenant cure the entire monetary default after judgment and deposits with the bankruptcy clerk the rent that comes due in the next 30 days; the tenant then has 30 days to certify a full cure, after which the exception doesn't apply unless the court orders otherwise. Washington law does let a tenant pay after a nonpayment judgment in some cases (`edu-redemption-wa`, `edu-forfeiture-redemption-wa`), so expect tenants to be able to make that certification. You may object to a certification; the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. (3) Endangerment or illegal drugs. An eviction based on endangering the property or illegal use of controlled substances there is excepted if you file and serve a certification under penalty of perjury that the eviction has been filed or that the tenant did so in the 30 days before; the exception applies 15 days later unless the tenant objects, in which case the court holds a hearing within 10 days. (4) Otherwise, ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay. (5) The lease. In a chapter 7 case the trustee must assume or reject a residential lease within 60 days after the order for relief (or a court-extended time) or it is deemed rejected; in chapter 13 (and chapters 9, 11 and 12) the decision can wait until plan confirmation, though you can ask the court to set a deadline. A lease in default can be assumed only if the default is cured, or adequate assurance of a prompt cure and of future performance is given. A lease term that makes bankruptcy or insolvency itself a default can't be used to end the tenancy after the filing. What to do: when you get notice of a filing, stop collection and eviction steps until you confirm that an exception applies or you have relief from the stay, and take advice. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Trespass Notices at Washington Rental Properties
bodyText: Washington's trespass rules are the general criminal trespass statutes; nothing in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the held court rules sets a special trespass-notice procedure for rental property. A person commits criminal trespass by knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building (first degree, a gross misdemeanor) or on other premises (second degree, a misdemeanor). A person enters or remains unlawfully when not then licensed, invited or otherwise privileged to be there, and permission to be in the part of a building open to the public isn't permission to be in the parts that aren't. Defenses include that the premises were open to the public and the person complied with all lawful conditions on access, and that the person reasonably believed the owner, or another person empowered to license access, would have let them in. What this means for you: (1) You may tell a person who is not a tenant, an occupant or a tenant's guest to leave your common areas and not come back, and call the police if they return; give the notice in person or in writing and keep a record. No statute prescribes a form. (2) A tenant can invite guests to the tenant's own unit, and a guest who reasonably believes the tenant could let them in has a defense, so a trespass notice alone may not keep a tenant's guest away; whether a tenant can license a guest's passage through common areas you have barred is not settled by any statute read, and no Washington case was searched. (3) Never use trespass to remove a tenant or a legal occupant: only a court order can (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`). The police may remove a squatter on your sworn declaration, but that procedure may not be used to remove an occupant entitled to occupy under a rental agreement, or that occupant's guests or invitees, and you are liable for false statements in it. (4) For a person who entered without your permission and without any claim of right, you can also serve a three-day written notice and bring an unlawful detainer. (5) Guest limits in the lease are covered by the guest policy clause (`guest-policy`). The library doesn't offer a Washington clause obliging the tenant not to admit a person you have barred; you may add one with advice, but enforce it only through the 10-day notice to comply, and don't end a tenancy because a tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking (`edu-dv-eviction-protection-wa`). Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Owner Move-In Is a Statutory Cause: No Lease Reservation Needed
bodyText: In Washington you don't need, and the library doesn't offer, a lease clause reserving a right to end the tenancy so you or your family can move in. Owner occupancy is already one of the just causes in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), on its own terms (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). The cause: you, as landlord, in good faith seek possession so that the owner or the owner's immediate family (a spouse or state registered domestic partner, parents, grandparents, children including foster children, siblings and in-laws) may occupy the unit as that person's principal residence, and no substantially equivalent unit is vacant and available for them in the same building. The notice: at least 90 days' advance written notice of the date the tenant's possession is to end, served the way eviction notices are served and stating the facts that support the cause (`edu-notice-delivery-wa`). Good faith: if the owner or family member doesn't occupy the unit as a principal residence for at least 60 consecutive days during the 90 days after the tenant leaves, the law presumes you didn't act in good faith, and removing a tenant other than as the statute allows makes you liable for the greater of the tenant's actual damages or three months' rent, plus attorneys' fees and costs. Fixed terms: owner move-in can't end a fixed term before it is completed unless you and the tenant both agree in writing to end it early and the tenant gets at least 60 days to vacate. Whether that written agreement can be given in advance, in a lease signed at move-in, is not settled by any statute read, and a lease term that waives part of the act is unenforceable, so don't rely on a lease reservation: if you need the unit before the term ends, ask the tenant for a separate written agreement at the time. For a month-to-month tenancy, the 90-day notice can be given at any time. Related causes have their own rules: selling a single-family home (90 days), and sharing the dwelling or its kitchen or bathroom with the tenant (20 days). Your city may add longer notice or relocation payments; local ordinances aren't covered here. Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Pending Foreclosure to Tenants in Washington
bodyText:
Washington doesn't require you to tell a prospective or new tenant that the property is in foreclosure. No statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws, and no held court rule, requires a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure, a notice of default or a notice of trustee's sale before signing a lease or at any other time.

The foreclosure rules that protect tenants put the duties on others and start later (`edu-foreclosure-wa`): the trustee must send the notice of trustee's sale to the occupants of a single-family home or a building with fewer than five units, and when it elects to foreclose the occupants' interests it also posts and mails a notice addressed to the "Resident of property subject to foreclosure sale" telling them the foreclosure process has begun and that a renter may get a new rental agreement or a sixty-day notice to vacate from the new owner; after the sale, the purchaser must send tenants a statutory notice, and a tenant or subtenant in possession at the time of the sale must get 60 days' written notice to vacate before removal (except for waste or nuisance, and not where the borrower stays on as an occupant). Federal law adds its own protections against the new owner (`edu-ptfa-foreclosure-tenants`).

If the unit is foreclosed during the tenancy and the deposit isn't transferred to the successor, you, as the foreclosed-upon owner, must refund the full deposit immediately after the sale or transfer.

Because a tenant who signs while a foreclosure is pending may soon face a new owner, an optional written disclosure can protect you against a later claim that keeping quiet was misleading; the library's optional foreclosure disclosure clause records one (`foreclosure-disclosure-nv`). Whether Washington's Consumer Protection Act reaches a landlord's silence about a pending foreclosure is a question for case law.

Mobile home lot tenancies (chapter 59.20 RCW) are outside this library.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporate Landlord in Washington
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a corporation, LLC, partnership or other entity, hire a Washington lawyer for an eviction (unlawful detainer) case. Washington's court rule defining the practice of law includes representing another entity or person in a court, and practicing law without being an active member of the state bar or otherwise authorized by the Supreme Court is a crime (a gross misdemeanor the first time, a class C felony after that). No Washington statute or court rule in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved state court rules and local superior court rules lets an officer, member, manager, employee or property manager who is not a lawyer appear for an entity in superior court or in district court outside small claims, and no Washington case on the point was searched. So don't send a manager to file, sign or argue an eviction for the company. Eviction cases are heard in the superior court of the county where the property is. The one place an entity speaks for itself is the small claims department of district court. There, no lawyer, legal paraprofessional or anyone other than the plaintiff and defendant may take part without the judge's consent, and a corporation may not be represented by a lawyer or legal paraprofessional (except in a case a defendant transferred from district court, where the plaintiff's lawyer of record may continue). Small claims hears claims for money only, up to $5,000 in a case brought by anyone other than a natural person (for example, an LLC landlord suing for unpaid rent or damage), the claim must be verified by the real claimant, and an assignee such as a collection agency can't file it there. It can't give you possession. The statute doesn't say which person speaks for a company in small claims, so send an officer or employee who knows the facts and can show authority to act. If you own the property in your own name, you may appear for yourself: a party not represented by a lawyer signs and dates its own pleadings and gives its address. Separately, a foreign (out-of-state) entity doing business in Washington can't maintain a lawsuit here until it registers with the Secretary of State (`edu-nonresident-owner-agent-wa`).

title: How Long You Have to Sue a Washington Tenant
bodyText: Washington's general time limits for suing a tenant are in chapter 4.16 RCW, and two landlord-tenant statutes shorten them. General periods: an action on a written lease (or a liability arising out of a written agreement) must be started within six years; an action for rent or for the use and occupation of real estate also has six years; an action on an oral agreement that does not arise out of a writing has three years; and an action for waste or trespass upon real property has three years. A claim runs from when it accrues, so each missed rent payment generally starts its own clock. Shorter landlord-tenant periods: for a tenancy whose rental agreement began on or after July 23, 2023, any lawsuit against a tenant to recover sums exceeding the deposit must be started within three years after the rental agreement ends or the tenant abandons the premises. The sentence sits in the deposit-and-damage section but its words reach any such suit, and no Washington case on whether it covers unpaid rent was searched, so treat three years from the end of the tenancy as your deadline for every money claim against a former tenant under one of those agreements (`edu-deposit-damage-claims-wa`). If the tenant paid a fee in lieu of a security deposit, any lawsuit or other collection activity to recover losses from that tenant after move-out (unpaid rent, unpaid fees or damage beyond ordinary wear) must be started within one year after the rental agreement ends or the tenant abandons. Payments and promises: a payment made on the debt after it is due, but before the period runs out, restarts the period from that payment; a payment made after the period has expired does not revive it. A promise or acknowledgment extends the period only if it is in a writing signed by the tenant, and never after the period has expired. Whether a payment restarts the three-year or one-year periods measured from the end of the tenancy is not settled by those statutes, so don't rely on it. Other points: if, after the claim accrues, the tenant departs from and resides out of the state, or conceals themselves, the time of that absence or concealment is not counted; a short trip out of state does not stop the clock. That rule extends the periods in the general limitations chapter; it doesn't say it extends the three-year or one-year periods measured from the end of the tenancy, so don't rely on it for those. A case counts as started when you file the complaint or serve the summons, whichever is first, but you must complete the other step within 90 days. A judgment can be enforced for 10 years from entry, and the court grants an additional 10 years if you apply within the 90 days before the original 10 years end. No Washington statute lets a residential lease shorten or lengthen these periods (the Uniform Commercial Code permission to shorten applies to leases of goods), and no case on such a clause was searched, so the library offers none.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Method in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no rule like Oregon's that lets you and the tenant agree on an extra way, such as a text message, to give "actual notice" where the law requires it, and the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) doesn't use the term actual notice at all. Each Washington notice carries its own method instead. Eviction and termination notices must be served in one of the ways the unlawful detainer statute lists, and a lease can't add another (`edu-notice-delivery-wa`). Where a law only requires a notice in writing and names no delivery method, the electronic transactions act lets you deliver it electronically, but only if both of you have agreed to conduct transactions electronically, the tenant can store and print what you send, and the tenant keeps a right, which can't be waived, to refuse to do other transactions electronically. A law that names a delivery method still controls, and a law requiring regular mail can be varied by agreement only as far as that law allows. The act itself shows the narrow places where your agreement matters: for example, a tenant who gets a payment-plan stay of an eviction writ serves the order on you by personal delivery, first-class mail, fax, or email if the two of you agreed to email. Notice through your rent collector: if you don't live in Washington and you don't name an agent in the county for service of notices and process, the person to whom rent is paid is treated as that agent, so a notice the tenant gives to your property manager or rent collector reaches you in law (`landlord-disclosure-wa`). Federal law: a servicemember ending a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act may deliver the written notice and orders by hand, private carrier, return-receipt mail, or electronic means, including any electronic means reasonably calculated to ensure actual receipt by you or your agent, so treat an emailed termination notice with orders as delivered. Outside landlord-tenant law, Washington statutes use actual notice for other purposes (probate creditor notices, protection orders, and a fair housing rule protecting a bona fide tenant who has no actual notice of a discrimination charge), and the Uniform Commercial Code's general definition of notice applies to the transactions that code governs, such as sales and leases of goods, not to a lease of a home. The library offers no agreed-notice-method clause for Washington; the shared `notices` clause defers to every method the law requires.

title: Which Washington Landlord-Tenant Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) has no single rule that every notice must be written; it requires writing notice by notice, and a lease term that turns a required written notice into an oral one waives part of the act and is unenforceable. Notices you must give in writing: every notice that starts an eviction or ends a tenancy for cause (the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice, the 10-day comply-or-vacate notice, the 3-day notice to quit for waste or nuisance and the other just-cause notices), each served by a method the unlawful detainer statute allows and stating the facts known to you when you issue it (`edu-termination-notice-wa`, `edu-notice-delivery-wa`); the 60-day notice ending a tenancy at the end of its initial term where the act allows that; at least 90 days' written notice of a rent increase (30 days for a subsidized tenancy whose rent is based on income) (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`); 30 days' written notice of a new rule (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`); at least two days' written notice before entering, except in an emergency or where it is impracticable (`landlords-access-wa`); written notice of the tenant's failure to carry out a statutory duty, and the 30-day written notice to fix a condition affecting health and safety before you may do the work and bill for it; the 90-day notice before excluding children and the 120-day notices before a condominium conversion, demolition, substantial rehabilitation or change of use; immediate written notice of any change in the landlord's name and address, delivered personally or mailed and posted (`landlord-disclosure-wa`); and the deposit paperwork (a written rental agreement and checklist before collecting any deposit, written notice of where the deposit is held, and the written statement within 30 days after the tenancy ends). The fire safety notice and the screening criteria notice are written too (the screening notice may be posted instead). One entry notice is different: to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers or tenants, the act asks for at least one day's notice without saying written. Give it in writing anyway, so you can prove it. Notices the tenant must give in writing: 20 days' written notice to end a month-to-month tenancy, or to end a fixed-term tenancy at the end of the term; the repair notice that starts your repair deadlines (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`); a servicemember's notice with orders; a victim's notice to terminate; and a threatened tenant's notice to terminate. Where a statute requires writing but names no delivery method, email can satisfy it only under the electronic transactions act's conditions (`edu-notice-delivery-wa`).

title: Telling Tenants About Foreclosure or Other Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: No Washington statute requires you to tell a tenant, before or during the tenancy, that the property is being foreclosed, taken by condemnation, sold for taxes or put into receivership, or that a lawsuit about the property is pending; and no statute requires a tenant to forward to you a summons or other notice about a claim against the property. Washington delivers the foreclosure notices to the tenant directly instead. In a nonjudicial (trustee's) foreclosure of a single-family home, condominium unit or a building with fewer than five units, the trustee must post the notice of sale on the property or serve it on an occupant at least 90 days before the sale, and, to the extent it elects to foreclose its lien or interest, must also mail it to the occupants (whether or not the rental agreement is recorded). If the trustee elects to foreclose the occupants' interest, it posts and mails a statutory notice to the "Resident of property subject to foreclosure sale" saying the property may be sold in 90 days or more and that a tenant may get a new rental agreement or a 60-day notice to vacate. After a sale, a tenant in possession must get 60 days' written notice to vacate before removal (except for waste or nuisance) (`edu-foreclosure-wa`; for federal rules, `edu-ptfa-foreclosure-tenants`). Your own duties when a foreclosure happens: if the deposit is not transferred to the successor, you must refund the full deposit to the tenant immediately after the sale or transfer, or you are liable for up to twice the deposit. A taking by eminent domain is handled in the condemnation case and through the condemning agency's relocation program (`edu-eminent-domain-wa`); a code-enforcement condemnation of the unit triggers your relocation duties (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). Optional clause: a lease term asking the tenant to send you promptly any court paper or official notice about the property that arrives at the unit is lawful in Washington, but the library offers none, because the statutes above put the foreclosure notices in the tenant's hands and a damages or fee term attached to a forwarding duty would have to stay within the act's limits on charges and attorneys' fees. You may add your own forwarding clause with advice.

title: Police Cooperation, Crime-Free Programs and Reporting Duties in Washington
bodyText: Washington makes you a partner of the police only in narrow, named situations. No duty to cooperate as such: no Washington statute in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules requires a landlord, as landlord, to report a tenant's suspected crime, to hand over tenant information on request, or to sign a crime-free lease, and none requires the tenant to do those things. You also have no right to let officers into a unit on your own say-so: you may enter without the tenant's consent only in an emergency or on abandonment, and otherwise only with the tenant's consent, a court order or an arbitrator's order, so an officer who wants in without consent needs a warrant. Crime-free rental housing programs: a city, town or county may run a crime-free rental housing program (training classes, environmental design surveys and awareness training under police supervision). It must be voluntary, except that the local government may require you to take part once criminal activity on the premises exceeds a reasonable threshold and you haven't made a good faith effort to deter it, such as serving a comply-or-quit notice, filing an unlawful detainer or completing an approved landlord training program; before that, the police department must send you a notice of each occurrence giving its date and location, its nature and the name of the person involved. A program may charge a fee, but it may not stop you from renting to or hiring a person solely because of criminal history. This state chapter preempts local rules on the subject (local rules adopted before July 1, 2010 are outside the section's requirements). Local program rules are municipal law, which this library did not search. Notices the police send you: a law enforcement agency that seizes illegal drugs at a rental, or arrests a tenant for threatening another tenant with a firearm or other deadly weapon, unlawfully using such a weapon on the premises or physically assaulting someone there, must try to find you and notify you in writing. If the arrest was for threatening another tenant with a weapon, the threatened tenant may end the lease without further obligation if you don't file an unlawful detainer within seven calendar days after that notice (`edu-statutory-early-termination-wa`, `edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-wa`). Neighbors endangered by gang activity may serve you a ten-day notice and demand, and you must investigate and tell them what you did. Court-ordered help: under a court order for a pen register or trap and trace device, a landlord must furnish the officer the information, facilities and technical assistance needed, and is reasonably compensated. If an officer damages your property while searching a tenant's home in a drug case, you may claim against the government and then the forfeiture proceeds, after first applying the tenant's deposit. Duties that bind everyone, you included: a person who witnesses a violent offense, a sexual offense against a child or an assault likely to cause a child substantial bodily harm must notify law enforcement or other officials as soon as reasonably possible (a gross misdemeanor if not, unless reporting would put you or your household in danger); anyone who knows of human remains must notify the coroner, medical examiner or police (a misdemeanor if not); and an adult must report severe abuse of a child who lives with them. Victims: you may not end, refuse to renew or refuse a tenancy because a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. No Washington statute separately bars a lease term penalizing calls to the police, but treating a victim's call for help as a lease violation risks that rule, so don't.

title: When Washington Rental Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
No Washington statute ends a lease, abates or reduces rent, or lets a court cancel a lease because the property is taken by eminent domain, and none says what happens on a partial taking; that is left to the lease (the library's optional condemnation clause, `eminent-domain-vi`, applies in Washington).

How a taking works: the condemning body files a petition in superior court naming each owner, encumbrancer and other person interested and asks the court or a jury to fix compensation for the owners and for all tenants, encumbrancers and others interested; a notice of the petition is served on each person named in it, tenants included, at least ten days before it is presented.

In a state taking the jury fixes one lump sum for everyone interested. In a city taking, where the title is divided by a lease, the damages to each interest may be found separately on any party's request: the jury finds the value of the whole property as if one owner held it and then apportions it among the interests. Whether a lease term giving you the tenant's share binds the condemnor and the court is not settled by statute; between you and the tenant the lease term controls.

Relocation: a displacing agency (the state, a local public agency, or anyone with eminent domain authority under state law) must pay a displaced residential tenant's actual reasonable moving expenses or a scheduled moving allowance, and, if the tenant lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least 90 days before negotiations began, a replacement housing payment to rent a comparable dwelling for up to 42 months (it can go toward a down payment instead), plus advisory help. To the greatest extent practicable, no lawful occupant should have to move without at least 90 days' written notice, and if the agency lets an owner or tenant stay on short-term after acquiring the property, the rent may not exceed fair rental value. These payments come from the agency, are not part of the condemnation award, and are reviewed administratively, not by a lawsuit. Some local projects without federal money that began on or before December 31, 2017 may be outside these payments.

Your own relocation duty under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act for a condemned unit does not apply when the tenant's displacement is a direct result of acquisition by eminent domain; that duty is for code-enforcement condemnations (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). A rental of a dwelling back to its former owner whose property was condemned for a highway (chapter 47.12 RCW), certified by the consumer protection division, is outside the act.

title: Construction Liens and Work Your Tenant Orders in Washington
bodyText: Washington's construction lien law is chapter 60.04 RCW. Anyone who furnishes labor, professional services, materials or equipment for the improvement of real property has a lien upon the improvement for the contract price of what was furnished at the instance of the owner, or the owner's agent or construction agent. The land itself is subject to the lien only to the extent of the interest of the owner at whose instance (directly or through a common law or construction agent) the work was furnished; if that interest can't be reached, the court may order the improvement sold and removed. Any contractor, subcontractor, architect, engineer or other person having charge of an improvement is deemed the owner's agent for the limited purpose of establishing the lien. Work your tenant orders: the chapter does not define owner and says nothing about leases, so it doesn't say whether your interest can be liened for an improvement a tenant ordered, or whether your consent to a tenant's alteration makes the work yours. That turns on whether the work was furnished at your instance through an agent, which only case law could settle, and no Washington case was searched. Washington has no notice-of-nonresponsibility procedure and no statute letting a lease keep your interest free of liens. Notice and deadlines: a supplier of professional services, materials or equipment who did not contract with the owner (other than a laborer, or a subcontractor hired directly by the prime contractor) must give the owner or reputed owner written notice of the right to claim a lien, which protects only what was supplied from 60 days before the notice (10 days for a new single-family home). A lien claim must be recorded within 90 days after the claimant stops furnishing, and it lapses after eight months unless a lawsuit is filed and the owner served within 90 days of filing. An owner can ask the superior court to release a frivolous or clearly excessive lien, and in a foreclosure the court may award the prevailing party attorneys' fees. A recorded lien also reaches the community interest of the owner's spouse or domestic partner. What to do: tenants of homes rarely commission construction, and alterations need your consent under the lease (`no-alterations`). If you agree to tenant work, ask for lien releases from everyone who sends you a notice, or pay by joint check. Repairs a tenant has done under the statutory repair-and-deduct remedy are repairs of your own duties, and the lease can't waive that remedy (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). The library's shared no-liens clause is not offered for Washington (see the decision for this topic); you may add your own clause with advice, without shifting your attorneys' fees to the tenant.

title: No Special-District Statement Required in a Washington Lease
bodyText: No Washington statute requires you to state in a lease, disclose, or have the tenant acknowledge that the rental lies within a special district (a local improvement district, water-sewer district, irrigation district, conservation district, park district, business improvement area or similar body), and none gives a residential tenant a voice in a district through the lease. Districts reach the owner, not the tenant: a city's local improvement assessment is a lien on the assessed property, and a water-sewer district's or irrigation district's charges for service to the property, with penalties and interest, are a lien on the property served. Voting follows each district's own statute: in an irrigation district of less than 200,000 acres the electors are the landowners (title holders of assessable land, including entities that own land there), so a tenant has no vote; a conservation district's electors are the registered voters who live in the district, so a tenant who is a registered voter there can vote. The one district rule that reaches you as a residential landlord concerns tenant utility accounts: a water-sewer district or an irrigation district that serves your rental must notify you of a tenant's delinquency if you have told it in writing that the property is a rental, asked to be notified and given a complete mailing address; if it fails to, it has no lien against the premises for that tenant's unpaid charges (see the `utility-disconnection-notice-authorization` and `utility-shutoff-statute` topics). Make that written request to each district that bills your tenants directly. If you want to pass a district assessment or charge through to the tenant, the lease must say so as a recurring charge, which makes it rent under the act, and later increases follow the rent increase notice rules (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). A district statement in the lease is optional: you may add one, but don't word it so that the tenant appears to take on an assessment the law places on you. Local district rules are outside what this library searched.

title: Out-of-State Owners and Entities Renting in Washington
bodyText:
Agent for notices and process: if the landlord named in the lease does not live in Washington, the landlord must also name a person who lives in the county where the rental is and is authorized to accept service of notices and process; if you name no one, the person to whom rent is paid is treated as that agent. The library's `landlord-disclosure-wa` clause carries this designation.

Being sued from out of state: whatever you designate, an owner living outside Washington who violates the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act is deemed to have submitted to Washington's courts, and can be personally served outside the state with a summons that gives 60 days to appear (60 days also for a small claims notice of claim). More generally, owning real property in Washington submits you to its courts for claims arising from that ownership, and personal service outside the state is valid on an affidavit that you couldn't be served here. A Washington or registered foreign entity must keep a registered agent in Washington, and serving that agent serves the entity.

Out-of-state LLCs and corporations: a foreign entity may not do business in Washington until it registers with the Secretary of State, and one doing business here can't maintain a lawsuit or proceeding (an eviction included) until it registers and pays the fees and penalties for the years it did business unregistered; the court may stay the case meanwhile. Not registering doesn't void your leases and doesn't stop you defending a suit. Owning property without more is not doing business, and neither is maintaining or defending a lawsuit, but renting homes to tenants is more than owning, so register before you file. Washington doesn't restrict foreign ownership itself (`edu-no-foreign-ownership-limit-wa`).

Trade names: anyone, resident or not, who carries on business under a trade name (a name such as "Maple Court Apartments" that is not the owner's true and real name) must register it with the Department of Revenue, and can't maintain any lawsuit until it does, though the leases stay valid and you can still defend.

Taxes: no Washington statute requires a tenant or manager to withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. Starting January 1, 2028, Washington taxes individuals' Washington taxable income at 9.9 percent after a $1,000,000 standard deduction (prorated for nonresidents), and a nonresident's Washington-source income includes rents from Washington real property; ask your tax adviser. No other registration, bond or in-state agent rule for nonresident residential landlords was found in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws; 

City rental registration programs are municipal law.

title: Lease Length, Signatures, Spouses and Recording in Washington
bodyText: Washington sets no maximum term for a private residential lease. What changes with length is form: Up to one year: a lease may be written or printed (or partly each) and is valid for any term up to one year without acknowledgment, witnesses or seals. Year-to-year tenancies exist only by express written contract (`edu-statute-of-frauds-wa`). Over one year: a lease is a conveyance of an interest in real estate and must be by deed, meaning in writing and signed by the party bound; since a 2024 amendment a lease needs no acknowledgment, witness or seal unless you want to record it, and to be recorded a lease or a memorandum of lease must have both your and the tenant's signatures acknowledged. Over two years: the recording act treats a lease for more than two years as a conveyance, so an unrecorded one is void against a later good-faith purchaser or mortgagee for value who records first. Recording protects mainly the tenant; it is not needed for the lease to bind you and the tenant, and leases of two years or less fall outside the recording act. Spouses and domestic partners: either spouse or domestic partner may manage community property alone, but neither may sell, convey or encumber community real property unless the other joins in and both acknowledge the instrument. The statute does not say whether a lease is a conveyance or encumbrance for this purpose (the separate-property statute lists lease separately from sell, convey and encumber), and no Washington case was searched. A homestead (the home the owner or a dependent actually lives in) of a spouse or domestic partner likewise can't be conveyed or encumbered unless both execute and acknowledge the instrument. Cautious course: if the rental is community real property and the term, counting any renewal or option the lease grants, is more than one year, or if you are renting part of your own home, have both spouses or domestic partners sign the lease, and have them acknowledge it if the term is long. Property owned by one spouse as separate property may be leased by that spouse alone. Single-family homes: a lease of a single-family dwelling for a year or more may be taken out of the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act only if the tenant's attorney approves the exemption on the face of the lease; the library doesn't offer that (`edu-scope-wa`). For the library's leases: a month-to-month agreement or a fixed term of one year or less needs only a written lease signed by the parties; a fixed term longer than a year needs the landlord's signature and, for community property, the spouse's or domestic partner's joinder on the cautious course; no lease term the library offers requires recording.

title: No Usufruct in Washington: Leasing When You Hold Less Than Full Ownership
bodyText: Washington has no usufruct. The words usufruct, usufructuary and naked owner appear nowhere in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution, the 2025-2026 session laws or the saved court rules; usufruct is a civil-law estate (the library's Louisiana and Puerto Rico rows), and those rows don't state Washington law. Washington's nearest equivalent is the life estate, and no Washington statute says whether a lease granted by a life tenant (or by anyone holding less than full ownership) survives the end of that interest, or what the life tenant owes the people who take the property next. The statutes only recognize that such estates exist: the seller disclosure form asks whether title is subject to a lease or a life estate, partition and recording statutes list life tenants and remainder holders among owners, and the waste statute lets anyone injured sue a tenant for life or for years, a subtenant or a tenant at will who commits waste, for treble damages or $50, whichever is greater, plus attorneys' fees, with forfeiture and eviction available to the person entitled to the reversion only where the injury equals the value of the tenant's estate or was done or suffered in malice. What follows from that is case law, which this library didn't search, so take the cautious course: if you hold the property only for your life (or for a term, or as one of several owners), don't sign a lease that runs past what you hold unless the people who will own the property after you (the remainder holders, or your co-owners) sign it too, and tell the tenant in writing what interest you hold. Once your interest ends, the next owners take the property, and the tenancy's continued rights under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, including the just-cause rules, would have to be sorted out with them; get advice before relying on the end of a life estate to end a tenancy. Co-owners: if several people own the property, have every owner sign the lease; community property follows the spouse-joinder rules in `edu-lease-term-limitation-wa`.

title: No General Duty to Rehouse a Washington Tenant During Repairs
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles makes you provide, find or pay for substitute housing (a hotel room or another unit) while you make repairs or while a unit is unfit to live in, whether or not the tenant asks. Washington handles a unit that can't be lived in through the tenant's repair remedies and two relocation-payment rules instead. Repair remedies: once the tenant gives you written notice of a defect, you must start remedial work within 24 hours if the tenant has no hot or cold water, heat or electricity or the condition is imminently hazardous to life, within 72 hours for a refrigerator, range and oven or major plumbing fixture you supplied, and within 10 days otherwise. If you then fail to fix it within a reasonable time, the tenant may end the rental agreement on written notice and move out, owing no rent after the move-out date and getting a pro rata refund of prepaid rent and the deposit accounting; or use repair-and-deduct, rent escrow or a court or arbitrator's reduction of rent to the diminished rental value (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). Condemned or unlawful units: if a code agency notifies you that a unit will be condemned or unlawful to occupy and you knew or should have known of the conditions, you must pay each displaced tenant relocation assistance of the greater of $2,000 per unit or three months' rent, plus deposits and prepaid rent, within seven days; this isn't owed where the order results from a natural disaster, from a tenant's or third party's illegal conduct you didn't know about, or from eminent domain (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). A condemnation also lets you end the tenancy on at least 30 days' written notice (or as much as the order allows) where continued habitation would expose you to civil or criminal penalties. Local programs: a city or county that plans under the Growth Management Act may require owners to pay up to half of a capped relocation payment to low-income tenants displaced by demolition, substantial rehabilitation (including for code enforcement), change of use, or removal of use restrictions in assisted housing; check your city's or county's rules before major work. Someone who moves in after you apply for the permit gets nothing under such a program only if you first gave them written notice describing the work that may displace them and that they aren't eligible for relocation assistance. What to do: if you must move a tenant out for repairs, agree in writing on where they stay, who pays, and what rent is owed for the days the unit can't be used. No statute sets that rent and no case was searched, so don't charge full rent for days the tenant can't live there without the tenant's written agreement.

title: Caring for a Tenant's Animal Left in a Washington Rental
bodyText: Washington gives you no special right to enter a tenant's home to feed, care for or remove the tenant's animal. Under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) you may enter without the tenant's consent only in an emergency or after abandonment; otherwise you have no right of access except by court order, an arbitrator or the tenant's consent, and except in an emergency or where it is impracticable you must give at least two days' written notice (`landlords-access-wa`). An animal shut in a unit without food or water while the tenant is hospitalized, detained or away may amount to an emergency, but no statute says so and no Washington case was searched, so the safer course is to call animal control or the police. An animal control officer or law enforcement officer who has probable cause to believe an animal is in imminent danger, is suffering serious physical injury or infirmity, or needs immediate medical attention may enter private property without a warrant to give emergency aid or seize the animal; otherwise the officer needs a warrant. Tenant's death: if a sole occupant dies, upon learning of the death you may enter and turn the animals over to a tenant representative or to an animal control officer, humane society, or other person or organization willing to care for them (`edu-tenant-death-wa`). Taking an animal in makes you its keeper in law: Washington's animal-cruelty chapter defines an owner to include anyone having control, custody, or possession of an animal, with no minimum number of days, and an owner, or a person in possession or control of an animal or who has accepted responsibility for it, who knowingly, recklessly or with criminal negligence fails to provide necessary food, water, shelter, rest, sanitation, space or medical attention so that the animal suffers, or who abandons it, commits animal cruelty in the second degree, a gross misdemeanor. So if you take in a tenant's pet, care for it until you hand it to the tenant, the tenant's representative or an animal agency. Don't hold an animal for rent: a lease lien or distress clause is void, and a landlord who takes or detains a tenant's personal property without the tenant's specific written consent to that taking, and doesn't return it promptly after written demand, owes its value and damages, and up to $500 a day (capped at $5,000) if the refusal is intentional (`edu-landlord-lien-wa`). The abandonment procedure that lets you store and later sell property found in an abandoned unit doesn't mention animals; hand an animal to animal control rather than storing it. No lease clause is offered: the library's optional animal-care clause (the tenant names a caretaker you may let in) isn't offered for Washington, because whether a standing lease consent meets the entry-notice rule and the specific-consent rule for taking a tenant's property isn't settled by any statute or case searched. You may ask tenants to name an emergency animal caregiver on a separate form, get the tenant's consent at the time when you can reach them, or add your own clause with legal advice.

title: Appliances You Supply, and Why Washington Leases Can't Exclude Them
bodyText: Washington has no rule presuming that appliances found in a unit are yours, and no rule letting a lease exclude them from your repair duty. The test in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) is whether you supplied the appliance: you must maintain all electrical, plumbing, heating, and other facilities and appliances supplied by you in reasonably good working order, and the tenant must properly use and operate them. Once the tenant gives written notice of a defect, you must start remedial work within 72 hours where the tenant loses the use of a refrigerator, range and oven, or major plumbing fixture you supplied (24 hours if the defect cuts off hot or cold water, heat or electricity) (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). The act doesn't make you supply a refrigerator, stove, washer or dishwasher at all, but you must provide facilities adequate to supply heat, water and hot water as reasonably required. So list what you supply in the appliances clause (`appliances-included`) and maintain it; appliances the tenant brings are the tenant's own. Leaving an item you won't maintain: the library's optional "items not included" clause is not offered for Washington. Any lease term waiving any section or subsection of chapter 59.18 RCW is unenforceable; a lease may not provide that the tenant waives rights or remedies under the act, or agrees to the exculpation or limitation of any liability you have under law; and knowingly using a prohibited term exposes you to the tenant's actual damages, statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). The act doesn't define supplied, and no Washington case was searched, so an item you leave in the unit for the tenant's use may well count as supplied by you, and a clause saying you won't repair it would then be a waiver of your repair duty. The only lawful waiver of repair duties is a negotiated exemption agreement that can't appear in a standard form lease (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). Cautious course: before move-in, either remove an item you don't want to maintain or keep it and maintain it. You owe no repair for damage the tenant, the tenant's family, invitee or other person under the tenant's control caused (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`). Move-in checklist: record each appliance's condition on the written checklist (`existing-condition-wa`); you can't keep any of the deposit for repair or replacement of appliances whose condition wasn't reasonably documented in it (`edu-condition-checklist-wa`).

title: No Required Association Disclosure in a Washington Lease
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires a lease of a condominium or homeowners' association unit to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, to carry an owner's statement about the association's law or bylaws, or to be sent to the board, and nothing treats a tenant, even under a long lease, as a purchaser entitled to the resale certificate an owner must give a buyer before a sale. What does matter for your lease (see `edu-hoa-wa` and the `hoa-compliance` clause): Rules bind the tenant only if shared at move-in. A tenant must follow reasonable obligations or restrictions concerning the use, occupation and maintenance of the unit and the property only if they don't violate the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, aren't otherwise unlawful, and are brought to the tenant's attention at the time of initial occupancy, which makes them part of the rental agreement. A new rule needs 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant and takes effect at the end of the term or sooner by mutual consent. So give the tenant the association's declaration restrictions, rules and fine schedule that affect occupants when the lease is signed. The association can act against your tenant. In a community under the Washington Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act (chapter 64.90 RCW: communities created on or after July 1, 2018 or that elect in, and every community from January 1, 2028), if a tenant violates the governing documents the association may enforce them directly against the tenant, fine the tenant and you after notice and an opportunity to be heard, and, if the violation isn't cured within 10 days of its notice, use rights you as landlord could have used under the lease; it can't end the lease or evict unless the declaration allows it. Screening and leasing limits. The association may require you, at your own cost, to screen a prospective tenant or get background information and to show it was done, but may not require a copy of the report (older condominium and homeowners' association acts carry the same rule until January 1, 2028). The declaration may restrict leasing, and board rules may restrict leasing only as needed to meet institutional lenders' underwriting requirements, so check the declaration and rules before you rent. Cooperatives: the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act doesn't apply to a cooperative's proprietary lease created after July 1, 2018 (or after the cooperative elects into chapter 64.90 RCW); those are outside this library.

title: No State Approval Rule for Leases of Tribal Land in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires a government officer to approve, or voids, a residential lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land; the state's assumption of jurisdiction over Indian country expressly doesn't authorize alienating or encumbering Indian trust or restricted property, so if the home is on tribal trust or restricted land, federal and tribal law govern (not held or read here) and you should check with the tribe and the federal agency before signing; leases of state public lands from the Department of Natural Resources are outside the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (`edu-scope-wa`).

title: You Can't Pick the Tenant's Repairer in Washington
bodyText: Washington doesn't let you name the repairer a tenant must use when the tenant uses the repair-and-deduct remedy; the statute chooses the qualification, not the person (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). If you fail to start remedial work within the required time after the tenant's written notice and estimate, the tenant may contract with a licensed or registered person, or, where no license or registration is required for the work, with a responsible person capable of doing the repair, and deduct the cost (up to two months' rent per repair and in any 12-month period) after completion and an opportunity for you or your designated agent to inspect. For a repair costing no more than one month's rent that doesn't by law require a licensed or registered person, the tenant may do the work personally in a workmanlike manner, within the unit only. All work must meet applicable codes, and you may sue for actual damages if the tenant's repair is negligent and damages your property. Because any lease term waiving a section or subsection of the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act is unenforceable and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under it, a clause requiring the tenant to use only your contractor, or barring repair-and-deduct, doesn't hold up, and knowingly using a prohibited term exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). What you can do: name your repair contact. The tenant's notice of a defect may go to the person named in the lease or posted notice as the landlord or to the person who collects the rent, and the estimate may go to you or your designated agent, so put a maintenance contact in the lease for convenience but don't make it the only valid way to give notice. You and the tenant may also agree that the tenant will do repairs for cash or a reasonable rent reduction; that agreement doesn't change your duties under the act. The landlord-tenant act names no qualification for repairers you hire yourself, but the licensing and code rules for the trade still apply.

title: No Disaster-Displaced Guest Rule in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood, earthquake or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, stops you from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or sets special rules for disaster-displaced guests in hotels or short-stay lodging. Washington's interstate emergency compact deals with evacuees between governments, not through private leases. So your guest and occupancy terms still apply (`guest-policy`, `guest-policy-day-limit`, `permitted-occupants`): a guest rule binds the tenant if it is reasonable, lawful and was brought to the tenant's attention at move-in, and a guest who becomes an unauthorized occupant is a lease breach you may act on only through the act's cause-based notices. Fair housing law still applies to how you treat the household (for example families with children status and disability accommodation). Hotels and motels: residence in transient lodging is outside the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, but a person who has lived in a hotel, motel or other transient lodging for 30 or more consecutive days with the owner's or manager's knowledge and consent is treated as a tenant for relocation assistance if the building is condemned or declared unlawful to occupy, and an interruption in occupancy meant mainly to avoid that rule doesn't count (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`).
