Cautious course after a disaster: if a tenant asks to shelter displaced family or friends, answer in writing with who may stay, for how long and any conditions, and apply the same answer to every household.

title: No Disaster-Specific Tenancy Rules in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws says what happens to a residential tenancy after a declared disaster: the tenancy doesn't end automatically, no rule suspends or abates rent while the unit is inaccessible, and no disaster price-gouging statute covers rent. The ordinary rules apply instead (`edu-casualty-termination-wa`). If the unit is damaged: the tenant gives written notice and you must start remedial work within 24 hours (no water, heat or electricity, or a condition imminently hazardous to life), 72 hours or 10 days, except where circumstances are beyond your control, in which case you must fix it as soon as possible. If you don't remedy the defect within a reasonable time, the tenant may end the rental agreement on written notice and owe no rent after moving out; a court or arbitrator may reduce rent to the diminished rental value; and if the defect is so substantial that it can't feasibly be fixed in time and the tenant shouldn't stay, a court or arbitrator may end the tenancy and set a reasonable time to vacate (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). Because no statute sets rent for days a disaster keeps the tenant out, agree with the tenant in writing on rent for that period rather than charging it in full. Ending the tenancy yourself: you need a listed cause, for example a unit certified or condemned as uninhabitable by a local agency where continued occupancy would expose you to penalties (at least 30 days' written notice, or as much as the order allows). Relocation assistance for condemned units isn't owed where the order results from a natural disaster such as an earthquake, tsunami, windstorm or hurricane (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). Emergency orders: after proclaiming a state of emergency the Governor may prohibit activities he or she reasonably believes should be prohibited to preserve life, health, property or the public peace, and may waive or suspend certain statutory obligations (a waiver or suspension under that second power lasts no more than 30 days unless the Legislature or its leaders extend it); willfully violating such an order is a gross misdemeanor. Washington's 2020-2021 eviction moratorium came from such a proclamation, so check current proclamations after a disaster. Rent increases stay subject to the statewide limit (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). Before a disaster: the move-in fire safety notice for a multifamily building must say whether the building has an emergency notification, relocation or evacuation plan and give the tenant a copy of any plan (`fire-safety-notice-wa`), and leases entered into after December 31, 2026 need the flood-risk disclosure (`flood-disclosure-wa`).

title: No Double-Letting Statute in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws deals specifically with double letting, whether renting the same unit to two tenants or letting part of a room to more than one household, and nothing gives a rent-abatement remedy for it. The general law covers it instead. If you sign leases with two tenants for the same unit, the tenant you can't put in possession has ordinary contract claims against you; the lease's delayed-possession terms (`possession-delay`: no rent until possession, and the right to cancel and get everything back if possession isn't delivered within 30 days) apply only to a delay through no fault of yours, so don't rely on them to limit what you owe when you rented the unit twice. Knowingly renting a unit you have already rented and taking the second tenant's money can also be a crime: Washington's theft statute covers obtaining another's property by deception, and deception includes knowingly transferring or encumbering property without disclosing an adverse claim or other legal impediment, or promising performance you don't intend to or know won't happen. Whether it is also an unfair or deceptive practice under the Consumer Protection Act is a case-law question (`edu-consumer-protection-act-wa`). What to do: don't accept a second application deposit, holding deposit or signed lease for a unit already committed, and if a prior tenant fails to move out, tell the incoming tenant in writing at once (`edu-holding-deposit-wa`).

title: No Emergency-Contact Duty in Washington, and the Contact Rules That Do Apply
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number, or to put a management website or social-services hotline notice in the lease. What Washington does require: your name and address (and, if you live out of state, an in-county agent for notices and process) in the lease or a conspicuously posted notice (`landlord-disclosure-wa`); a telephone number in every notice of entry for the tenant's objections or rescheduling requests (`landlords-access-wa`); in any notice disconnecting electric or water service you resupply, clear information on how to ask for reconnection during a heat alert, including how to contact you (`edu-heat-alert-utility-wa`); and, in a multifamily building, the move-in fire safety notice saying whether the building has an emergency notification, relocation or evacuation plan, with a copy of each plan (`fire-safety-notice-wa`). The tenant's emergency contact: if a tenant who is the sole occupant dies, you must send the death notice to, among others, any emergency contact the tenant listed on the rental application, so keep the application on file (`edu-tenant-death-wa`). A separate written designation of a person to act on the tenant's death may be requested but must be kept separate from the lease. Good practice, not a legal duty: give tenants a maintenance or after-hours number for urgent repairs, because the tenant's repair notice clock (24 hours for loss of water, heat or electricity) runs from your receipt of written notice. Short-term rental operators must post emergency and operator contact information, but short-term rentals are outside this library.

title: No Washington Mandate to Screen Rental Staff, and the Fair Chance Limits When You Do
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires a residential landlord or management company to run background checks on employees, such as maintenance staff or managers with keys to units, and no rule ties employee screening to the lease. Two rules do bear on it. Keys: you must maintain and safeguard with reasonable care any master key or duplicate keys to the unit, so control which staff hold keys and keep a record of who has them (`keys`, `edu-security-devices-wa`); entry by staff follows the same notice rules as your own entry (`landlords-access-wa`). Hiring limits: Washington's Fair Chance Act applies to you as an employer. In its current form (applying to employers with 15 or more employees from July 1, 2026 and to all other employers from January 1, 2027), you may not ask about or obtain an applicant's criminal record, including through a background check, until you have decided the applicant is otherwise qualified and made an offer conditioned on the record; you may not advertise "no felons" or similar, or use a policy that automatically excludes people with criminal records; you may not take an adverse action based on an arrest record or juvenile record; and you may act on an adult conviction record only for a legitimate business reason, after notifying the person of the record you rely on, holding the job open at least two business days for an explanation, and giving a written decision assessing the listed factors. The act doesn't apply to hiring for a position with unsupervised access to children, vulnerable adults or vulnerable persons, or where another law requires or permits the inquiry. The Attorney General enforces it with penalties of up to $1,500 for a first violation, $3,000 for a second and $15,000 for each later one, per aggrieved person; there is no private lawsuit under it. Federal and state credit-reporting rules apply if you use a consumer report for hiring. Screening tenants is a separate subject (`edu-tenant-screening-wa`).

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no rule letting you (or the tenant) end a residential tenancy because of an environmental or public health event such as wildfire smoke, a chemical spill or contamination, and a lease clause giving you that right can't be used here. Under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act you may not evict a tenant, refuse to continue a tenancy or end a periodic tenancy except for the causes the act lists, and any lease term waiving a section of the act is unenforceable; a clause adding an environmental-event cause would be one of those, and knowingly using a prohibited term risks statutory damages of up to twice the monthly rent (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). The library offers no such clause for Washington (the same reasoning as the declined casualty clause in `edu-casualty-termination-wa`). What does apply after an event: if a local agency certifies or condemns the unit as uninhabitable and continued occupancy would expose you to civil or criminal penalties, you may end the tenancy on at least 30 days' written notice, or as much notice as the order allows (`edu-condemned-premises-wa`). If a property is contaminated by hazardous chemicals, the local health officer posts a warning, inspects and, if it is contaminated, orders it unfit and prohibits its use until it is decontaminated; if you believe a tenant contaminated a unit that is now vacated or abandoned, you must contact the local health officer (`edu-meth-contamination-wa`). If the event leaves the unit defective, the tenant's repair-notice remedies apply, including ending the rental agreement if you don't remedy the condition within a reasonable time, and a court or arbitrator may end the tenancy if the defect can't feasibly be fixed in time (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). Check any Governor's emergency proclamation in force (see the `disaster-duties` topic).

title: Tenant Family Home Child Care in a Washington Rental
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles makes a landlord allow a tenant to run a licensed family home child care (a family day care provider caring for up to 12 children in the provider's home), or sets conditions a landlord may impose on one. So the lease decides: the `residential-use-only` clause bars commercial use, and if you are willing to allow child care, do it in a written addendum. Who can't stop it: a city or county may not prohibit using a residential dwelling in a residential or commercial zone as a family day-care provider's home facility (it may impose building, fire, safety, health, business licensing, loading-area, signage, hours and neighbor-notice conditions), and a condominium or homeowners' association may not adopt or enforce a rule that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts the use of a unit as a licensed family home child care. The association may still impose reasonable rules applied equally to similar units, limit child care to units with direct access, and require the provider to be licensed, indemnify the association, obtain parents' signed (not notarized) liability waivers for the association, carry day care insurance or self-insurance, and pay the costs of operating; an association that willfully violates this owes actual damages and a civil penalty of up to $1,000. Those rules bind the association, not you as landlord. Insurance: a licensed family day care provider must either show the licensing agency day care insurance or give each enrolled child's parents written notice of its insurance status, so if you allow child care, ask to see the license and the insurance (or the parent notice) and consider requiring liability coverage that protects you. Apply the same terms to every tenant who asks. The state's child care licensing rules (Title 110 WAC) aren't held here, so whether a renting applicant must show the licensing agency the landlord's permission wasn't checked.

title: Hunting Rights on Leased Land in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles says whether a tenant of rented farmland or rural land has hunting or fishing rights, or that those rights stay with the owner unless granted in writing; the lease decides. (A rental of a house that is incidental to a lease of land used primarily for agriculture is outside the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act altogether (`edu-scope-wa`).) Rules that touch the question: hunting on someone else's premises after knowingly entering or remaining there without license or privilege is a misdemeanor and costs the hunter's licenses for two years if wildlife is killed, and one defense is a reasonable belief that the owner or other person empowered to license access would have allowed it, so the law contemplates that someone other than the owner, such as a tenant in possession, may be able to give permission. Only a person who owns or leases the land, or someone with the permission of the person who owns, leases or controls it, may post signs against hunting or fishing. Unfenced, unimproved and apparently unused land is open to entry unless notice against trespass is given, but cultivated or fenced fields are not treated that way. A landowner or other person in lawful possession and control who lets the public hunt or fish without charging a fee isn't liable for unintentional injuries, except for a known dangerous artificial latent condition with no conspicuous warning sign. State lands leased by the Department of Natural Resources for grazing or agriculture stay open to public hunting and fishing unless the department approves the lessee's posting. What to do: if you lease land with a home, state in the lease who holds the hunting and fishing rights, whether the tenant may hunt or allow others to, and whether you or people you authorize may come onto the land to hunt.

title: How Long a Washington Lease Guarantor Is Bound
bodyText:
No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles says how long a lease guarantor stays bound: nothing limits a guaranty to the original term, extends it to renewals, makes it revocable, or caps what a guarantor may be asked to pay. Those questions turn on the guaranty's wording and on case law. So draft the guaranty to answer them (the optional `guaranty-as` clause is tagged for Washington and makes you choose).

Writing: a promise to answer for another person's debt or default is void unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor.

Continuation: in Washington a fixed term usually rolls into a month-to-month tenancy by law when it ends, unless you used one of the narrow options to end it without cause (`lease-end-continuation-wa`, `fixed-term-end-without-cause-wa`), so say expressly whether the guaranty covers that continuation, renewals and later rent changes, and have the guarantor sign each new lease.

Surety statutes: a person bound as surety on a written contract for the payment of money may, once the right to sue has accrued, require you in writing to sue at once, and if you don't bring the action within a reasonable time and pursue it to judgment and execution, the surety is discharged. If you sue the tenant and the surety together, the surety can have the suretyship decided and the court will order the tenant's property exhausted first. No statute says whether a lease guarantor counts as a surety for these rules, so if a guarantor sends you a written demand to sue, act promptly.

Screening and deposits: approving an applicant on condition of a qualified guarantor is a conditional approval you must give on the statutory adverse action notice (`edu-tenant-screening-wa`). Washington has no deposit cap (`edu-no-security-deposit-cap-wa`); the act's deposit rules speak of money paid by the tenant, and whether money a guarantor pays as security falls under them isn't settled, so the cautious course is to handle it the same way (written terms, checklist, trust account and the 30-day accounting).

title: Guest Rights in Washington Rentals
bodyText: This is a pointer: Washington's guest rules are covered by the `guest-policy` and `guest-policy-day-limit` clauses, which are tagged for Washington. In short, no Washington statute gives tenants a stated right to have guests, caregivers or suppliers visit, bars guest fees, or limits how long a guest may stay in a building under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (unlike New York's rule for buildings with three or more households). The fair housing law preserves your right to post and enforce reasonable rules of conduct and safety for all tenants and their guests, as long as the rules don't discriminate and you make reasonable accommodations for a tenant with a disability, which can include allowing a live-in aide or caregiver. A guest rule binds the tenant only if it is reasonable, lawful and brought to the tenant's attention at move-in; a new rule needs 30 days' written notice and takes effect at the end of the term or sooner by mutual consent (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). A guest who overstays becomes an unauthorized occupant, which you may act on only through the act's breach notices (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-wa`). Any recurring guest or occupant charge identified in the rental agreement counts as rent, with the rent notice and increase rules that follow (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). If you use a smart access system, from January 1, 2027 your written policy must say what data about tenants' guests it collects (`edu-smart-access-wa`). Mobile home lots have their own guest-fee and care-provider rules under chapter 59.20 RCW, outside this library.

title: Home Businesses in Washington Rentals
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented dwelling, or says a lease must state a restriction on one, as West Virginia's and Missouri's statutes do. The Residential Landlord-Tenant Act says nothing about tenants working from home, so the lease decides: the `residential-use-only` clause (tagged for Washington) bars commercial use, and if you're willing to allow a home business, say so in writing with any limits (customer visits, signs, parking, deliveries, inventory, insurance). Whether a home business is allowed at the property at all is a local zoning and business-licensing question: Washington law lets a city treat home-based businesses as a type of business needing a regulatory license, and city and county codes aren't searched in this library, so the tenant must check them. One state rule overrides local zoning for a specific home business, family home child care, and associations can't prohibit or unreasonably restrict licensed family home child care either; that subject is covered under the `family-child-care` topic. A private residence or home-based business is not a place of employment under the state's indoor smoking law unless it is used to provide licensed child care, foster care, adult care or similar care on the premises, so those uses bring the smoking ban into the home (`edu-smoking-wa`).

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW or the held WAC titles requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, or ties insurance to a landlord registration program; any local registration or licensing rule would be in a city or county code, which this library doesn't search (`edu-no-landlord-registration-wa`). Insurance comes up in the landlord-tenant act in four other ways. Disclosure: for leases entered into after December 31, 2026 you must tell tenants that your insurance does not cover the loss of the tenant's personal possessions and that they should consider renter's and flood insurance (`flood-disclosure-wa`, `edu-renters-insurance-wa`). No shifting your liability: a lease may not make the tenant agree to exculpate you or limit your liability under law, or indemnify you for that liability or its costs, so don't use an insurance clause to do either (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Fee in lieu of deposit: if you offer one, you must disclose in writing the terms of any insurance you buy for your losses from unpaid amounts, including exclusions and caps, and whether the insurer requires you to try the tenant first (`edu-fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). Cooling devices: you may restrict a window-mounted portable cooling device if your insurance policy for the tenant's dwelling expressly restricts or prohibits it and you give the tenant written evidence of that restriction (`portable-cooling-device-wa`). Short-term rental operators must carry at least $1,000,000 in primary liability insurance, but short-term rentals are outside this library.

title: No Initials Requirement for Washington Lease Terms
bodyText: Washington has no general rule that a tenant must initial particular lease provisions or notices for them to be valid. The one lease term that needs a separate tenant acknowledgment is a nonrefundable fee in lieu of a security deposit: the fee may be entirely or partly nonrefundable only if that is disclosed in the lease and separately acknowledged by the tenant (`fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). Other formal steps the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act requires: the fire safety and smoke detection notice must be signed by you (or your agent) and the tenant, with copies to both (`fire-safety-notice-wa`); the move-in condition checklist must be signed and dated by both of you, with a copy to the tenant, before you may collect a deposit (`existing-condition-wa`); any nonrefundable fee must be in a written rental agreement that clearly says it is nonrefundable (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`); an agreement to arbitrate is barred unless you pay the entire cost and the agreement is notarized (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`); and a tenant's designation of a person to act on the tenant's death must be in a signed writing separate from the lease (`edu-tenant-death-wa`). Beyond those, having the tenant initial key terms (pets, smoking, parking, late fees) is good practice for proof, not a legal requirement.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Washington Leases
bodyText: This is a pointer: the answer is in `edu-no-plain-language-rule-wa`. Washington sets no minimum type size or typeface for a printed residential lease, and no rule like New York's that keeps small-print documents out of evidence. The only type rules in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act and the unlawful detainer statutes are for court-stage papers and statewide notices: the writ of restitution and its accompanying notice must state the partial-payment information conspicuously in boldface type, all capitals, at least 12 points (a court and sheriff document, not your lease), and the Attorney General's translated versions of the 14-day pay-or-vacate notice must be available in print on one letter-size page in an easily readable font size. Statutory forms you use, such as the 14-day notice and the rent increase notice, follow their own prescribed wording (`edu-statutory-forms-wa`). Mobile home lot agreements carry their own boldface park-closure statement under chapter 59.20 RCW, outside this library. Good practice: print the lease in a readable size (the library's default output is), because a court weighing whether a term was fairly disclosed may look at how it was presented; no Washington case on that was searched.

title: Giving Tenants Parking Rules and Changing Them in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no statute written for parking rules, so your parking rules work like any other house rule under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) (`edu-rules-regulations-wa`). A parking rule binds the tenant only if it is reasonable, doesn't violate chapter 59.18 RCW or other law, and was brought to the tenant's attention when the tenant first moved in, which makes it part of the rental agreement. So hand the tenant your parking rules with the lease and keep a signed receipt. A new or changed parking rule needs at least 30 days' written notice to each affected tenant and takes effect at the end of the rental agreement's term, or sooner only if the tenant agrees. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires the lease to say whether parking is provided, prescribes a heading or form for parking rules, limits what vehicle information you may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term. Parking charges: a recurring parking charge identified in the rental agreement is part of the rent, because rent means the recurring and periodic charges for the use and occupancy of the premises, and the premises include facilities held out for the tenant's use. Raising it or adding a new one is a rent increase: at least 90 days' written notice on the state Rent and Fee Increase Notice form, not effective before a fixed term ends, and within the statewide annual limit unless an exemption applies (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). Towing: Washington's towing chapter defines residential property as property with no more than four living units. On such property you may have an unauthorized vehicle impounded immediately by giving a registered tow truck operator a signed written authorization that contains the statutory liability statement. A complex with five or more units isn't residential property under that chapter: a vehicle there may be towed in less than 24 hours only if signs are posted near each entrance and on the property showing when vehicles may be impounded and the towing firm's name, telephone number and address; without signs the vehicle must have been left unattended for 24 hours. No statute gives a waiting period before towing a vehicle with expired registration from a private lot (the 45-day rule covers only police impounds from public streets). Never boot a vehicle: it is a gross misdemeanor (`edu-towing-wa`). For lease wording use `parking-vehicle-rules`. Mobile home lots (chapter 59.20 RCW, outside this library) have their own rule that the rental agreement state reasonable guest parking rules.

title: Entering for Scheduled Services in Washington Still Takes Two Days’ Written Notice
bodyText:
Washington has no special rule for regularly scheduled services such as pest treatment, filter changes or smoke alarm checks.

Every non-emergency entry into a tenant's unit follows the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act's entry rule (`landlords-access-wa`): except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least two days' written notice and enter only at reasonable times. The notice must state the exact date or dates and time of entry, or a period on that date or dates with the earliest and latest possible times, and the telephone number the tenant can call to object or reschedule. Only one day's notice is needed to show the unit to prospective or actual buyers or tenants.

Beyond that you have no right of entry except by court order, an arbitrator or the tenant's consent; you may enter without consent only in an emergency or after abandonment.

A lease clause letting you enter for scheduled services on shorter notice, without written notice, or without any notice is unenforceable, because a lease term that waives any section of chapter 59.18 RCW is void and no lease may make the tenant give up rights under the chapter. The written exemption procedure in RCW 59.18.360 doesn't reach the entry section and can't be used in a standard form lease anyway. Knowingly using a lease with a prohibited term can cost you actual damages, up to two times the monthly rent, costs and attorneys' fees (`edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`).

What to do: send a written notice at least two days before each visit. The statute lets one notice list several dates, so you may give the tenant a written service schedule with exact dates and time windows, the telephone number, and at least two days' lead time before the first date; the cautious course is a short written reminder two days before each visit.

A tenant may also agree to a particular visit. A tenant who keeps refusing reasonable entry, or a landlord who keeps violating these rules after one written notice listing the violation, can owe up to $100 per later violation.

title: No Pets-and-Eviction Fact Sheet in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws makes you give a tenant a state fact sheet about pets and eviction, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and no Washington law sets special eviction steps for a household with animals. Your pet rules, pet deposits and pet rent follow the ordinary rules (`pet-policy-wa`, `edu-pet-fees-wa`), and an eviction follows the usual notice and court process (`edu-eviction-process-wa`). After the sheriff executes a writ of restitution, the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act's property procedure speaks of the tenant's property in general and says nothing about animals (`edu-post-eviction-property-wa`). Because a live animal can't be stored or sold like furniture and no statute or Washington case searched for this row tells you what to do, the cautious course is to warn the tenant in writing before the eviction date that animals must be removed, and to call your local animal control agency or humane society for any animal left behind rather than keeping or disposing of it yourself. The only animal rule in chapter 59.18 RCW is for a tenant's death: on learning of the death you may enter the unit and turn over animals to the tenant representative or to an animal control officer, humane society, or another person or organization willing to care for them (`edu-tenant-death-wa`).

title: No Plain-Language Consumer Statement for Washington Leases
bodyText: Washington has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts or leases: no readability test, no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up, no attorney general preapproval of lease forms and no dollar threshold for such a regime (`edu-no-plain-language-rule-wa`). No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires one. Two things do the work instead. First, a lease can't take rights away from the tenant at all: any term that waives a section of the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act is unenforceable, and the listed prohibited terms can cost you damages if you knowingly use them (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-knowing-use-penalty-wa`), so there is no list of consumer waivers to disclose. The one written-approval procedure in the Act, an exemption from certain repair and duty sections approved in writing by the county prosecutor, the attorney general's consumer protection division or the tenant's attorney, can't appear in a standard form lease (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). Second, specific notices carry their own form rules, for example the rent and fee increase notice form, and from January 1, 2027 a smart access building's data policy must be written in plain language (`edu-smart-access-wa`). Writing your lease in short, clear sentences is still good practice, but it is your choice, not a Washington requirement.

title: Washington Duties Turn on the Building, Not Your Portfolio Size
bodyText: Apart from one accessibility rule (item 6), Washington doesn't tier your landlord duties by how many units you own in total. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws gives a small-landlord exemption from the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), adds duties once your portfolio passes a set number of units (other than the accessibility rule in item 6), or limits large investors buying single-family homes. The Act applies the same way to a landlord with one rental house and one with a thousand apartments. Where Washington law does use a number, it looks at the building, the owner's own occupancy or the owner's legal form, and except possibly for item 6 not your portfolio: (1) Rent increase limit: the statewide cap doesn't apply to a unit where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives there, to a single-family owner-occupied residence where the owner rents no more than two units or bedrooms, or to a duplex, triplex or fourplex where the owner lived in one unit when the tenancy began and still does. Those three exemptions are unavailable if the owner is a real estate investment trust, a corporation, or an LLC with at least one corporate member, so both conditions must be met (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). (2) City rental inspections: at a property with 20 or fewer units a city may select no more than four units for a certificate of inspection; with 21 or more, no more than 20 percent of the units, up to 50, if the first inspection finds no dangerous conditions (`edu-rental-inspection-wa`). (3) Towing: property with no more than four living units counts as residential property, where an unauthorized vehicle may be impounded immediately; larger complexes need posted signs for a tow within 24 hours (`edu-parking-rules-notice-wa`). (4) Pools: the health rules' exemptions turn on a single-family home, an owner-occupied duplex or a group of fewer than 15 rental units (`edu-pool-rules-wa`). (5) Construction liens: the protections that limit a lien to what the owner still owes the prime contractor cover only an existing owner-occupied single-family residence. On your rental property, a supplier who doesn't contract directly with you must send you a notice of the right to claim a lien, but that notice protects its lien for everything supplied from 60 days before the notice, and a person who contracts directly with you, a laborer, or a subcontractor who contracts directly with your prime contractor needs no notice at all, so not receiving a notice doesn't mean there is no lien. Ask your contractor for lien releases before paying. (6) Accessibility: under the Human Rights Commission's rules, if you own four or more units of rental property and make nonstructural changes, it is an unfair practice to install, replace, relocate or modify a fixture or component in a way that is not accessible to people with disabilities, or to fail to eliminate barriers, where this can be done without substantially changing the scope or cost of the project or requiring structural changes the law doesn't otherwise require. The rule doesn't say whether units in different buildings are added together, so if you own four or more rental units in total, follow it. Check local ordinances: some cities set their own thresholds.

title: No Written-Repair-Promise Rule in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws says that a promise to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, must carry a completion date or must be given before the lease is signed, and no Washington statute lists a false or unkept repair promise as an unlawful practice in renting. What does apply: (1) Your repair duties under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act exist whether or not you promised anything; you must keep the premises fit to live in and make the repairs RCW 59.18.060 lists, and a lease term waiving them is unenforceable (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`, `edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`). (2) The Act expects agreed repairs: the tenant must not unreasonably refuse you entry to make necessary or agreed repairs, alterations or improvements, on the usual two days' written notice (`landlords-access-wa`). (3) Washington's Consumer Protection Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade and commerce include the sale of assets, which include real property; whether a particular broken repair promise to a tenant is a deceptive practice is a question for the courts, and no Washington case was searched (`edu-consumer-protection-act-wa`). (4) The library's lease says the lease and its addenda are the entire agreement and can be changed only in a signed writing (`entire-agreement`), so an oral promise you make at a showing may be disputed later. What to do: if you promise any cleaning, repair or improvement before move-in or during the tenancy, put it in a signed addendum that says what will be done and by when, and do it. Don't advertise or promise work you don't intend to do.

title: Illegal Use Doesn’t Void a Washington Lease by Itself
bodyText: Washington lets you limit the unit to residential use and forbid illegal use in the lease; the library's clause does this (`residential-use-only`). No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws makes a residential lease void or annulled by operation of law because the tenant uses the premises for a prohibited purpose, such as gambling, prostitution or drug dealing. The lease stays in force until you end the tenancy through the ordinary process. How a prohibited use ends a tenancy: under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act you may end a tenancy only for a listed cause (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Waste, nuisance, unlawful activity that affects the use and enjoyment of the premises, or other substantial or repeated and unreasonable interference with your or the neighbors' use and enjoyment supports at least three days' advance written notice to quit; breach of a material lease term, such as a residential-use-only clause, needs a written notice giving the tenant at least 10 days to cure or leave (`edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-wa`). Drug-related activity, imminently hazardous assaults or weapons use, and gang-related activity are also statutory tenant duties (`edu-criminal-activity-wa`, `edu-drug-free-housing-wa`). If the tenant doesn't leave, you must go to court; you can't lock the tenant out (`edu-self-help-eviction-wa`). Police seizures: a law enforcement agency that seizes illegal drugs on rental premises must make a reasonable attempt to identify and notify you in writing; respond within seven days, because ignoring the notice can defeat your claim for damage officers cause in a later seizure. Real property used with the owner's knowledge for felony drug manufacturing or sales can be forfeited, but an owner's interest isn't forfeited for acts done without the owner's knowledge or consent.

title: No Notice Exempts You From Washington Rent Escrow
bodyText: Washington has no notice you can give to opt out of the tenant's rent escrow remedy, and no small-landlord exemption from it. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws exempts a landlord from rent escrow, or from the other repair remedies, by giving the tenant notice or because the landlord owns few units. How rent escrow works (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`): if you fail to fulfill a substantial repair obligation that substantially endangers or impairs the tenant's health or safety (for example structural, weather exposure, plumbing and sanitation, no water or hot water, heating, electrical, exits or fire risk), the tenant gives you written notice. If you don't remedy it within the statutory time, the tenant may ask the local government to inspect; it must inspect and certify within five days, and should give you 24 hours' notice of the inspection where practicable. You can't prohibit entry for it. If the condition is certified, the tenant may pay rent into an escrow account and must notify you within 24 hours on the sworn statutory form. You may get the money released once the repairs are certified, or go to court; you can't file an eviction for nonpayment while the tenant keeps paying the full rent into escrow on time. The only exemption route in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act is a written agreement exempting both parties from certain repair and duty sections, and it can't appear in a standard form lease, requires no substantial inequality in bargaining power, and needs written approval from the county prosecutor, the attorney general's consumer protection division or the tenant's attorney (`edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`). It doesn't list the escrow section itself, and no library lease can use it.

title: Seasonal Leases Get Full Tenant Protection in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no seasonal-tenancy category. A lease for a season (a summer at the lake, a ski season) is an ordinary tenancy under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) if the tenant is entitled to occupy the unit primarily for living or dwelling purposes, and it gets the same protections as any other lease (`edu-scope-wa`). No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws lets a seasonal lease end automatically at the end of the season or excuses it from the eviction-cause rules. The season end is the hard part. You may end a tenancy without cause when its term expires only in two cases, each with at least 60 days' advance written notice before the term ends: a lease for a specified period that doesn't continue month to month, where the first rental agreement was for 12 months or more (or every agreement since the tenancy began was for six months or more for a specified period) and the tenancy has never been month to month (`fixed-term-end-without-cause-wa`); or a lease whose initial term was between six and 12 months and which continues month to month after it, ended at the end of that initial term (`lease-end-continuation-wa`). A three- or four-month seasonal lease meets neither test, so when it ends the tenancy becomes month to month and you may end it only for a listed cause, such as the owner or the owner's immediate family moving in as a principal residence, a sale of a single-family residence, or the tenant refusing to sign a proposed new rental agreement (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`, `edu-termination-notice-wa`). The tenant may leave at the end of the term on 20 days' written notice. What the Act doesn't cover: residence in a hotel, motel or other transient lodging defined in RCW 19.48.010 (a building held out to the public as a hotel or lodging house with three or more rooms for transient guests), and housing for seasonal agricultural employees provided in conjunction with their employment (temporary worker housing has its own health rules). Washington regulates short-term rentals (a dwelling unit offered for fewer than 30 consecutive nights) under chapter 64.37 RCW, but that chapter doesn't say whether a short-term rental guest is a tenant, and no Washington case was searched. What to do: for stays under 30 nights, rent as a short-term rental with a guest agreement. For anything longer, assume the Act applies: use a lease of 12 months or more, or a six-to-12-month lease that continues month to month, if you need the right to end it without cause at the end of the term, or plan for a month-to-month tenancy after the season.

title: No Work Card for Staff at Washington Senior Rentals
bodyText: Washington has no work card or background-check requirement for people who work at senior (55-plus or 62-plus) apartments or any other rental housing. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires a landlord, manager or maintenance worker at housing for older persons to get a work card, be fingerprinted or pass a background check. Washington's only senior-housing rule for landlords is the fair housing exemption: the state's ban on discrimination based on families with children doesn't apply to housing for older persons as defined in the federal Fair Housing Act (as amended by the Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995), and Washington allows no requirements for such housing different from the federal ones (`edu-fair-housing-wa`, `edu-children-occupancy-wa`). The federal definition (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)) isn't in this library's saved federal sections, so check it before advertising a property as 55-plus. Fingerprint-based background checks are required for long-term care, direct care and similar workers paid through the state's social and health services or children's agencies; those settings are care facilities, not tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. Screening your own staff is your choice, subject to employment law, which this row doesn't cover.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty for Washington Landlords
bodyText: You have no duty in Washington to tell tenants or applicants about registered sex offenders living nearby or in the building, and no duty to put a registry notice in the lease. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires either (`edu-sex-offender-wa`). Public notification is a law enforcement job: public agencies may release information about sex and kidnapping offenders when they decide it is relevant and necessary to protect the public, and the Washington Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs keeps a public statewide website listing level II and level III registered sex offenders, level I offenders only while out of compliance with registration or lacking a fixed residence, and all registered kidnapping offenders. You may point tenants to that website if you choose. Where an offender is your tenant: a tenant's being required to register as a sex offender during the tenancy, or failing to disclose a registration requirement when the rental application asked or when it was otherwise known to the property owner at the start, is a cause to end the tenancy on at least 60 days' advance written notice before the end of the rental period or rental agreement (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). A comprehensive reusable tenant screening report includes a sex offender registry search (`edu-tenant-screening-wa`). Screen consistently and follow the fair housing rules (`edu-fair-housing-wa`).

title: Student Rentals Are Ordinary Tenancies in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no separate student-housing law for landlords. Off-campus apartments and houses rented to students are ordinary tenancies under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW), with every protection the Act gives other tenants: eviction only for a listed cause, the statewide rent increase limit and notice rules, deposit rules and repair duties. The rent-limit exemptions don't include student housing (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). The Act's only exclusion that can reach students covers residence at an institution, public or private, where residence is merely incidental to the institution's educational (or medical, religious, recreational or similar) services, unless the arrangement was set up primarily to avoid the Act (`edu-scope-wa`). That fits a college's own residence hall, where living there is part of attending. So if you own or manage private student housing, assume the Act applies in full. Two school-specific rules: a public or private educational institution may separate the sexes in, or limit, dormitories, residence halls and other student housing to one sex, and make distinctions based on marital or families with children status, without violating Washington's fair housing law (`edu-fair-housing-wa`); and each public institution of higher education must tell students applying for college- or university-owned housing about liquor-free housing and provide it on request. For private landlords: you may rent by the bedroom and use joint or individual leases (`joint-liability`), but don't refuse or steer applicants because they are students in a way that tracks a protected class, and screen every applicant the same way.

title: Inspection Refusals in Washington Subsidized Housing Follow the Ordinary Rules
bodyText: Washington has no special rule for a tenant in subsidized housing who refuses an inspection: no two-refusal trigger, no special warning notice and no emergency eviction. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws provides one. The ordinary rules apply. Your own inspections: the tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, on at least two days' written notice stating the date and time or time window and a telephone number for rescheduling (`landlords-access-wa`). For a city's rental inspection program, your written notice must also say who is doing the inspection and that the tenant may see the inspector's identification. A landlord or tenant who keeps violating the entry rules after one written notification listing the date and time of the violation can owe up to $100 for each later violation. Ending the tenancy: a substantial breach of a material program requirement of subsidized housing, a material lease term or a tenant obligation imposed by law is a cause to end the tenancy, but only after a written notice that specifies the breach and gives the tenant at least 10 days after service to fix it (`edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-wa`). In a housing choice voucher tenancy, the federal rule allows termination during the lease only for serious or repeated lease violations, violations of law tied to the occupancy, or other good cause, so follow the program's process too (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`). The voucher family's own program obligations also require it to allow the housing agency to inspect the unit at reasonable times and after reasonable notice; a refusal is a matter between the family and the agency under the program rules, not an added ground for you to end the tenancy. Your side: you can't refuse a voucher holder because the voucher requires an inspection unless the written estimate of repairs needed to pass is more than $1,500 and you haven't received landlord mitigation program money for them (`edu-source-of-income-wa`). You also can't retaliate against a tenant who lets a code enforcement official inspect (`edu-retaliation-wa`).

title: No Subsidy Split for Washington Habitability Rent Reductions
bodyText: Washington has no rule on how a habitability rent reduction is split between a housing subsidy and the tenant's own share. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws prorates a rent reduction or abatement between the subsidy and the tenant. The ordinary repair remedies apply to subsidized tenants as to everyone else (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`): if you fail to carry out your repair duties within a reasonable time after notice, a court or arbitrator may set the diminished rental value and enter judgment for rent paid above it, and the tenant need not pay rent above the diminished value until you fix the defect or the court or arbitrator decides otherwise. The tenant may also use repair-and-deduct or rent escrow. In a housing choice voucher tenancy, federal rules add a floor: the family isn't responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, the agency's failure to pay isn't a lease violation by the tenant, and you may not end the tenancy during the lease for the agency's nonpayment (`edu-voucher-tenancy-addendum`). The voucher rules also govern the agency's share when the unit fails: if you don't correct a deficiency within the cure period (24 hours for a life-threatening deficiency, otherwise 30 days or a longer period the agency approves), the agency must abate its payments, it pays you nothing for the abated period even after you repair, and you may not end the family's tenancy because of the withholding or abatement; the family may end the tenancy during an abatement. So if the agency stops its payments because the unit fails inspection, don't bill the tenant for the missing subsidy or treat it as unpaid rent in a 14-day notice. Because no statute or Washington case searched for this row says whether a court's diminished-value reduction comes off the tenant's share, the subsidy or both, the cautious course is to fix the condition promptly and, if a reduction is ordered or agreed, document in writing how it applies to the tenant's share.

title: No Tenancy at Will in Washington
bodyText: Washington statutes don't recognize a tenancy at will that either side can end at any moment. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws creates or defines one; the term appears only in the waste statute, which lets anyone injured sue a tenant "at will", among others, who commits waste. Under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, when premises are rented for an indefinite time with monthly or other periodic rent, the tenancy is month to month (or period to period, by the rent period). The tenant ends it by written notice of 20 days or more before the end of a rental period. You may end it only for a cause listed in RCW 59.18.650, on the notice that cause requires (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`, `edu-termination-notice-wa`). A lease clause letting you end the tenancy at will is unenforceable, because a lease can't waive the Act (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Older general rules in chapter 59.04 RCW (a month-to-month tenancy ended by 30 days' written notice by either party, and a tenant by sufferance) don't apply to any rental agreement covered by chapter 59.18 RCW. They matter only for arrangements outside the Act (`edu-scope-wa`). A tenant by sufferance is someone who got possession without the consent of the owner or another person entitled to give it; that person owes reasonable rent for the time occupied and must surrender possession on demand. Someone you let live in a unit without a written lease, such as a relative or a friend paying something toward rent, may well be a tenant under the Act. No statute says when a rent-free occupant is a tenant, and no Washington case was searched, so put any occupancy arrangement in writing and get legal advice before treating anyone as removable on demand (`edu-unauthorized-occupants-wa`).

title: Housing Your Own Employee in Washington
bodyText: If you house your own employee, such as a resident manager, caretaker or maintenance worker, the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (chapter 59.18 RCW) doesn't govern the arrangement when the employee's right to occupy is conditioned on employment in or about the premises, unless you set it up primarily to avoid the Act (`edu-scope-wa`). If the employee simply rents a unit and keeping it doesn't depend on the job, the employee is an ordinary tenant with every protection of the Act. Housing for seasonal agricultural employees provided in conjunction with their employment is also outside the Act; temporary worker housing with five or more units, or housing ten or more occupants, falls under the separate temporary worker housing law, which this library doesn't cover. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to give an employee-occupant a signed disclosure of the occupancy terms, to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, or to file a rent agreement for a sponsored worker, and none says how quickly an employee must leave after the job ends or which court procedure removes a holdover employee. The unlawful detainer statute speaks of a tenant of real property for a term less than life, and no Washington case was searched on whether it reaches an employee whose occupancy ended with the job. What to do: put the housing terms in a written agreement separate from the lease library, stating that occupancy is conditioned on employment on the premises, what (if anything) is charged, and how long the employee has to move out after the job ends. Don't lock out or remove a former employee yourself; get legal advice and use the courts. If you also charge rent for a unit and the right to stay doesn't depend on the job, use a normal Washington lease.

title: Insurance Claims Between You and Your Washington Tenant
bodyText: Washington has no statute on insurance claims between you and your tenant: no accidental-fire rule that shields a tenant from your or your insurer's claim, no general limit on your insurer's subrogation against a tenant, and no rule letting a lease shift your repairs onto the tenant's renter's insurance. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws provides one. Four rules still shape what you can do. (1) Fault: a tenant must not intentionally or negligently damage the dwelling or let family, invitees, licensees or anyone under the tenant's control do so, and must restore the unit at move-out except for wear from ordinary use (`tenant-caused-damage-wa`). No statute says whether a tenant owes anything for a fire caused without fault, and no Washington case was searched; bill only damage you can tie to the tenant's conduct. (2) No shifting your liability: a lease may not make the tenant agree to exculpate you, limit your liability arising under law, or indemnify you for it; such a term is unenforceable and knowingly using it can cost you damages (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`, `edu-renters-insurance-wa`). So the tenant's half of a mutual waiver of insured losses (the tenant releasing you, or waiving claims to the extent of insurance) can't go in a Washington lease. Waiving your own claims against the tenant, or your insurer's subrogation, is your choice; the library doesn't offer that clause, and you may add your own with advice. (3) Your repairs stay yours: your repair duties can't be waived, so a lease can't require the tenant to claim on renter's insurance for repairs you must make (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`). (4) Fee-in-lieu insurance: if you offer a fee instead of a deposit and an insurer pays you for a valid claim, you may not collect those amounts from the tenant, and an insurer with subrogation rights may recover from the tenant only what the tenant owed under the lease, never repairs of ordinary wear (`edu-fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`).

title: Tenant Records, Receipts and Data Security in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no rent-ledger statute and no rule that you keep tenant files for a set time or produce them on a records request. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws imposes either. Your record duties come from four narrower rules. (1) Receipts: you must give a receipt for any cash payment you accept, a written receipt for any other payment when the tenant asks, and a written receipt for a security deposit along with written notice of where it is held (`edu-rent-receipts-wa`, `deposit-depository-wa`). (2) Nonpayment notice: the 14-day notice to pay or vacate must list, by month, the rent, utilities and other recurring or periodic charges due and the total, so keep records that let you itemize them (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`). In a nonpayment eviction the court may weigh the tenant's payment history in deciding whether to stay the writ, so your ledger becomes evidence. (3) Data breaches: any person or business that conducts business in Washington and owns or licenses personal information, such as an applicant's name with a Social Security, driver's license or bank account number or full date of birth, must notify each affected Washington resident of a breach of unsecured data within 30 calendar days of discovery (unless the breach isn't reasonably likely to subject consumers to a risk of harm) and must notify the attorney general within 30 days if more than 500 Washington residents are affected. No Washington statute requires a written information security program; keeping notification procedures in an information security policy is optional and counts as compliance if they meet the statute's timing. (4) Disposal: when you dispose of records you no longer keep, you must take all reasonable steps to destroy personal financial and health information and government-issued identification numbers, for example by shredding, or face a $200 penalty or actual damages for negligence and more for willful failure. Screening reports and tenant confidential information are covered under `edu-tenant-confidential-information-wa` and `edu-tenant-screening-wa`.

title: No Lease Exemption Notice in Washington: Claim Rent-Limit Exemptions in the Increase Notice
bodyText: Washington has no lease-stage exemption notice. Some states make an owner who is exempt from a statewide rent cap or just-cause rule say so in the lease; no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires that, and Washington's just-cause eviction rule has no exemption you can claim by notice. It covers every tenancy under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Washington's exemption statement comes later, with each rent increase. The statewide rent increase limit doesn't apply to seven kinds of tenancies: a unit whose first certificate of occupancy was issued 12 or fewer years before the increase notice; units owned by a public housing authority, public development authority or qualifying nonprofit with regulated rents; qualifying low-income and tax-credit developments; a unit where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner living there; a single-family owner-occupied residence where the owner rents no more than two units or bedrooms; and an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or fourplex. The three owner-occupied exemptions are unavailable if the owner is a real estate investment trust, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member. To raise rent above the limit under an exemption, you must check the exemption on the state Rent and Fee Increase Notice form and include facts or documents supporting it (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). What to do: don't put an exemption statement in the lease as a substitute; keep the evidence (the certificate of occupancy date, ownership and occupancy records) and attach it to any increase notice that claims an exemption. These rent-limit sections expire July 1, 2040 (`edu-tpa-sunset-wa`).

title: No Tenant Right to Buy Before Sale in Washington, Except Conversions
bodyText: Washington gives tenants of apartments and rental houses no right to buy the property before you sell it, and no statewide notice of an opportunity to purchase. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws creates one for ordinary rentals; you may sell freely, and the tenancy continues under the new owner (`edu-sale-or-management-change-wa`). Three narrower rules come close. (1) Condominium or cooperative conversion: if you convert a building to a common interest community, you must give each residential tenant 120 days' notice with the public offering statement, and for 60 days after that notice you must offer to convey the tenant's own unit to the tenant. If the tenant doesn't buy, for the next 180 days you may offer that unit to others at a better price or on better terms only after offering the same price and terms to the tenant in writing and giving the tenant 10 days to accept (`edu-conversion-notice-wa`). (2) Federally assisted housing: an owner who plans to prepay a federally assisted mortgage or let a rental assistance contract expire must give tenants and public agencies at least 12 months' written notice, but the notice gives tenants no right to buy, and the owner remains free to prepay or end the contract (`edu-subsidized-housing-notice-wa`). (3) Manufactured/mobile home communities have a notice of opportunity to compete to purchase under chapter 59.20 RCW, which this library doesn't cover. No lease notice of rights: Washington also doesn't require a lease notice telling tenants about the statewide rent increase limit or the just-cause eviction rule (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-wa`). Tenants learn about the rent limit from the Rent and Fee Increase Notice form you must use for any increase (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`).

title: Washington’s Rent Increase Limit Expires July 1, 2040
bodyText: Washington's statewide rent increase limit is on a repeal clock: RCW 59.18.700 (the limit, lease-type parity and enforcement), RCW 59.18.710 (the exemptions) and RCW 59.18.720 (the Rent and Fee Increase Notice form) each expire July 1, 2040 (`edu-rent-increase-limit-wa`). Until then, a landlord may not raise rent during the first 12 months of a tenancy or, in any 12-month period, by more than seven percent plus the Seattle-area consumer price index or 10 percent, whichever is less, unless an exemption applies. What doesn't expire: the just-cause eviction rule in RCW 59.18.650 has no expiry date (`edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`). Neither does the 90-day written notice of any rent increase in RCW 59.18.140(3), which Laws of 2025, ch. 209 amended but didn't put on the clock (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). Some sections change on fixed dates rather than expiring: new versions of RCW 59.18.200 and RCW 59.18.650 take effect January 1, 2028, and a new version of the definitions in RCW 59.18.030 takes effect January 1, 2027. No other section of the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, the unlawful detainer chapter or chapter 59.04 RCW carries an expiry or repeal date in the RCW or the 2025-2026 session laws. What to do: diary July 1, 2040, and check before then whether the Legislature has extended or changed the limit.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement in Washington
bodyText: Washington has no truth-in-renting statement: no state-prepared booklet of landlord and tenant rights that you must hand to tenants or post. No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires one for ordinary residential rentals (`edu-no-tenant-rights-statement-wa`). What you do hand out are specific notices whose contents the statutes set, tied to particular events: the 14-day notice to pay or vacate in the statutory form, which the attorney general translates into the top ten languages spoken in Washington and posts online with information on where tenants can get legal or advocacy help (`edu-nonpayment-notice-wa`); the Rent and Fee Increase Notice form for any rent increase (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`); and the move-in fire safety notice (`fire-safety-notice-wa`). One rights package does exist, for federally assisted housing only: an owner who plans to prepay a federally assisted mortgage or let a rental assistance contract expire must include, with the 12-month notice to tenants, the Department of Commerce's written information on the legal rights, responsibilities and options of owners and tenants (`edu-subsidized-housing-notice-wa`). Manufactured/mobile home lot tenancies have their own disclosure rules under chapters 59.20 and 59.30 RCW, which this library doesn't cover. Some cities require a local rights handout; check your city's ordinances.

title: No Statewide Unbundled-Parking Rule in Washington
bodyText: No Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles or the 2025-2026 session laws requires you to offer parking separately from rent, to let tenants decline a parking space, or to list parking as a separate charge. Whether to bundle parking into the rent or charge for it separately is your choice, subject to the rules below and to local law. Local option near transit: in a station area of a city planning under the Growth Management Act, the city may not require off-street parking for residential or mixed-use development (with exceptions for disability and delivery parking, safety studies certified by the Department of Commerce, and areas near the largest airport). If a development provides more residential parking than that, the city may adopt rules requiring a share of the parking to be distributed between affordable and market-rate units and folding all or part of the cost of unbundled parking charges into the monthly cost of units designated as affordable housing. Check your city's code if you build or own near light rail or commuter rail. Separately, cities over 30,000 people are being phased into limits on minimum parking requirements (no more than 0.5 space per multifamily unit, none for affordable or senior housing), which changes how much parking new buildings must have, not how you charge for it. If you charge separately: a recurring parking charge identified in the rental agreement is part of the rent, so it counts toward the statewide rent increase limit and needs 90 days' notice on the Rent and Fee Increase Notice form to increase (`edu-parking-rules-notice-wa`, `edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`). Where a regional transit authority adopts a parking tax in an enhanced service zone, it doesn't apply to an exclusive residential stall in the tenant's own building, whether provided as an inseverable condition of the lease or charged separately from the rent. For lease wording on assigned spaces use `assigned-parking-space`.

title: Washington Lease Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Washington's required disclosures, by when they fall due. Before you screen an applicant: in writing or by posting, the types of information you will check, the criteria that may lead to denial, the consumer reporting agency you use and the applicant's rights, and whether you accept a comprehensive reusable screening report (`edu-tenant-screening-wa`, `edu-application-fees-wa`). If you take a fee or deposit to hold a unit after offering it: a receipt and a written statement of the conditions under which it may be retained, immediately upon payment (`edu-holding-deposit-wa`). At or before signing, in the lease or a document signed with it: your name and address for notices and service, plus an agent living in the county if you live outside Washington (`landlord-disclosure-wa`); the fire safety and protection notice, signed by you and the tenant (`fire-safety-notice-wa`); the Department of Health information on indoor mold, given or posted (`mold-disclosure-wa`); for leases entered into after December 31, 2026, the flood and renter's insurance disclosure (`flood-disclosure-wa`); if you take a deposit, a written lease stating when it may be withheld, a receipt and where it is held (`security-deposit-use-wa`, `deposit-depository-wa`), and before you collect it, a move-in condition checklist signed and dated by both of you (`existing-condition-wa`); any nonrefundable fee, called nonrefundable in the written lease (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`); if you offer a fee in lieu of a deposit, the statutory disclosure form (`fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`); if you restrict window-mounted cooling units, a notice in the lease (`portable-cooling-device-wa`); and for housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet (`lead-based-paint`). Rules of tenancy bind the tenant only if they are brought to the tenant's attention at initial occupancy (`edu-no-association-disclosure-wa` covers association rules). From January 1, 2027, in a smart access building: the system developer's or operator's privacy policy, and your own plain-language data policy at lease signing or within five days of installing the system (`edu-smart-access-wa`). During the tenancy: 90 days' notice of a rent increase on the state form (`edu-rent-increase-notice-wa`), 30 days' written notice of a new rule (`edu-term-change-notice-wa`), and the other notices the act requires in writing (`edu-written-notice-required-wa`). Where they apply: if you authorize a utility's conservation work recovered through an energy savings charge on the bill, notice to the tenant at least 30 days before the work starts (`edu-meter-conservation-charge-wa`, optional clause `meter-conservation-charge-wa`); a copy of an environmental covenant to each person in possession when the covenant is signed (`edu-hazardous-contamination-disclosure-wa`); the conversion notices and the tenant's purchase offer when you convert to a condominium or cooperative (`edu-conversion-notice-wa`, `edu-no-tpa-notice-wa`); and 12 months' notice before a federally assisted mortgage is prepaid or a rental assistance contract expires (`edu-subsidized-housing-notice-wa`). Not required: a foreclosure disclosure (`edu-foreclosure-disclosure-wa`), a sex offender registry notice (`edu-no-sex-offender-disclosure-wa`), a plain-language rights statement (`edu-no-plain-language-consumer-statement-wa`), or tenant initials on particular terms (`edu-no-lease-initials-requirement-wa`). City and county rules: a local rule requiring landlords to give tenants information about the property or area takes effect only after a summary and link are posted on the state's municipal research website, which lists those requirements by jurisdiction, so check it for your city or county.

title: Where Washington Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Washington rules turn on what your written lease says, so the lease, not the statute, decides. Deposits and fees: you may take a deposit only under a written lease stating when it may be withheld (`security-deposit-use-wa`); a fee is nonrefundable only if the written lease clearly says so, or it is treated as a refundable deposit (`nonrefundable-fees-wa`); interest on a deposit held in an account belongs to you unless you and the tenant agree otherwise in writing (`deposit-depository-wa` keeps that default on purpose); and a fee in lieu of a deposit is available only as the option the statute sets out (`fee-in-lieu-of-deposit-wa`). Rent: rent is due when and in the amounts the lease provides, and "rent" means the recurring and periodic charges your lease identifies for use and occupancy, so a recurring fee you list is rent for the increase notice and the rent limit (`edu-fees-as-rent-wa`). No late fee may be charged for rent paid within five days after its due date, but once rent is more than five days past due, late fees may run from the first day after the due date (`late-fee-wa`); a tenant whose main income is monthly government assistance that arrives after the due date can make you move the due date by up to five days, and only where late fees may be charged (`edu-rent-due-date-change-wa`). Length and end of the tenancy: a fixed term becomes month-to-month by law unless the lease uses one of the two statutory options, a six-to-12-month first term you may end at its close on 60 days' notice (`lease-end-continuation-wa`) or a term of 12 months or more that doesn't continue month to month (`fixed-term-end-without-cause-wa`). Rules: rules bind the tenant only if they are lawful and brought to the tenant's attention at initial occupancy; later rules need 30 days' written notice and take effect at the end of the term unless the tenant agrees. Repairs: a duty you take on in the lease becomes a duty the tenant's repair remedies can enforce, and appliances you supply must be kept working (`appliances-included`). Disputes: you and the tenant may agree in writing to mediation by an independent third party, and the optional `informal-dispute-resolution-or` clause adds an informal pre-suit meeting step, but a lease may not require arbitration unless you pay its entire cost and the agreement is notarized (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`). Agreements that can't be in your standard lease: an exemption from the repair and duty sections (only in a separate, approved writing, `edu-tenant-repair-agreement-wa`), an opt-out of the act for a single-family lease (only with the tenant's attorney's approval on its face, `edu-scope-wa`), and a tenant-death designation (a separate writing, `edu-tenant-death-wa`). Spouses and recording: no lease term the library offers needs recording, and recording any lease is optional; if the rental is community property, have both spouses sign a lease longer than one year as the cautious course (`edu-lease-term-limitation-wa`). Every other right or duty in the act applies whatever the lease says, and a term waiving one is unenforceable (`edu-prohibited-lease-terms-wa`).

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have: What Washington Has and Lacks
bodyText: Washington's habitability law is broad (`edu-landlord-maintenance-wa`), so most features other states are known for are present here; three are not. Present: smoke detection devices in every unit, working before each new occupancy, and carbon monoxide alarms under the building code (`edu-alarm-duties-wa`); repair deadlines that start running on the tenant's written notice, 24 hours for loss of heat, hot or cold water or electricity (`edu-tenant-repair-remedies-wa`); a rent escrow procedure that no notice of yours can exempt you from (`edu-no-repair-escrow-exemption-wa`); pest control at the start of the tenancy and, except in a single-family residence, during it (`edu-pest-control-wa`); and a tenant's right to install a portable cooling device, within the statutory limits (`portable-cooling-device-wa`). Absent, first: a minimum indoor temperature you must keep. Your duty is to provide facilities adequate to supply heat as reasonably required by the tenant and to keep the heating you supply working (`edu-heating-wa`); no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws sets a number of degrees a landlord must maintain. The state building code does require new dwellings to have heating facilities capable of maintaining 68 degrees Fahrenheit in habitable rooms where the winter design temperature is below 60 degrees, but that is a design standard for construction, not a temperature you must keep in an existing rental, and city housing codes, which this library did not search, may set one. Second: a duty to supply air conditioning; there is none (`edu-heating-wa`). Third: a duty to supply appliances. Your repair duty reaches the appliances you supply, which you must keep in reasonably good working order, and a lease can't exclude them from that duty (`edu-appliances-excluded-wa`, `appliances-included`). Practical course: keep heat working at a level the tenant reasonably needs, respond to a loss of heat within 24 hours, and list in the lease the appliances you supply.

title: Other Rules Washington Has and Lacks: Subletting, Double Letting, Application Fraud, Grace Periods
bodyText: Four questions landlords often ask, answered for Washington. Subletting and assignment: no Washington statute gives a residential tenant a right to sublet or assign, requires you to be reasonable about consent, or sets a deadline for your answer; no Washington statute or regulation in the RCW, the held WAC titles, the Constitution or the 2025-2026 session laws does (manufactured/mobile home lots, outside this library, have their own transfer rule). Your lease decides (`no-sublet-assign`). A tenant who sublets in breach of a covenant not to sublet is handled through the 10-day comply-or-vacate notice, not ended at once (`edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-wa`), and fair housing law applies to your consent decisions as to any rental decision. Double letting: no statute deals with renting the same unit to two tenants; the general law covers it, including the theft-by-deception statute where it is knowing (`edu-no-double-letting-rule-wa`). Rental application fraud: present. Intentional, knowing and material misrepresentations or omissions on the application at the start of the tenancy, which would have led you to ask for more information or take an adverse action, are a cause to end the tenancy on at least 30 days' written notice to vacate (`rental-application-accuracy-wa`, `edu-for-cause-eviction-wa`).
